card.headline: Bright red comb, alert and busy bird
card.look: A healthy laying hen has a bright red, waxy comb and wattles, clear shining eyes, smooth tight feathers and spends her day scratching, pecking, drinking and dust-bathing. Her droppings are firm, brown to grey-green, with a white cap on top.
card.action: Walk through your flock every morning before feeding, watching how the birds move, eat, drink and breathe, and look closely at any bird that sits apart.

detail.summary: This page describes what a normal, healthy chicken looks, sounds and behaves like, so you can spot trouble early. Most poultry diseases in Kenya, such as Newcastle disease, Gumboro, coccidiosis and fowl typhoid, start with small changes in behaviour, droppings or feed and water intake before birds start dying. A farmer who knows what 'normal' looks like in their own flock can call the vet a day or two earlier, and that often decides whether you lose a few birds or the whole house.
detail.cause: A chicken stays healthy when several things come together. First is good nutrition: a balanced feed for the bird's age and purpose (chick mash, grower, layer or broiler feed), with enough protein, energy, vitamins, minerals and calcium for egg shells. Second is clean, cool water available all day, because chickens drink roughly one and a half to two times as much water as the feed they eat, and more in hot weather. Third is a clean, dry, well-ventilated house with dry litter, enough space and no draughts at bird level; wet litter and ammonia smell damage the airways and allow coccidia (tiny gut parasites) and bacteria to multiply. Fourth is protection from disease through vaccination, biosecurity (keeping germs out of the farm) and control of worms, mites and lice. Finally, low stress matters: steady routines, no overcrowding, shade and airflow in the heat, and gentle handling. When any of these fail, the bird's immune system weakens and the first signs you see are usually quiet ones: less eating, less drinking, ruffled feathers or a change in droppings.
spread: Health is kept or lost through daily management: good feed, clean water, dry litter and fresh air keep birds strong, while mouldy feed, dirty drinkers and damp, crowded houses wear them down.
Most infections enter the farm on new or returning birds, so buying birds from markets or neighbours without a quarantine period is one of the biggest risks to a healthy flock.
Germs also arrive on people's shoes, clothes and hands, on egg trays, crates, sacks and bicycles or motorbikes that visit other farms or markets.
Wild birds, rats, stray dogs and cats can carry diseases and parasites into the house and contaminate feed and water.
Sudden changes such as heat waves, cold nights during the long rains, transport, a change of feed or vaccination day can stress birds and make hidden problems show.

Feed stored in damp conditions can grow moulds that produce mycotoxins (poisons made by moulds, such as aflatoxin), which quietly lower immunity, growth and egg production even before any bird looks sick.
detail.atRisk: Knowing the baseline matters for every flock, but some birds show problems fastest and need the closest watching. Day-old to three-week-old chicks have little reserve and can go from normal to dead in a day if they are cold, hungry or thirsty. Growing birds between about three and eight weeks are the classic age for coccidiosis and Gumboro. Laying hens at the start of lay and at peak production need high-quality feed and calcium, and show stress through drops in eggs and pale combs. Broilers grow very fast and are sensitive to heat, poor ventilation and leg problems. Kienyeji (indigenous) and improved kienyeji birds kept free-range are hardy but meet more wild birds, neighbours' chickens and worms, and are often unvaccinated. Risk rises in the long and short rains, when litter gets wet and coccidiosis increases, and in the hot dry months, when heat stress and dehydration are common. Small farms that keep mixed ages together, buy birds from markets, or share equipment with neighbours are also at higher risk.

early: Comb and wattles: in a laying hen they are bright red, full, soft and slightly waxy; in young birds, non-layers and moulting hens they are smaller and paler pink, which is normal for their stage.
Eyes: bright, round, clear and alert, with no swelling, bubbles, tears or crusts; the bird follows movement and reacts quickly when you enter.
Nostrils and beak: clean and dry with no discharge, no crusting and no smell; breathing is quiet, with the beak closed when the bird is resting in cool weather.
Feathers: smooth, tight and glossy, lying flat against the body; the vent (the opening under the tail) feathers are clean and not pasted with droppings.
Behaviour: birds are busy all day scratching, pecking, dust-bathing, preening and moving around the house or compound, and they crowd to the feeder when fresh feed arrives.
Posture and walking: the bird stands upright on both legs, walks evenly without limping, and the tail is held up; chicks spread out evenly under the brooder, not huddled or pressed against the walls.

Droppings: mostly firm, brown to grey-green and shaped, with a white cap of urates (the bird's form of urine); about once in every several droppings you will see a softer, sticky, darker brown caecal dropping with a stronger smell, which is normal.

Feed, water and production: birds eat and drink steadily through the day; a commercial layer in lay typically eats around 110–130 grams of feed a day depending on breed and feed, water use rises in hot weather, and egg numbers stay steady from day to day.
advanced: A bird standing alone, hunched, with ruffled feathers, eyes half closed or head tucked in during the day is not normal and should be picked up and checked at once.
A drop in feed or water intake across the flock, even before birds look sick, is one of the earliest warnings of disease or heat stress; a sudden rise in water use can also signal fever or heat.
A sudden drop in eggs, or eggs with thin, soft, wrinkled or pale shells, often points to disease, stress or a feed problem.
Changes in droppings: watery, very green, yellow, white and chalky, or blood-stained droppings, or pasted vents, mean something is wrong and should be reported to the vet.
Breathing changes: sneezing, gurgling, coughing, open-mouth breathing in cool weather, swollen faces or discharge from the eyes and nostrils point to respiratory disease.
A comb that turns pale, shrunken, dark purple or blue, or develops scabs and wart-like spots, needs attention.
Nervous signs such as twisted necks, circling, paralysis of legs or wings, or trembling are serious and need the vet urgently.
Any unexplained deaths, even one or two birds in a day in a small flock, should be taken seriously, recorded and the body taken to a vet or laboratory for a post-mortem.

lookalikes.name: Moulting
lookalikes.howToTell: Once a year, usually after a laying season, hens lose and regrow feathers, stop or reduce laying and the comb shrinks and goes pale. The bird still eats, drinks and moves normally, the new pin feathers are visible growing in, and the droppings are normal. Sick birds with feather loss are usually dull, eat less and may have mites, lice or other signs.

lookalikes.name: Normal caecal droppings
lookalikes.howToTell: Chickens empty their caeca (two blind pouches of the gut) every so often, producing a sticky, shiny, dark brown, smelly dropping. This is normal if most other droppings are firm with a white cap. Blood in droppings, many watery droppings or birds that look dull are not normal and may mean coccidiosis or another gut disease.

lookalikes.name: Panting in hot weather
lookalikes.howToTell: On hot afternoons healthy birds open their beaks, hold their wings away from the body and drink more, then return to normal in the cool of the evening. If birds pant in cool weather, gasp, gurgle or have swollen faces, or if many birds lie down and stop moving in the heat, call the vet.

lookalikes.name: Broody hen
lookalikes.howToTell: A broody hen sits in the nest for long periods, fluffs up, growls or pecks when disturbed and leaves the nest only briefly to eat, drink and pass a very large, smelly dropping. She is alert and strong when handled. A sick hen is weak, dull and does not defend the nest.

detail.diagnosis: A home health check is simple and takes a few minutes a day. Each morning, before you put out fresh feed, stand quietly at the door or in the compound and watch the whole flock for a minute: are the birds spread out, active and coming to the feeder, and is anyone sitting apart? Listen for sneezing, rattling or coughing, especially at night when the house is quiet. Smell the house; a strong ammonia smell means the litter is too wet. Look at fresh droppings on the litter or droppings boards. Check feeders and drinkers, and if you can, measure how much feed and water is used each day and write it down with egg numbers and any deaths. For a closer check, pick up any dull bird gently, holding the wings against the body, and look at the eyes, nostrils, comb, beak and mouth, feel the crop (the pouch at the base of the neck, which should be full and soft after feeding and empty by morning), feel the keel (breastbone) to judge body condition, look under the wings and around the vent for lice and mites, and check the feet for swelling or sores. Taking a chicken's temperature is not routine on farms and is hard to interpret, because birds run naturally hot, at roughly 40.5–42 °C, and stress from catching raises it. If you do use a digital thermometer, it is placed gently just inside the vent and the reading is used only as a rough guide; behaviour, feed and water intake and droppings tell you much more. If something looks wrong, separate the bird, write down what you saw and when it started, the age and number of birds, vaccination history, feed type and any deaths, and share this with your vet or County Veterinary Officer. Fresh dead birds kept cool, not frozen, are very useful for a post-mortem examination.
firstSteps: Make a daily flock check a habit: same time every morning, before feeding, watching behaviour, breathing, droppings, feed and water.
Keep simple records in a notebook or on your phone: number of birds, daily feed and water used, eggs collected, any sick or dead birds and any treatments or vaccinations given.
Move any bird that looks dull, hunched or off its feed into a separate, clean, dry pen with its own feeder and water, away from the main flock.
Give sick or separated birds easy access to clean, cool water and fresh feed, with shade and good airflow, and keep them calm and quiet.
Do not give antibiotics or other drugs on your own; call your vet or a qualified animal health officer to examine the birds first.
If several birds fall sick or die quickly, stop selling or moving birds and eggs, stop visitors from entering, and call the vet the same day.
Wash your hands with soap after handling birds, droppings or dead birds, and wear dedicated shoes or boots inside the poultry house.
detail.vetTreatment: For a healthy flock, the vet's role is mostly prevention and advice. A vet or animal health officer can help you plan a vaccination programme suited to your area and type of bird. In Kenya this commonly covers Marek's disease (usually given at the hatchery on day one), Newcastle disease, Gumboro (infectious bursal disease), infectious bronchitis, fowl pox and fowl typhoid, with boosters for long-lived birds such as layers and kienyeji breeders; the exact vaccines and ages vary, so follow your hatchery's and vet's schedule. The vet can also advise on worm control, using a prescribed dewormer at suitable intervals, and on treating mites and lice. They can check that your feed, housing, lighting and stocking density suit the birds' age. When birds die unexpectedly, a post-mortem by the vet or a veterinary laboratory is the quickest way to find the cause and protect the rest of the flock. Any medicine, including antibiotics, coccidiostats and dewormers, must be prescribed by a vet, used exactly as directed, and the egg and meat withdrawal period on the label (the time after treatment when eggs and meat must not be eaten or sold) must be followed. Antibiotics should never be used routinely to keep healthy birds healthy, because overuse leads to antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to the drugs that people and animals need.
prevention: Buy chicks only from reputable, registered hatcheries that vaccinate against Marek's disease, and ask for records of the vaccines given.
Follow a vaccination programme agreed with your vet, keep vaccines cool from the agrovet to the farm, use clean, chlorine-free water to mix them, and record every vaccination date.
Feed the right ration for each stage, from chick mash to grower to layer or broiler feed, store feed off the floor in a cool, dry place, use it within a few weeks and never feed mouldy or caked feed.
Provide clean, cool water all day, wash drinkers daily and place them in shade; in hot weather add extra drinkers so no bird has to compete.
Keep litter dry and loose by fixing leaking roofs and drinkers, adding fresh litter in the rainy seasons and removing wet patches, and keep the house ventilated without draughts at bird level.
Practise biosecurity: limit visitors, use a footbath or dedicated boots, keep new or returning birds in quarantine for at least two weeks, and keep different ages apart where possible.
Control rats, wild birds and stray animals, keep the house fenced or netted, and remove and safely dispose of dead birds by burying deeply or burning.
Clean and disinfect the house, feeders and drinkers between batches and leave it empty for a rest period before new birds arrive.
detail.impact: Knowing what a healthy chicken looks like is one of the cheapest and most powerful tools on any Kenyan poultry farm. A flock that is checked daily loses fewer birds, because problems such as coccidiosis, Gumboro or heat stress are caught early when treatment or management changes still work. Healthy layers keep laying steadily with strong shells, which means better income from trays sold to neighbours, hotels and markets. Healthy broilers reach market weight on time on less feed, and feed is usually the biggest cost on the farm. Early warning also protects your reputation with buyers and your neighbours' flocks, and it helps you use medicines only when truly needed, saving money and reducing drug residues in eggs and meat. Record keeping turns your daily check into data you can show the vet, the bank or an extension officer.
detail.humanHealth: Even healthy-looking chickens can carry germs such as Salmonella and Campylobacter in their gut and on their feathers and feet, which can cause stomach illness in people. Wash hands with soap after handling birds, eggs, litter or equipment, especially before eating, and supervise children. Collect eggs often, keep them clean and cool, and do not wash dirty eggs in cold water; discard cracked or heavily soiled eggs. Cook eggs and chicken meat thoroughly. If birds have been treated with any medicine, follow the egg and meat withdrawal period on the label before eating or selling products.
detail.outlook: A flock that is well fed, watered, housed, vaccinated and checked every day has a very good outlook, with steady growth, good laying and low deaths. No flock is ever completely free of risk, but the earlier you notice a change from normal, the better the chances that the vet can find the cause and that most birds will recover. Flocks that are not checked often, or where sick birds are left among healthy ones, tend to suffer heavier losses when disease arrives.

faqs.q: My hen's comb has gone pale. Is she sick?
faqs.a: Not always. A pale, smaller comb is normal in young pullets before they start laying, in hens that have stopped laying, in moulting hens and in broody hens. If the hen is still alert, eating and drinking, and her droppings are normal, it is probably her stage of life. If the pale comb comes with dullness, weight loss, poor appetite, diarrhoea or many birds affected at once, it can point to worms, mites, poor feed or disease, and you should ask your vet to check.

faqs.q: How much should my chickens eat and drink each day?
faqs.a: It depends on age, breed, feed and weather. As a rough guide, a commercial layer in production often eats around 110–130 grams of feed a day, and chickens usually drink about one and a half to two times as much water as feed, more on hot days. Kienyeji birds on free range eat less bought feed because they forage. The most useful thing is to measure what your own flock normally uses and write it down, so that you notice when it suddenly drops or rises.

faqs.q: Are watery droppings always a sign of disease?
faqs.a: No. In hot weather birds drink more and droppings become wetter, and some feeds also cause looser droppings. Caecal droppings, which are sticky, dark and smelly, are also normal now and then. Be concerned if many droppings are watery, coloured bright green, yellow or white, contain blood, or if birds look dull, have pasted vents or are eating less. Those birds should be isolated and the vet called.

faqs.q: Should I give my healthy chickens antibiotics to keep them from getting sick?
faqs.a: No. Antibiotics do not prevent viral diseases such as Newcastle or Gumboro, and using them routinely in healthy birds wastes money, leaves residues in eggs and meat, and helps germs become resistant to the drugs people and animals need. Protect your flock with vaccination, clean water, good feed, dry litter and biosecurity, and only use antibiotics when a vet has examined the birds and prescribed them.

faqs.q: How often should I check my flock?
faqs.a: At least once a day, ideally every morning before feeding, with a quick look again in the evening. Chicks under three weeks old need checking several times a day to make sure they are warm, eating and drinking. The morning check only takes a few minutes but is the best early warning you have.

faqs.q: Do I need to take my chicken's temperature?
faqs.a: Usually not. Chickens naturally run very hot, around 40.5–42 °C, and simply catching them can push the temperature up, so a thermometer reading on its own is hard to interpret. Watching behaviour, appetite, water intake, breathing and droppings tells you far more. If you are worried about a bird, isolate it, note what you see and let your vet decide on further checks.

products.role: Mouldy or damp-stored feed is a common hidden drain on flock health in Kenya. Adding this mycotoxin binder to feed can help reduce the effect of aflatoxin and ochratoxin on birds' immunity, growth and laying, alongside proper dry feed storage and never feeding visibly mouldy feed.

A liquid vitamin and mineral supplement that can help healthy birds cope with stressful periods such as vaccination, transport, heat or peak lay, supporting steady productivity. It is an addition to a balanced feed and vaccination programme, not a replacement for them.

healthy.imagePrompt: A healthy brown laying hen with a bright red waxy comb and wattles, clear bright eyes and smooth glossy tight feathers, scratching alertly on clean dry wood-shaving litter inside a simple, well-lit Kenyan smallholder poultry house, with a few other active hens in the background.
healthy.seoDescription: Learn what a healthy chicken looks like: bright comb, clear eyes, tight feathers, normal droppings, feed and water intake. A daily flock check guide for Kenya.

card.headline: Twisted neck and sudden flock deaths
card.look: Birds gasp, sneeze and stop eating, then pass green watery droppings. Some twist their necks, walk in circles or become paralysed, egg laying crashes, and many birds die within a few days.
card.action: Lock down the flock immediately, stop all bird and egg movement, and report to your County Veterinary Officer today, because Newcastle disease is notifiable.

detail.summary: Newcastle disease is a highly contagious viral disease of chickens and many other birds. Severe strains can kill most of an unvaccinated flock within days, which is why kienyeji farmers often describe whole villages losing their chickens to 'kideri' at once. There is no cure, but good vaccination works well and is the main protection. It is a notifiable disease in Kenya, so every suspected outbreak must be reported to the veterinary authorities.
detail.cause: Newcastle disease is caused by a virus called avian orthoavulavirus 1, still widely known by its older name, avian paramyxovirus type 1 (APMV-1). A virus is a tiny germ that can only multiply inside living cells, so antibiotics cannot kill it. Strains differ a lot in how dangerous they are. Mild (lentogenic) strains cause little or no illness and some of them are used to make vaccines. Moderate (mesogenic) strains mainly cause breathing problems and egg drop. Severe (velogenic) strains are the ones behind most outbreaks in East Africa and cause high deaths. After the bird breathes in or swallows the virus, it multiplies in the airways and gut, then spreads through the blood. It damages the lining of the airways, causing gasping and coughing. It damages the gut wall and blood vessels, causing bleeding in the gut and the green watery diarrhoea. In many birds it also attacks the brain and nerves, which causes the twisted neck, trembling, circling and paralysis. It damages the egg-making organs, so eggs drop suddenly and those laid are often soft, thin-shelled or misshapen. The time from infection to signs (the incubation period) is usually around 2 to 15 days, most often about 5 to 6 days.
spread: Sick and recovering birds shed huge amounts of virus in their droppings and in mucus from the beak and nose, and healthy birds pick it up by breathing it in or eating contaminated feed and water.
Buying new birds from markets, neighbours or traders and adding them straight to your flock is one of the most common ways kideri enters a farm.
Free-ranging kienyeji chickens mix with neighbours' birds at feeding spots, rubbish heaps and water points, so the virus moves quickly from homestead to homestead.
People carry the virus on their shoes, clothes, hands and bicycles or motorbikes, especially chicken traders, egg collectors and visitors who move between farms.
Contaminated egg trays, crates, sacks, feeders, drinkers and vehicles can carry the virus from one farm or market to another.
Wild birds, pigeons and other poultry such as ducks and guinea fowl can carry the virus, sometimes without looking sick.
The virus survives for weeks in droppings, litter and on surfaces, especially in cool, shaded places, so a dirty house can infect new birds long after an outbreak.
Carcasses of birds that died of the disease, if thrown in the bush or eaten by dogs, can spread the virus further around the village.
detail.atRisk: All chickens of any age can be affected, and turkeys, guinea fowl, pigeons, quails and many other birds are also susceptible. Ducks and geese usually show fewer signs but can still carry the virus. The birds most at risk are unvaccinated ones, especially free-range kienyeji flocks where vaccination is irregular, and young growers whose protection from their mother's antibodies has worn off. Layers that missed booster vaccinations are at high risk of severe egg drop. In Kenya outbreaks are often reported during the dry and windy months and around festive seasons, when many birds are bought, sold and moved through markets. Farms that mix birds of different ages, buy birds often, share equipment or sit near busy live-bird markets face extra risk. Stress from poor feeding, heavy worm burdens, heat or transport makes birds less able to respond to vaccines and more likely to fall sick.

early: Birds suddenly become dull, sit with ruffled feathers and eat and drink much less than usual.
You hear gasping, sneezing, coughing or rattling breathing, and some birds breathe with their beak open.
Layers show a sudden, sharp fall in egg numbers within a few days.
Eggs become pale, thin-shelled, soft-shelled, rough or misshapen, and the egg white may be watery.
Watery eyes, nasal discharge and some swelling around the eyes or head.
A few birds die suddenly with little warning, often before other signs are obvious.
advanced: Green or greenish-white watery diarrhoea, sometimes with a strong smell, soiling the feathers around the vent.
Twisted neck (torticollis), with the head turned sideways, backwards or upside down, or the bird looking up at the sky ('star-gazing').
Trembling of the head and neck, walking in circles, falling over or walking backwards.
Drooping wings and paralysis of one or both legs, so birds sit or lie and cannot reach feed or water.
Many birds die within a few days, and in an unvaccinated flock losses can reach nearly the whole flock.
Some birds that survive stay permanently with a twisted neck or weak legs and never return to normal production.

lookalikes.name: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (bird flu)
lookalikes.howToTell: Bird flu can look almost the same, with sudden deaths, breathing trouble and egg drop. It more often causes swollen heads, blue or purple combs and wattles, and red spots on the shanks, but you cannot reliably tell the two apart on the farm. Both are notifiable, so only laboratory tests arranged by the vet can confirm which one it is.

lookalikes.name: Infectious bronchitis (IB)
lookalikes.howToTell: IB causes coughing, sneezing and egg drop with wrinkled or misshapen eggs, but it does not cause twisted necks or paralysis, and deaths in adult birds are usually low. Newcastle disease in unvaccinated birds spreads faster and kills far more birds.

lookalikes.name: Fowl cholera
lookalikes.howToTell: Fowl cholera is a bacterial disease that also causes sudden deaths and green diarrhoea, but birds often have hot, swollen wattles, swollen joints and it usually affects adult birds more. It does not usually cause nerve signs, and a vet can confirm it in the lab and treat it with suitable antibiotics, unlike Newcastle disease.

lookalikes.name: Marek's disease and vitamin deficiencies
lookalikes.howToTell: Marek's disease causes paralysis, typically with one leg stretched forward and the other back, but it spreads slowly, affects a few young birds at a time and does not cause sudden flock-wide deaths or breathing signs. Vitamin E deficiency ('crazy chick disease') can cause twisted necks in young chicks, but there is no gasping, green diarrhoea or rapid spread, and it relates to poor or stale feed.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will first look at the pattern: how fast birds are falling sick, the mix of breathing, gut and nerve signs, the egg drop and the vaccination history. At post-mortem (opening a dead bird) the vet often finds pinpoint bleeding at the tips of the glands in the proventriculus (the stomach before the gizzard), bleeding or ulcers in the intestines and caecal tonsils, and inflammation in the windpipe. These findings are strongly suggestive but not proof, because bird flu and some other diseases can look similar. Confirmation needs laboratory tests such as PCR (a test that detects the virus's genetic material), virus isolation, or blood tests for antibodies, done through regional veterinary investigation laboratories or the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete. To help, the farmer can prepare: a written record of when signs started, how many birds are sick and dead each day, egg production records, the dates and type of each vaccination, the vaccine batch number and where it was bought, and any recent purchases or movement of birds. Keep two or three freshly dead or very sick birds in a sealed double plastic bag in a cool place (not frozen) for the vet, and do not open carcasses yourself.
firstSteps: Report the suspected outbreak immediately to your County Veterinary Officer, local veterinary office or an extension officer; Newcastle disease is notifiable under Kenyan law, so reporting is required, not optional.
Stop all movement: do not sell, give away, buy or slaughter birds, and do not take eggs, manure, trays or crates off the farm until the vet tells you it is safe.
Confine your birds in their house or a fenced area so they cannot mix with neighbours' chickens, ducks or wild birds, and keep visitors and traders away.
Separate visibly sick birds from the rest where possible, and give all birds clean drinking water, easy-to-reach feed, shade and a quiet, dry place.
Protect yourself and avoid carrying the virus: use dedicated boots or a footbath, wash hands with soap after handling birds, and wear gloves and a mask when handling sick or dead birds or droppings.
Collect dead birds promptly, keep them in sealed bags, and follow the vet's instructions on disposal, usually deep burial with lime or burning; never throw them in the bush or feed them to dogs.
Write down the number of sick and dead birds each day, the date signs began, your vaccination records and recent purchases, so the vet can act quickly.
Do not give antibiotics or other medicines on your own; they will not kill the virus and may hide the true problem, so wait for the vet's advice.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no treatment that cures Newcastle disease, and antibiotics do not kill the virus. Because it is notifiable, the government veterinary service leads the response. Depending on the situation, the vet may confirm the diagnosis, place the farm or area under quarantine, and advise or order humane culling of affected flocks to stop the spread, followed by cleaning and disinfection. In some outbreaks, vets may advise emergency vaccination of healthy birds on nearby farms, or of the still-healthy birds in a flock, to build protection quickly, though birds already incubating the virus may still fall sick. For birds that are kept, care is supportive: clean water, good feed, warmth or shade, and keeping stress low. If secondary bacterial infections are a real problem, a vet may prescribe an antibiotic, but this only treats the extra bacterial infection, not the virus, and should be used only when truly needed to limit antimicrobial resistance (germs becoming resistant to medicines). Any antibiotic must be prescribed by a vet, and the egg and meat withdrawal periods on the label must be followed, meaning eggs and meat cannot be eaten or sold until that time has passed. Expect losses to continue for several days even with good care, and expect some survivors to have lasting nerve damage and poor laying.
prevention: Vaccinate every bird, including kienyeji chickens; vaccination is the single most important protection against kideri, and schedules vary by vaccine type and local disease risk, so follow the vaccine label and your vet.

A common pattern in Kenya is a first Newcastle vaccine (often a live strain such as LaSota or Hitchner B1, by eye drop or drinking water) in the first one to two weeks of life, a booster around three to four weeks later, then regular boosters about every three months for layers, breeders and kienyeji flocks; layers are often also given an inactivated (killed) injectable vaccine by trained personnel before laying starts.

Handle vaccines carefully: keep them cold from the agrovet to the farm, use clean water free of chlorine, use a stabiliser such as skimmed milk powder if the label advises, give vaccine in the cool of the morning, and make sure all the vaccine water is drunk within the time stated on the label.

For village chickens, ask your vet or agrovet about heat-tolerant (thermostable) Newcastle vaccines, which cope better where there is no fridge, and consider organising vaccination with neighbours so the whole village is protected at once.
Quarantine all new birds away from your flock for at least two weeks, buy only from trusted sources, and never bring birds back from the market and put them straight into your house.
Keep a footbath at the entrance, limit visitors and traders, clean and disinfect crates, trays and equipment, and do not share equipment with other farms.
Keep birds healthy so vaccines work: good feed, clean water, regular deworming, dry litter and protection from heat and overcrowding.
After any outbreak, remove all litter and manure, clean and disinfect the house and equipment, leave it empty for the period your vet advises, and only restock with vaccinated birds.
detail.impact: Newcastle disease is one of the most damaging poultry diseases in Kenya and across East Africa. In unvaccinated kienyeji flocks, an outbreak can wipe out most or all of a family's chickens within days, taking away a key source of eggs, meat, school fees and emergency cash. In commercial layers, even vaccinated flocks with weak protection can suffer a sharp egg drop and poor shell quality that lasts for weeks, and some birds never return to full production. Broiler farmers lose birds close to market weight and may be unable to sell during quarantine. Movement restrictions can stop sales of live birds and eggs from the farm and sometimes from the whole area, and markets may be closed. Costs add up from dead birds, lost production, cleaning and disinfection, delayed restocking and the price of replacement stock. Compared with these losses, regular vaccination is cheap insurance.
detail.humanHealth: Newcastle disease is not a serious threat to people, but the virus can occasionally cause a mild eye infection (conjunctivitis, with red, watery, sore eyes) in people who handle large amounts of virus, such as vaccinators, poultry workers and laboratory staff. It usually clears by itself within days. Avoid rubbing your eyes when handling sick birds or live vaccine, wash your hands with soap afterwards, and see a health worker if your eyes become sore. Do not eat or sell sick or dead birds; besides spreading the disease, this is against the rules during an outbreak. If a vet prescribes antibiotics for secondary infections, respect the egg and meat withdrawal periods so that drug residues do not reach people.
detail.outlook: For unvaccinated flocks infected with a severe strain, the outlook is poor: many or most birds may die, and survivors often have permanent nerve damage or reduced laying. Well-vaccinated flocks usually show much milder signs, often only a drop in eggs or some breathing problems, and losses are far lower. Recovery depends on the strain of virus, the bird's vaccination status and age, how quickly the flock is locked down, and whether other problems such as worms, poor nutrition or bacterial infections are present. Once a farm is cleaned, disinfected and restocked with properly vaccinated birds, and good biosecurity is kept up, the risk of another outbreak drops greatly.

faqs.q: Can I treat kideri with antibiotics or local remedies?
faqs.a: No treatment cures Newcastle disease. It is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only work against bacteria. A vet may sometimes prescribe an antibiotic to control extra bacterial infections in surviving birds, but this does not stop the virus itself. Giving antibiotics without a vet wastes money, leaves residues in eggs and meat, and helps germs become resistant to medicines. Local remedies may help birds feel more comfortable but will not stop an outbreak. The right steps are to report, lock down, and follow the vet's advice.

faqs.q: My birds were vaccinated. Why did they still get sick?
faqs.a: Vaccines greatly reduce illness and deaths but do not give perfect protection. Common reasons for failure are a broken cold chain (vaccine got warm on the way from the agrovet), using chlorinated tap water that kills the live vaccine, not all birds drinking enough vaccine water, giving the vaccine to birds already incubating the virus, missing booster doses, or birds being stressed, wormy or poorly fed. Keep records of the vaccine batch, date and method, and discuss them with your vet so the schedule and handling can be improved.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell birds or eggs from a flock with Newcastle disease?
faqs.a: During a suspected or confirmed outbreak you must not sell or move birds or eggs off the farm unless the veterinary officer allows it. Selling sick or in-contact birds is one of the main ways kideri spreads to other farms and markets. Sick or dead birds should not be eaten; they should be disposed of as the vet directs. Newcastle disease itself is not a major food safety risk to people, but the main concern is stopping the spread to other flocks.

faqs.q: Why do I have to report it, and what do movement restrictions mean for me?
faqs.a: Newcastle disease is notifiable in Kenya, which means the law requires anyone who suspects it to report it to the County Veterinary Officer or the Directorate of Veterinary Services. Reporting lets vets confirm the disease, warn neighbours and stop it spreading across the area. Movement restrictions, or quarantine, mean that no birds, eggs, manure, litter or used equipment can leave or enter your farm, and sometimes the whole area, until the vets lift the order. Markets may also be closed for a time. These measures can be hard, but they protect your neighbours and the wider poultry industry, and early reporting usually means a shorter, smaller outbreak.

faqs.q: Do kienyeji chickens really need vaccination?
faqs.a: Yes. Kienyeji chickens are hardy, but they are not naturally protected against Newcastle disease, and it is the main reason whole village flocks are lost. Because they roam freely and mix with other birds, they are often at higher risk than caged birds. Regular vaccination, with boosters about every three months or as your vet advises, and vaccinating together with neighbours, gives the best protection. Heat-tolerant vaccines can be useful where there is no fridge.

faqs.q: How long should I wait before restocking after an outbreak?
faqs.a: Wait until the veterinary officer lifts any restrictions and tells you it is safe. Before that, remove all litter, manure and feathers, clean and disinfect the house, feeders, drinkers and equipment, and leave the house empty for the period the vet recommends, commonly several weeks. When you restock, buy healthy birds from a trusted source, make sure they are vaccinated or vaccinate them on time, and keep strict biosecurity so the virus does not come back.

newcastle-disease.imagePrompt: A brown kienyeji hen standing on bare earth in a rural Kenyan backyard with its neck twisted sideways and its head turned upside down, ruffled feathers, other chickens blurred in the background, natural daylight, realistic photo.
newcastle-disease.seoDescription: Newcastle disease (kideri) in chickens: spot twisted necks, gasping, green diarrhoea and egg drop, report it, and protect your flock with vaccination.

card.headline: Swollen head, purple comb, sudden deaths
card.look: Many birds die suddenly, often overnight, with little warning. Survivors may have swollen heads and eyelids, a dark purple or blue comb and wattles, and red or purple blotches on the legs.
card.action: Lock the farm down, do not sell, move or eat any birds, and report immediately to your County Veterinary Officer.

detail.summary: Avian influenza is a viral disease of chickens, turkeys, ducks, geese, quail and wild birds, caused by influenza A viruses. The severe form, called highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), can kill most of a flock within a few days. It is a notifiable disease in Kenya, so any suspected case must be reported to government vets by law. Some strains can also infect people and cause serious illness, which makes fast reporting and careful handling a matter of family and public health, not only farm profit.
detail.cause: Avian influenza is caused by influenza A viruses. Scientists name them by two surface proteins, H and N, which gives names like H5N1 or H5N8. Viruses are grouped into two kinds. Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI) usually causes mild breathing problems or a drop in eggs, and may go unnoticed. Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), usually of the H5 or H7 types, is the deadly form. Some low pathogenic H5 and H7 viruses can change into the highly pathogenic form after circulating in poultry, which is why both are taken seriously. Once a bird breathes in or swallows the virus, it multiplies first in the nose, throat and gut. The highly pathogenic form then spreads through the blood to almost every organ. It damages the lining of small blood vessels, so they leak and bleed. This is what causes the swelling of the head and the purple colour of the comb, wattles and legs: blood and fluid pool under the skin because the vessels are damaged and oxygen is not reaching the tissues. The virus also attacks the heart, brain, lungs, kidneys and pancreas, which is why birds can die very quickly, sometimes before any clear sign appears. There is no drug that cures the infection in poultry.
spread: Wild water birds such as ducks and geese can carry the virus, often without looking sick, and spread it through their droppings into dams, ponds, lakes and pasture where poultry drink or scratch.

Sick and infected birds shed large amounts of virus in their droppings and in mucus from the nose, mouth and eyes, so healthy birds catch it by direct contact or by eating and drinking contaminated feed and water.
People carry the virus on their shoes, clothes, hands and vehicles from one farm or market to another; live-bird markets and poultry traders moving between villages are a major risk.
Buying new birds, especially from markets, or bringing back unsold birds from the market, can bring the virus home.
Contaminated equipment such as egg trays, crates, feeders, drinkers, sacks and bicycles or motorbikes used for transport can move the virus between farms.
Feeding or throwing dead birds, offal or feathers where dogs, cats, rats or wild birds can reach them spreads the virus further.
The virus survives longer in cool, damp conditions and in droppings, so contaminated litter and manure remain dangerous for days to weeks if not handled properly.
detail.atRisk: All poultry can catch avian influenza. Chickens and turkeys usually get the most severe disease and die in large numbers. Ducks and geese often carry and spread the virus while showing few or no signs, which makes mixed flocks of ducks and chickens especially risky. Kienyeji (free-range indigenous) chickens that roam, scavenge and share water with wild birds face high exposure, while commercial broiler and layer farms face the biggest financial losses because so many birds are kept together. Farms near lakes, rivers, dams, wetlands and rice schemes, such as around Lake Victoria, Lake Naivasha and other Rift Valley lakes, are at higher risk because migratory and resident water birds gather there. Risk can rise during the months when migratory birds pass through East Africa, roughly from around October to April, though timing varies. Farms that buy birds from live-bird markets, mix birds from different sources, or have poor fencing and no footbath are also at greater risk. Outbreaks of HPAI have been reported in the wider East African region, including in Uganda, so Kenyan farmers should stay alert even though the situation changes over time.

early: Sudden death of several birds, sometimes overnight, often with no earlier signs of illness; this is frequently the first thing a farmer notices.
Birds that are quiet, sleepy and huddled, with ruffled feathers and drooping wings.
A sharp drop in feed and water intake across the flock.
A sudden fall in egg production in layers, with soft-shelled, thin-shelled or misshapen eggs.
Watery eyes, sneezing, mild coughing or gurgling breathing.
In low pathogenic infections, only mild breathing signs and a small drop in eggs may be seen, which can be easy to miss.
advanced: Swelling of the head, face, eyelids and the skin around the eyes, sometimes with fluid under the skin.
Comb and wattles turning dark red, purple or bluish, and sometimes swollen, with dark dead patches at the tips.
Red or purple blotches (bleeding under the skin) on the shanks and feet, which are normally yellow or pale.
Discharge from the nose and mouth, heavy laboured breathing and gasping.
Watery green or white diarrhoea.
Nervous signs such as trembling, twisted neck, loss of balance, walking in circles or paralysis, more often seen in ducks and turkeys.
Very high deaths, which can reach most or nearly all of the flock within a few days in highly pathogenic outbreaks.

lookalikes.name: Newcastle disease (kideri)
lookalikes.howToTell: Virulent Newcastle disease can look almost exactly like bird flu, with sudden deaths, breathing problems, green diarrhoea and swollen heads. Twisted necks and paralysis are more typical of Newcastle, while severe swelling of the head and purple legs lean towards bird flu, but the signs overlap so much that only a laboratory test can tell them apart. Both diseases are notifiable, so report either one.

lookalikes.name: Fowl cholera
lookalikes.howToTell: Fowl cholera is a bacterial disease that can cause sudden deaths and swollen, purple wattles, usually in older birds and layers. It tends to spread more slowly through a flock, swollen wattles may be on only one side, and it can come back on the same farm. A vet can confirm it with lab tests; unlike bird flu, it responds to vet-prescribed antibiotics.

lookalikes.name: Infectious laryngotracheitis (ILT)
lookalikes.howToTell: ILT mainly affects the windpipe. Birds stretch their necks to gasp for air and may cough up bloody mucus. Deaths are usually lower and spread more slowly than in bird flu, and swollen heads and purple legs are not typical.

lookalikes.name: Heat stress
lookalikes.howToTell: Heat stress causes sudden deaths on very hot afternoons, with birds panting, holding wings away from the body and lying near walls or drinkers. Deaths stop when the house is cooled, and birds do not have swollen heads or bleeding on the legs.

detail.diagnosis: Bird flu cannot be confirmed by looking at birds alone, because Newcastle disease and other conditions look very similar. When you report a suspected case, a government veterinary officer will visit, examine the flock and record the signs and death pattern. They will collect samples, usually swabs from the throat and the vent (cloaca) of sick and dead birds, and sometimes whole carcasses or blood. Samples are sent under strict safety rules to a government laboratory, such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete, where tests such as PCR (a test that detects the virus's genetic material) and virus isolation confirm the virus and its type, such as H5N1. Results can take a few days, and movement restrictions apply while you wait. To help the vet, keep a written record of when the first birds fell sick, how many have died each day, the ages and types of birds, any recent purchases, market visits or visitors, and whether wild birds visit your water or feed. Keep a few fresh dead birds in sealed, double plastic bags in a cool, shaded place away from animals and children, but do not open them yourself. Never cut open carcasses to look inside, because this exposes you to the virus.
firstSteps: Report immediately to your County Veterinary Officer, the nearest government vet, or your area extension officer; this is required by law and is the most important step.
Stop all movement: do not sell, give away, slaughter or move any birds, eggs, manure, litter or equipment off the farm, and do not bring new birds in.
Keep all birds confined in their house or pen so they cannot mix with neighbours' birds or wild birds, and keep ducks separate from chickens.

Protect yourself and your family: wear gloves or plastic bags on your hands, a mask or cloth over your nose and mouth, and boots or dedicated shoes when handling birds, and wash hands with soap and water afterwards.
Keep children, elderly people, pregnant women and anyone who is sick away from the birds, and do not let anyone eat sick or dead birds.

Collect dead birds with protected hands, place them in sealed bags, and keep them in one safe spot for the vet; do not throw them in rivers, dumps or bushes, and never feed them to dogs, cats or pigs.
Close the farm gate to visitors and traders, place a footbath with disinfectant at the entrance, and change clothes and wash before visiting any other farm or market.
Write down daily deaths, signs seen, feed and water intake, egg numbers and any recent bird purchases, visitors or market trips to share with the vet.
Keep water and feed available to the remaining birds, but cover them so wild birds, rats and other animals cannot reach them.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no cure for avian influenza in poultry, and birds are not treated with drugs. Antibiotics do not kill the virus and will not save birds or stop the outbreak, so do not waste money on them; using them carelessly also adds to antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to medicines. Human antiviral medicines are not used in poultry. Because the highly pathogenic form spreads fast and threatens people, the government response under Kenya's animal disease laws usually focuses on control rather than treatment. Once confirmed, the Directorate of Veterinary Services may order humane killing (culling) of infected and exposed flocks, safe disposal of carcasses by deep burial or burning, cleaning and disinfection of houses and equipment, and a quarantine around the farm. Movement restrictions mean that no birds, eggs, poultry products, manure or equipment can leave or enter the affected farm and surrounding zone without permission, and markets in the area may be closed for a time. Officers will also check neighbouring farms for signs of disease. Vaccination against bird flu is not routinely used in Kenya and may only be used under government control in specific situations, so farmers should never buy or use bird flu vaccines on their own. Expect officials to ask questions, take samples and give instructions; cooperating fully helps the area recover faster and allows markets to reopen sooner. Ask the County Veterinary Officer whether any compensation scheme applies, because this depends on government policy at the time.
prevention: Keep a closed flock where possible: avoid buying birds from live-bird markets, buy chicks only from reputable, licensed hatcheries, and keep any new birds separate for at least two weeks before mixing.
Never bring unsold birds back from the market into your flock; if you must, keep them fully separate and watch them closely.
Keep poultry away from wild birds: house or fence birds, net open sides of houses, and do not let chickens and ducks drink from dams, ponds or swamps used by wild water birds.
Give clean, safe water from a covered tank, borehole or treated supply, and store feed in closed containers or rooms that wild birds and rats cannot enter.
Keep ducks and geese separate from chickens and turkeys, because ducks can carry the virus without showing signs.
Limit visitors, use a footbath with disinfectant at the poultry house door, and keep dedicated boots and clothes for working with birds.
Clean and disinfect crates, egg trays, feeders, drinkers and vehicles, and avoid sharing equipment with other farms; use new or disinfected egg trays.
Remove litter and manure regularly and compost or dispose of it away from the poultry area, and dispose of dead birds safely by burial or burning.

Vaccinate against Newcastle disease, Gumboro and other diseases your vet recommends; this does not protect against bird flu but keeps birds healthier and makes unusual deaths easier to notice and investigate.
Watch your flock every day, record deaths and egg numbers, and report any unusual or sudden deaths early, especially during the migratory bird season.
detail.impact: Bird flu is one of the most costly poultry diseases. In a highly pathogenic outbreak, most or all of the flock can die within days, wiping out the farmer's investment in chicks, feed, vaccines and housing. Layer farmers lose their daily egg income at once, and broiler farmers can lose a whole batch just before sale. Even birds that survive are usually culled under government control to stop the spread. Quarantine and movement restrictions stop sales of birds and eggs for weeks or longer, and restocking is delayed until the farm has been cleaned, disinfected and cleared by veterinary authorities. Neighbouring farms and traders in the zone also suffer from closed markets and falling prices, and fear of bird flu can reduce demand for poultry products across a region even where birds are healthy. For a family relying on kienyeji chickens as savings, food and school fees, losing the flock can be a serious setback. Countries with confirmed outbreaks can also face trade restrictions on poultry exports.
detail.humanHealth: Some avian influenza viruses, especially H5N1, can infect people. Human cases are rare, but they can cause severe pneumonia and death. People usually catch it through close, unprotected contact with sick or dead birds, their droppings, or contaminated surroundings, especially when slaughtering, plucking, cleaning or preparing infected birds. Never slaughter, sell, give away or eat birds that are sick or died of unknown causes. Handle birds only with gloves or plastic bags on your hands, cover your nose and mouth, and wash hands well with soap and water afterwards. Keep children away from poultry during an outbreak and from dead birds at any time. Change and wash clothes after working with birds. If you or anyone in your household develops fever, cough, sore throat, breathing difficulty or red eyes after contact with sick or dead birds, go to a health facility promptly and tell the health worker about the bird contact. Properly cooked poultry meat and eggs from healthy flocks are considered safe, but food from an infected farm must not enter the food chain. Cats, dogs and other mammals can also catch the virus from eating infected birds, so never feed carcasses to them.
detail.outlook: For chickens and turkeys infected with highly pathogenic avian influenza, the outlook is very poor. Most affected birds die, often within a few days, and surviving birds are normally culled to stop the spread and protect people. Ducks and geese may survive but can keep spreading the virus. Low pathogenic strains cause milder disease and most birds survive, though egg production may fall, and these strains are still reported and managed because some can change into the deadly form. For the farm and the community, the outlook depends on how quickly the disease is reported: early reporting, strict movement control and good cleaning limit the outbreak to fewer farms and allow markets to reopen sooner. Farms that are properly cleaned, disinfected and left empty for the period set by the veterinary authorities can restock and recover.

faqs.q: Can I sell or eat chickens or eggs from my farm if I suspect bird flu?
faqs.a: No. Do not sell, give away, slaughter or eat any birds or eggs from a flock you suspect has bird flu. Handling and preparing infected birds is how most people catch the virus, and selling them spreads the disease to other farms and families. Wait for the government vet's instructions and test results. Poultry and eggs from healthy flocks, properly cooked, are considered safe.

faqs.q: Will antibiotics, herbal remedies or immune boosters save my birds?
faqs.a: No. There is no cure for bird flu in poultry. Antibiotics do not kill viruses, and no supplement, herbal product or immune booster has been shown to protect birds from or cure highly pathogenic avian influenza. Spending money on them delays the right action, which is reporting to your County Veterinary Officer and locking down your farm.

faqs.q: Why do I have to report it? Will I lose all my birds?
faqs.a: Bird flu is a notifiable disease in Kenya, which means the law requires anyone who suspects it to report it to the County Veterinary Officer or the Directorate of Veterinary Services. Reporting protects your family, your neighbours' flocks and the whole poultry industry. If the disease is confirmed, the government may order culling of infected and exposed birds, because they are likely to die anyway and are a danger to people. Hiding an outbreak can lead to far bigger losses for you and your whole area. Ask the vet about any compensation that may be available.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine for bird flu that I can buy at the agrovet?
faqs.a: Bird flu vaccination is not routinely used in Kenya, and where it is used anywhere, it is controlled by government veterinary services. Do not buy or use any product sold as a bird flu vaccine on your own. The best protection for your flock is good biosecurity: keeping wild birds away, controlling visitors and movements, buying from trusted sources, and reporting unusual deaths quickly. Keep vaccinating against Newcastle disease and Gumboro as your vet advises.

faqs.q: How do I tell bird flu from Newcastle disease?
faqs.a: You cannot reliably tell them apart by eye. Both can cause sudden deaths, breathing problems, green diarrhoea and swollen heads. Swollen heads, purple combs and red or purple legs point more towards bird flu, while twisted necks and paralysis point more towards Newcastle, but the signs overlap. Only a laboratory test can confirm which it is. Both are notifiable, so report sudden high deaths either way.

faqs.q: When can I restock after an outbreak?
faqs.a: Only after the veterinary authorities say it is safe. Before restocking, all birds, carcasses, litter and manure must be safely disposed of, and the house and equipment must be cleaned, disinfected and left empty for the period set by the County Veterinary Officer. Restocking too early, or with birds from unknown sources, risks bringing the disease straight back. Use this time to improve fencing, netting, footbaths and water supply so your new flock is better protected.

avian-influenza.imagePrompt: A close-up realistic photo of a sick chicken standing in a simple Kenyan poultry house, its head and eyelids swollen, its comb and wattles dark purple, and red-purple blotches visible on its yellow shanks, with ruffled feathers and a drowsy posture.
avian-influenza.seoDescription: Bird flu in poultry: spot swollen heads, purple combs and sudden deaths, report to your County Vet, protect your family and prevent avian influenza in Kenya.

card.headline: Ruffled, huddled chicks with white diarrhoea
card.look: Chicks of about 3 to 6 weeks suddenly sit huddled together with ruffled feathers, sleepy eyes and white, watery droppings stuck around the vent. Some peck at their own or others' vents, and deaths rise quickly over a few days.
card.action: Separate sick chicks and keep them warm with clean water close by, stop all visitors and bird movement, and call your vet or County Veterinary Officer today.

detail.summary: Gumboro is a highly contagious viral disease of young chickens. It attacks the bursa of Fabricius, a small organ near the vent that builds the chick's immune (defence) system. Outbreaks can kill many chicks within a week, and the birds that survive often have weak immunity for life, so vaccines work poorly and other diseases hit harder. It is one of the most important diseases of broilers, layers and improved kienyeji chicks in Kenya.
detail.cause: Gumboro is caused by infectious bursal disease virus, a birnavirus. The virus is swallowed by the chick and travels to the bursa of Fabricius. The bursa is a small pouch just above the vent where young chicks make B-cells, the white blood cells that produce antibodies against disease. The virus multiplies inside these cells and destroys them. Within a few days the bursa swells, becomes inflamed and may bleed, then later shrinks and is left almost empty of immune cells. During the sudden phase, chicks become weak, stop eating and drinking, and lose water through diarrhoea. Dehydration and waste products build up and damage the kidneys, and small bleeds can appear in the leg and breast muscles. Very virulent strains, which are present in Africa including Kenya, can kill a large share of a flock. Chicks infected before about 3 weeks of age often show few signs, but their bursa is badly damaged, leaving them with long-term immune suppression. This means they respond poorly to vaccines such as Newcastle disease vaccine and fall sick more easily with coccidiosis, E. coli, respiratory infections and others.
spread: Sick and recovering birds pass large amounts of virus in their droppings, which contaminate litter, feed and drinking water.
Chicks catch it mainly by eating or drinking material contaminated with infected droppings.
The virus is very tough and can survive for months in poultry houses, old litter, soil and equipment, so a new batch of chicks can be infected from a previous flock's house.
People carry the virus on shoes, clothes and hands when moving between farms, markets and houses.
Shared or second-hand equipment such as feeders, drinkers, crates and egg trays can bring the virus onto a farm.
Vehicles, feed sacks and chick delivery boxes from other farms can carry contaminated dust and droppings.
Litter beetles (darkling beetles), rodents and wild birds can carry the virus around and between houses.
Stress, poor vaccination timing and weak maternal (mother-passed) antibodies make outbreaks more likely and more severe.
detail.atRisk: Chicks between about 3 and 6 weeks of age are most likely to show clear sickness and deaths, although outbreaks can occur somewhat earlier or later. Chicks under 3 weeks may be infected without obvious signs but suffer lasting immune damage. Older birds that have passed the age of bursa activity are rarely affected. Layer-type breeds often suffer more severely than broilers, and improved kienyeji breeds such as Kuroiler and KALRO improved kienyeji are commonly affected, especially when unvaccinated or poorly vaccinated. Local kienyeji chickens can also get Gumboro; how resistant they are varies. Highest risk is on farms that raise batch after batch of chicks in the same house without thorough cleaning and a rest period, in areas with many poultry farms close together, and where chicks come from hatcheries with unknown breeder vaccination. Outbreaks happen all year round, but stress from cold nights during the rains, overcrowding and poor ventilation can make them worse.

early: Sudden onset: chicks that looked fine yesterday are sleepy and dull today.
Ruffled, standing-up feathers and drooping wings.
Chicks huddle together near the heat source or in corners, even when the brooder is warm.
Reduced feeding and drinking; feed is left in the feeders.
White or creamy, watery diarrhoea, often with a sticky, soiled vent.
Some chicks peck at their own vent or at other chicks' vents, which is a typical sign of an irritated bursa.
Slight trembling or unsteady walking in some birds.
advanced: Severe weakness: chicks lie down, with eyes closed, and do not move away when approached.
Signs of dehydration: shrunken eyes, dry shanks and a thin, light-feeling body.
Daily deaths rise sharply over 3 to 4 days, peak, and then fall again within about a week.
Dead birds may show darkened, dehydrated muscles with small red streaks or spots on thighs and breast (seen by the vet at post-mortem).
Survivors recover but grow slowly and unevenly, with poor feathering.
Weeks later, the flock may suffer repeated outbreaks of other diseases, or vaccinations such as Newcastle may seem to fail, because of immune damage.

lookalikes.name: Newcastle disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Newcastle affects chickens of all ages, not mainly 3 to 6 week chicks. It usually causes breathing problems, gasping, greenish diarrhoea, twisted necks or paralysis, and a sharp drop in eggs in layers. Newcastle is notifiable in Kenya, so if you see nervous or breathing signs, report to your County Veterinary Officer. A vet can tell them apart at post-mortem and with lab tests.

lookalikes.name: Coccidiosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Coccidiosis also affects young chicks and causes huddling and ruffled feathers, but droppings are often bloody, brown or mucky rather than white and watery. Deaths tend to continue rather than following the sharp rise-and-fall of Gumboro. At post-mortem, the gut (especially the caeca, the two blind pouches) is damaged and bloody, while in Gumboro the bursa is swollen. Both can occur together, because Gumboro weakens the defence against coccidia.

lookalikes.name: Kidney form of infectious bronchitis
lookalikes.howToTell: Some infectious bronchitis strains damage the kidneys and also cause wet droppings, dehydration and deaths in young birds. However, there are usually breathing signs such as sneezing, snicking or rattling first. The vet finds swollen pale kidneys without the swollen, yellowish bursa typical of Gumboro.

lookalikes.name: Mycotoxin poisoning (aflatoxins in feed)
lookalikes.howToTell: Mouldy feed causes poor growth, weakness, pale or yellow birds and weak immunity, but it usually builds up slowly and affects birds of different ages eating the same feed. It does not spread from bird to bird and does not have the sudden peak of deaths seen with Gumboro. Changing to fresh, good-quality feed often helps. Mycotoxins can also make Gumboro worse.

detail.diagnosis: A vet usually suspects Gumboro from the age of the chicks, the sudden start, white watery diarrhoea, vent pecking and the typical pattern of deaths rising then falling within about a week. The most useful step is a post-mortem (opening dead or very sick birds). In early cases the bursa of Fabricius is swollen, yellowish or jelly-like and sometimes bloody; in later cases it is small and shrunken. The vet may also see bleeding in thigh and breast muscles, bleeding where the glandular stomach joins the gizzard, and swollen kidneys with white deposits. To confirm, samples such as the bursa can be sent to a laboratory, for example a county or regional veterinary laboratory or the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete, for tests such as PCR (detects the virus genes), tissue examination under a microscope, or blood tests (ELISA) to check flock antibody levels. Blood tests on day-old chicks or young birds can also help the vet plan the best vaccination age. To help your vet, keep a daily record of deaths and sick birds, note the age and breed of the flock, the hatchery source, all vaccines given (with dates, batch numbers and how they were given), feed and any medicines used. Keep two or three freshly dead or very sick birds cool (not frozen) in a sealed bag for post-mortem.
firstSteps: Call your vet, agrovet animal health worker or County Veterinary Officer as soon as you see several chicks huddled with white diarrhoea, because a quick diagnosis helps protect the rest of the flock and future batches.
Separate the sickest chicks into a warm, clean, well-bedded pen, and keep the whole flock warm and free of draughts, especially at night, while still allowing fresh air.
Make sure every chick can easily reach clean, fresh drinking water; add extra drinkers and place them close to where weak birds sit so they do not have to walk far.
Keep fresh, good-quality feed available and avoid sudden changes of feed during the outbreak.
Do not give antibiotics or any other medicine on your own; they do not kill the virus and wrong use builds drug resistance, so wait for your vet's advice.
Stop all visitors, do not sell or move birds, and do not share equipment with neighbours until the vet has assessed the flock.
Wear separate boots and overalls for the chick house, wash hands after handling birds, and work with healthy birds before sick ones.
Remove dead birds promptly, keep a few for the vet, and dispose of the rest by deep burial or burning away from water sources, never by throwing them to dogs or into rubbish pits.
Record daily deaths, feed and water use, and the signs you see, so the vet can judge how the outbreak is progressing.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no medicine that cures Gumboro, because it is a virus and antibiotics do not kill viruses. Most outbreaks run their course in about a week, and the vet's aim is to keep as many chicks alive as possible and limit damage. Treatment is mainly supportive: keeping birds warm, encouraging them to drink, and giving electrolytes (rehydration salts) and vitamins in water to replace lost fluids and support recovery. Your vet may advise temporary changes to feed to reduce strain on the kidneys. Because Gumboro weakens immunity, chicks often pick up bacterial infections such as E. coli at the same time. If the vet confirms or strongly suspects these, they may prescribe an antibiotic for a short period. Antibiotics must only be used on a vet's prescription, at the correct dose and for the full course, to avoid antimicrobial resistance, which makes medicines useless for animals and people. Any drug used will have a withdrawal period, meaning meat and eggs from treated birds must not be sold or eaten until that time has passed; ask your vet and read the label. If coccidiosis is also present, the vet may prescribe an anticoccidial drug. After the outbreak, the vet will review your vaccination programme and may advise checking flock immunity or revaccinating against other diseases, such as Newcastle, because earlier vaccines may not have worked well in immune-damaged birds.
prevention: Vaccinate every batch of chicks against Gumboro using a good-quality live vaccine from a trusted agrovet, following the timing advised by your vet or the hatchery, commonly during the second and third weeks of life; many flocks need two doses because mother-passed antibodies can block a single early dose.

Handle vaccines carefully: keep them cold in a cool box from the shop to the farm, use clean drinkers without soap or disinfectant residue, use clean water without chlorine (or add a vaccine stabiliser or skimmed milk powder as directed), and make sure all chicks drink the vaccine water within the time on the label.
Buy chicks only from reputable hatcheries that vaccinate their breeder flocks and can tell you which vaccines the chicks or parents received, including any given at the hatchery.

Practise 'all-in, all-out': raise one age group at a time in a house, and after each batch remove all litter, scrub and wash surfaces, disinfect with a product your vet recommends as effective against Gumboro virus, and leave the house empty for at least two weeks before new chicks arrive.

Keep strict biosecurity: a footbath or separate boots at the house door, limited visitors, no birds or equipment from markets or neighbours entering the chick house, and fencing or netting to keep out wild birds, rodents and stray chickens.
Control litter beetles and rodents, and do not reuse old litter for new chicks; compost it well away from the poultry houses.
Reduce stress during the first six weeks: avoid overcrowding, keep good brooding temperature, provide good ventilation, and give clean water and balanced feed at all times.
Protect feed from moisture and mould, because aflatoxins in mouldy maize or feed weaken immunity and make Gumboro and vaccine failure more likely.
Keep vaccination and flock records for every batch so you and your vet can spot patterns and adjust the programme if problems repeat.
detail.impact: Gumboro can be very costly for Kenyan poultry farmers. In a sudden outbreak, many chicks may die in a few days, wiping out the money spent on chicks, feed, brooding fuel and vaccines. Survivors often grow slowly and unevenly, so broilers take longer to reach market weight and use more feed per kilo of meat. Layer and improved kienyeji pullets may come into lay late or perform poorly. The hidden cost is often bigger: immune damage means later vaccines, especially for Newcastle disease, may not protect properly, and the flock suffers more from coccidiosis, E. coli, respiratory disease and other infections, increasing treatment costs and deaths later. Because the virus lingers in houses, farms that do not clean and vaccinate properly may see the problem return with every new batch.
detail.humanHealth: Gumboro virus does not infect people, and it is not a risk to human health. The main human concern comes from medicines: if a vet prescribes antibiotics or other drugs for secondary infections, follow the withdrawal period strictly and do not sell or eat meat or eggs from treated birds until it has passed, to avoid drug residues and the spread of antibiotic resistance.
detail.outlook: Most outbreaks follow a clear pattern: deaths rise for a few days, peak, then fall, and most surviving birds begin to eat and drink again within about a week. How many die depends on the virus strain, the age of the chicks, the breed, and how well they were vaccinated and cared for. Very virulent strains can kill a large part of a flock, especially in layer-type chicks. Warmth, plenty of clean water, good nutrition and quick vet support improve survival. Survivors may never fully regain normal immunity, so they need extra care, good biosecurity and attention to their other vaccinations. With proper cleaning, a rest period between batches and a correct vaccination programme, future batches can usually be well protected.

faqs.q: I vaccinated my chicks against Gumboro, so why did they still get sick?
faqs.a: Vaccine failures are common and usually have a reason. The vaccine may have been damaged by heat if it was not kept cold, or by chlorine or soap in the water. Some chicks may not have drunk enough vaccine water. The timing may have been wrong, because mother-passed antibodies in young chicks can block the vaccine if it is given too early. The strain on your farm may also be a very virulent type that needs a stronger vaccine or a different programme. Share your records with your vet so they can adjust the schedule and vaccine type.

faqs.q: Can I use antibiotics to cure Gumboro?
faqs.a: No. Gumboro is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not kill viruses. A vet may prescribe an antibiotic only if there are also bacterial infections, which are common because the birds' immunity is weak. Using antibiotics without a vet's advice wastes money, leaves residues in meat and eggs, and helps germs become resistant to medicines.

faqs.q: How long does the virus stay in my poultry house?
faqs.a: The Gumboro virus is very hardy and can survive for months in litter, dust, soil and equipment. That is why outbreaks often come back with the next batch. Remove all litter, scrub and wash everything, disinfect with a product your vet confirms works against this virus, and leave the house empty for at least two weeks before bringing in new chicks.

faqs.q: Can my adult hens or kienyeji chickens get Gumboro?
faqs.a: Adult birds rarely show signs, because the bursa that the virus attacks shrinks as chickens mature. However, older birds can still carry the virus on their feathers and feet and in their droppings, and contaminate the ground. Keep chicks separate from adult and free-range birds, especially in the first six weeks.

faqs.q: Is it safe to eat chickens or eggs from a flock that had Gumboro?
faqs.a: Gumboro does not infect people, so recovered birds and their eggs are not a disease risk to humans. Do not eat or sell birds that are sick or died of disease. If any medicine was given, wait until the withdrawal period on the label or from your vet has passed before eating or selling meat or eggs.

faqs.q: Should I vaccinate my chicks during an outbreak?
faqs.a: This depends on the age of the chicks, the vaccine and the situation on your farm, so ask your vet before doing it. Vaccinating birds that are already sick will not cure them and can sometimes add stress. Your vet may advise vaccinating healthy, younger groups on the farm, and will certainly help you plan a better programme for the next batch.

products.role: An oral rehydration solution that can help sick chicks replace fluids and salts lost through white watery diarrhoea, supporting kidney function and drinking during the outbreak, alongside warmth, vet advice and good care. It does not kill the virus.

A liquid vitamin and mineral supplement that can support appetite and recovery in surviving chicks after the outbreak peak and around revaccination stress, as part of good nutrition and a proper vaccination programme. It is a support, not a treatment for Gumboro.

gumboro.imagePrompt: A realistic photo of a group of four-week-old chicks huddled together on wood-shaving litter under a brooder lamp, with ruffled feathers, half-closed eyes and white watery droppings soiling the feathers around their vents.
gumboro.seoDescription: Gumboro (IBD) in chicks: spot ruffled, huddled birds with white watery diarrhoea, act fast, and prevent outbreaks with vaccination and clean housing.

card.headline: Gasping, sneezing chicks and wrinkled eggs
card.look: Young chicks huddle near the heat, stretch their necks to gasp, sneeze and make wet rattling sounds when breathing. In layers, egg numbers drop suddenly and the eggs come out soft, thin, wrinkled or pale, with watery whites.
card.action: Separate the sick birds, keep them warm with clean water and good ventilation, stop all bird movement, and call your vet or County Veterinary Officer the same day.

detail.summary: Infectious bronchitis (IB) is a fast-spreading viral disease of chickens caused by a coronavirus. It mainly attacks the breathing tubes, but some strains also damage the kidneys and the egg-making organs. It can sweep through a whole flock within a few days. Chick deaths, slow broiler growth, a sharp fall in egg numbers and poor shell quality make it one of the most costly poultry diseases in Kenya, even when few birds die.
detail.cause: IB is caused by infectious bronchitis virus (IBV), an avian coronavirus. It is a different virus from the one that causes COVID-19 in people, and it infects chickens, not humans. The virus enters through the nose and eyes and multiplies in the lining of the windpipe (trachea). It destroys the tiny hair-like cells (cilia) that normally sweep dust and germs out of the airway. Mucus then builds up, causing the rattling sounds called 'rales', and bacteria such as E. coli and Mycoplasma can move in. These bacteria cause secondary infections of the air sacs and lungs, and they cause most of the deaths. Some strains, called nephropathogenic strains, travel to the kidneys and cause swelling, white urate deposits and death, especially in young birds. In laying hens the virus attacks the oviduct, the tube where the egg white and shell are formed. This is why eggs come out thin-shelled, soft, misshapen, pale or with watery whites. If chicks are infected in their first two weeks of life, the oviduct can be permanently damaged. Those birds may grow up looking like normal hens but never lay properly. Farmers call them 'false layers'. IBV has many types (serotypes and variants), and a vaccine against one type does not always protect well against another.
spread: Breathing in virus-laden droplets and dust: sick birds cough and sneeze the virus into the air, and it moves quickly through a poultry house.
Droppings from infected birds carry the virus. It can contaminate litter, feeders and drinkers, and recovered birds may keep shedding virus for weeks.
People, shoes, clothes, egg trays, crates, sacks, bicycles and vehicles moving between farms or markets carry the virus on dirty surfaces.
Buying in birds from markets, neighbours or unknown sources, or bringing back unsold birds from the market, brings infection into a clean flock.
Keeping chickens of different ages on one farm, or restocking without cleaning out, lets the virus pass from older birds to new chicks.
