Stress makes outbreaks worse. This includes cold brooders, poor ventilation, strong ammonia from wet litter, overcrowding and sudden weather changes during the long and short rains.
Badly handled vaccines can fail. Vaccine left in the sun, mixed with chlorinated water or used after expiry leaves birds unprotected.
detail.atRisk: All chickens can catch IB, but the effects depend on age and use. Chicks under about six weeks suffer the worst breathing problems and deaths, and those infected in the first two weeks risk lifelong egg-laying damage. Broilers often get air sac infections as a complication, which slows growth and raises deaths and condemnations. Laying hens show the egg drop and poor shell and egg-white quality. Commercial layer and broiler units with many birds close together see fast spread. Kienyeji (indigenous) and improved kienyeji flocks are also at risk, especially when birds mix at markets or roam freely with neighbours' flocks, and they are often unvaccinated. Flocks are more at risk in cold, damp weather during the rains, in poorly ventilated or overcrowded houses, and on farms that keep several ages together or skip vaccination.

early: Chicks gasp with open beaks and stretched necks, and you hear wet rattling or gurgling sounds (rales) from the chest, clearest at night when the house is quiet.
Birds sneeze, cough and shake their heads, and you may see a watery discharge from the nostrils or watery, slightly swollen eyes.
Chicks crowd together under the heat source, look dull with ruffled feathers, and eat and drink less than usual.
Many birds show signs within a day or two of each other, because the virus spreads very fast.
In layers there is a sudden drop in daily egg collection, often with mild breathing sounds, or sometimes almost no breathing signs at all.
Eggs begin to show thin, rough or wrinkled shells, and brown eggs look pale or washed out.
advanced: Breathing becomes very laboured in young birds, and some die, especially where E. coli or Mycoplasma infections follow.
With kidney strains, birds drink more, droppings become wet and white with urates, litter gets soaked, and young birds may die without obvious breathing signs.
Broilers grow unevenly, feed conversion worsens, and at slaughter the air sacs may be cloudy or filled with yellow cheesy material.
Layers produce misshapen, soft-shelled or shell-less eggs. When you crack them, the white is thin and watery instead of firm, and it spreads widely on a plate.
Egg numbers may take weeks to recover, and in some flocks they never fully return to the expected level.
Months later, hens that were infected as chicks may look healthy, with red combs and a good body, but lay few or no eggs (false layers).

lookalikes.name: Newcastle disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Newcastle disease (kideri) also causes breathing signs and egg drop, but it usually brings many more deaths. It also causes nervous signs such as a twisted neck, circling or paralysis, and green watery diarrhoea. IB rarely causes nervous signs. Newcastle is a notifiable disease. If you see nervous signs or sudden heavy deaths, call the County Veterinary Officer immediately. Only lab tests can reliably separate the two.

lookalikes.name: Infectious coryza
lookalikes.howToTell: Coryza is a bacterial disease. It causes a swollen face and wattles, a sticky nasal discharge with a bad smell, and eyes that may stick shut. It mostly affects growing and adult birds. IB spreads faster, usually does not cause marked face swelling, and in layers is strongly linked to poor egg shells and watery whites.

lookalikes.name: Chronic respiratory disease (Mycoplasma gallisepticum)
lookalikes.howToTell: Mycoplasma spreads slowly through a flock over weeks. It causes long-lasting snicking, swollen sinuses under the eyes and frothy eyes. IB comes on suddenly and spreads within days. The two often occur together, which makes the disease much worse, so a vet may test for both.

lookalikes.name: Egg drop syndrome
lookalikes.howToTell: Egg drop syndrome is caused by an adenovirus. It causes thin-shelled, soft or shell-less eggs in apparently healthy layers, usually without breathing signs. The inside of the egg is usually normal. IB more often brings breathing signs, wrinkled shells and watery egg whites, and can affect young birds too.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will look at the flock's age, vaccination history, how fast the signs spread and egg production records, then examine live birds. A post-mortem (opening dead or sick birds) may show mucus in the windpipe, cloudy or cheesy air sacs, swollen pale kidneys with white urates, or a fluid-filled or under-developed oviduct in false layers. Because IB looks like Newcastle disease, coryza, Mycoplasma and others, lab tests are needed to confirm it. These include PCR tests on throat or cloacal swabs to detect the virus and identify its type, virus isolation in fertile eggs, and blood tests (ELISA or HI) on samples taken a few weeks apart to show rising antibodies. In Kenya samples can go through your vet or County Veterinary Officer to county labs, the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete, or university diagnostic labs. You can help by writing down when signs started, how many birds are sick and dead each day, daily egg counts and egg appearance, feed and water changes, and every vaccine given, with dates, brand and method. Keep a few freshly dead birds cool, but not frozen, in a sealed bag, or keep a few sick live birds separate for the vet.
firstSteps: Move visibly sick birds to a separate, warm, draught-free pen. Keep the rest of the flock in its house and stop all buying, selling and moving of birds until the vet has seen them.
Keep chicks warm at the correct brooding temperature and watch their behaviour. Huddling under the heat means they are cold; spreading away and panting means they are too hot.
Improve ventilation without creating cold draughts. Remove wet, ammonia-smelling litter and add fresh dry litter, because ammonia further damages already injured airways.
Give plenty of clean, fresh drinking water at all times and make sure every bird can easily reach drinkers and feeders. Sick birds eat little, and kidney strains make them very thirsty.

Do not give antibiotics or other drugs from the agrovet on your own. Antibiotics do not kill the virus, and the wrong drug wastes money, leaves residues in eggs and meat, and builds antibiotic resistance.
Tighten biosecurity: one person cares for the sick birds last, change or disinfect footwear at the door, keep visitors and other farmers' birds away, and do not lend crates or egg trays.
Record daily deaths, number of sick birds, egg numbers and egg quality. Remove dead birds quickly and bury them deeply or burn them, away from water sources.
Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer the same day. Call immediately if many birds die suddenly or you see twisted necks or paralysis, which could mean Newcastle disease or bird flu.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no drug that cures infectious bronchitis. Antibiotics do not kill the virus. Treatment aims to keep birds comfortable, reduce secondary infections and protect the rest of the flock. A vet may prescribe an antibiotic, such as a tetracycline, a macrolide like tylosin, or another suitable drug, only if there is evidence of secondary bacterial infection such as E. coli or Mycoplasma. Ideally the choice is guided by lab results. Use antibiotics only as prescribed and for the full course, because careless use breeds resistant bacteria that are harder to treat in animals and people. Every antibiotic has a withdrawal period, the time after the last dose during which eggs and meat must not be eaten or sold. Some products are not allowed at all in laying hens whose eggs are eaten. Your vet will tell you the correct period, so follow it strictly. Supportive care usually includes warmth, good ventilation, dry litter, electrolytes and vitamins in the water. For kidney strains, the vet may also suggest temporary feed adjustments. The vet may advise on vaccinating unaffected or future flocks, and may send samples to identify the virus type so the right vaccine can be chosen next time. Expect breathing signs to settle over one to three weeks. Egg production in layers may recover slowly, often only partly.
prevention: Vaccinate every flock according to a programme agreed with your vet or hatchery. Chicks usually receive a live IB vaccine, often combined with Newcastle disease vaccine, at the hatchery or in the first days of life, followed by boosters. Layers and breeders are commonly given an inactivated (killed) injectable vaccine before they start laying.

Handle vaccines correctly. Keep them cold from the agrovet to the farm, protect them from sunlight, use them before expiry, and use them within the time stated once mixed. Use clean, non-chlorinated water (a vaccine stabiliser or skimmed milk powder helps). Make sure every bird drinks during the vaccination period.
Ask your vet whether the vaccine type matches the strains found in your area. Variant IB strains occur, and a vaccine based on one type may not fully protect against another.
Buy day-old chicks only from reputable, licensed hatcheries that vaccinate and give vaccination records, and avoid restocking with market or roadside birds.

Practise all-in, all-out where possible: keep one age group per house. Between batches, remove all litter, clean and disinfect the house and equipment, and leave it empty for a rest period. The virus is killed by common disinfectants but can survive for some time in dirty litter.
Keep the house well ventilated, dry and not overcrowded. Control ammonia by managing wet litter, and give chicks correct brooding temperatures, especially in the cold months and the rains.

Practise everyday biosecurity: a footbath or dedicated shoes at the house entrance, limited visitors, a fence or run that stops contact with neighbours' and wild birds, and quarantine of any new birds for at least two weeks before mixing.
Feed a balanced ration with correct vitamins, minerals and protein, and store feed dry. Well-nourished, low-stress birds respond better to vaccines and recover faster.
detail.impact: IB hits a Kenyan farm's income in several ways. In chicks and broilers, deaths, especially with secondary E. coli or kidney strains, plus slow and uneven growth, mean more feed spent per kilo of meat and lighter birds at sale. In layers, the sudden drop in egg numbers, combined with soft, cracked, misshapen and pale eggs that traders reject or buy at a low price, can wipe out the profit margin for weeks. False layers are a hidden loss: you keep feeding hens that will never lay well, and you may only find out months later. Extra spending on vet visits, lab tests and treatment of secondary infections adds to the cost. For smallholders who depend on eggs for daily cash, an outbreak can seriously disrupt household income.
detail.humanHealth: Infectious bronchitis virus infects chickens only and does not cause disease in people. It is not the same coronavirus as the one that causes COVID-19. Eggs and meat from affected flocks are safe to eat when properly cooked. The main human risk comes from drug residues. If birds are treated with antibiotics or other drugs for secondary infections, do not eat or sell eggs or meat until the vet's withdrawal period has passed. Always wash your hands after handling sick or dead birds.
detail.outlook: Most adult birds survive IB, and breathing signs usually settle within about one to three weeks. Deaths are generally higher in young chicks, in flocks hit by kidney strains, and where secondary bacterial infections or poor housing, cold and ammonia make things worse. Broilers that recover may stay smaller than expected. In layers, egg numbers and quality often improve over several weeks but may not return fully to the previous level, and shell and egg-white problems can linger. Chicks infected very young may become permanent false layers. Recovery is best when the flock was vaccinated, the vet is involved early, secondary infections are managed properly, and birds are kept warm, dry and well fed.

faqs.q: Can we eat or sell eggs from hens with infectious bronchitis?
faqs.a: The virus does not infect people, so properly cooked eggs from affected hens are safe to eat. The problem is quality: many eggs will be soft, wrinkled or have watery whites, so they crack easily and buyers may reject them. Sort eggs carefully and do not sell cracked or dirty eggs. If your vet prescribes an antibiotic or other drug, you must stop eating and selling the eggs for the full withdrawal period the vet gives you.

faqs.q: I vaccinated my chicks against IB. Why did they still get sick?
faqs.a: There are several common reasons. The vaccine may have been damaged by heat, sunlight or chlorinated water before it reached the birds. Not every bird may have drunk enough of the vaccine water. Boosters may have been missed. The virus on your farm may also be a different type from the one in the vaccine, because IB has many strains and protection between them is not always good. Stress, poor ventilation and other diseases also weaken the response. Talk to your vet about your vaccine handling, your schedule, and whether lab testing could identify the strain.

faqs.q: Will antibiotics from the agrovet cure IB?
faqs.a: No. IB is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not kill viruses. A vet may prescribe an antibiotic only when bacteria such as E. coli or Mycoplasma are causing secondary infections. Giving antibiotics without a vet's advice wastes money, leaves residues in eggs and meat, and helps create bacteria that resist treatment. Good care, warmth, ventilation, water and nutrition matter most, together with vaccination for the future.

faqs.q: My hens look big and healthy with red combs, but they hardly lay. Could this be IB?
faqs.a: It could be. If the flock caught IB in their first two weeks of life, the virus may have permanently damaged the oviduct, the egg-forming tube. Such 'false layers' look normal but lay few or no eggs. Other causes, such as poor feed, lighting problems, parasites or other diseases, are possible too. A vet can examine a few birds, including by post-mortem, to check whether the oviduct is damaged and advise whether to cull non-layers.

faqs.q: Will my egg production come back after an outbreak?
faqs.a: Usually it improves over several weeks as the birds recover, but it often does not return fully to the level the flock had before. Shell quality and watery whites may take longer to improve. How well hens recover depends on their age when infected, the virus strain, whether secondary infections were controlled, and good feeding and management afterwards. Keep egg records so you and your vet can judge whether the flock is worth keeping.

faqs.q: Do my kienyeji chickens need IB vaccination?
faqs.a: Indigenous chickens can catch IB too, especially when they roam with neighbours' birds or are taken to and from markets. Many farmers vaccinate kienyeji and improved kienyeji flocks against Newcastle disease, and combined Newcastle and IB vaccines are widely available. Ask your vet or extension officer which vaccination programme suits your flock size, system and local disease situation.

products.role: Its plant-extract blend is labelled to relieve respiratory problems and post-vaccination reactions. It can help ease breathing discomfort in birds recovering from IB, or after IB vaccination, alongside vet care, warmth and good ventilation. It does not kill the virus or replace vaccination.

A liquid vitamin and mineral supplement for stress recovery and layer productivity. Given in the water, it can help support appetite and recovery after an outbreak and support layers as egg production picks up again. It is an aid to good nutrition and vet-guided care, not a treatment for IB.

infectious-bronchitis.imagePrompt: A realistic close-up photo of a small group of young brown chicks huddled under a warm brooder lamp on wood-shavings litter in a simple Kenyan poultry house, one chick in front stretching its neck upward with its beak open as if gasping, with a few pale, wrinkled, thin-shelled eggs in a tray softly blurred in the background.
infectious-bronchitis.seoDescription: Infectious bronchitis in chickens: spot gasping, sneezing and soft, wrinkled eggs early. A Kenyan guide to first steps, vet care and vaccination.

card.headline: Lame bird, one leg forward, one back
card.look: A young bird, often 6 to 20 weeks old, lies or sits with one leg stretched forward and the other stretched back, and cannot stand. Some birds also have a drooping wing, grey cloudy eyes with an irregular pupil, or are thin and pale.
card.action: Separate the affected bird at once, keep feed and water within its reach, and call your vet to confirm the cause before more birds are affected.

aka: Grey eye or pearl eye (eye form)
detail.summary: Marek's disease is a common and serious viral disease of chickens caused by a herpesvirus. It damages nerves and causes cancer-like tumours, so birds become paralysed, blind or waste away, usually between 6 and 20 weeks of age. There is no cure, and once the virus is on a farm it stays in dust and litter for a long time. It is prevented by vaccinating chicks at day old, usually at the hatchery, and by keeping young chicks away from older birds.
detail.cause: Marek's disease is caused by Marek's disease virus, a herpesvirus of chickens (scientific name Gallid alphaherpesvirus 2). A herpesvirus is a type of virus that stays in the body for life once a bird is infected. Chicks usually breathe the virus in with dust from the farm. The virus first attacks the bird's white blood cells, the cells that fight infection. This weakens the bird's immune system, so it catches other diseases more easily and may respond poorly to other vaccines. Later, some infected white blood cells turn into cancer cells. These multiply and gather in nerves, the eyes, skin and internal organs. In nerves, especially the big nerves to the legs and wings, they cause swelling that stops messages reaching the muscles, which leads to paralysis. In the eye they make the iris (the coloured ring) grey and the pupil irregular, causing blindness. In organs such as the liver, spleen, kidneys, ovary, heart and lungs they form tumours (lumps of cancer tissue). Meanwhile the virus grows in the feather follicles (the small pockets in the skin where feathers grow) and is shed in feather dander, so infected birds keep releasing virus for the rest of their lives, even if they look healthy.
spread: The main route is breathing in dust: infected birds shed the virus in tiny flakes of skin and feather dander, which float in the air and settle in litter, on walls, sacks and equipment.
The virus survives for many months in dry dust and old litter in a poultry house, so a house that once had Marek's can infect new chicks long after the sick birds are gone.
Infected birds carry and shed the virus for life, including vaccinated birds and birds that look healthy, so older birds on the farm are a constant source for young chicks.
Mixing ages is a major risk: brooding new chicks in the same house, or near, older birds lets the virus reach chicks before their vaccine immunity has developed.
People, egg trays, crates, sacks, feeders and vehicles can carry contaminated dust from one house or farm to another.
Buying adult or grower birds from markets or neighbours, and returning unsold birds from the market, can bring the virus onto a farm.
It is not spread through the egg, so chicks hatch free of the virus; they get infected from their surroundings after hatching.
Stress from transport, crowding, poor ventilation, other diseases such as Gumboro, and mouldy feed can make infected birds more likely to show disease.
detail.atRisk: All chickens can be infected, but disease is seen most often in birds between about 6 and 20 weeks old, though it can appear from around 3 to 4 weeks and occasionally in older layers. Layers, breeders and kienyeji or improved kienyeji birds (such as Kuroiler, Kenbro and KALRO improved kienyeji) are at highest risk because they live long enough for tumours to develop and because they are often bought unvaccinated or hatched at home under a hen. Broilers are usually slaughtered before signs appear, but can still be affected. Unvaccinated chicks, chicks vaccinated with poorly stored vaccine, and chicks exposed to heavy virus loads in their first two weeks are the most likely to fall sick. Farms that keep birds of many ages together, reuse litter, or brood chicks in old houses without thorough cleaning carry more risk. Free-range and backyard flocks are exposed because birds of all ages mix freely. Some breeds and strains are naturally more resistant than others, but no chicken is fully protected without vaccination. Marek's can occur in any season, as it depends on dust and management rather than rains.

early: A bird that walks unevenly, limps, or rests a lot without an obvious injury to the foot or joint.
Weakness in one leg or one wing, often on one side only, which slowly gets worse over days.
Duller, slower birds that eat less and lag behind the rest of the flock at feeding time.
Gradual loss of weight; you can feel a sharp keel (breastbone) when you pick the bird up.
Pale comb and wattles in birds that should be bright red as they approach laying.
One or both eyes looking greyer or cloudier than normal, with a pupil that is not perfectly round.
In some birds, enlarged, raised or reddened feather follicles on the skin, best seen after plucking.
advanced: The classic posture: the bird lies with one leg stretched forward and the other stretched backward, and cannot stand.
A wing that hangs down, or a neck that is twisted or held low, because the nerves are damaged.
Blindness: the bird bumps into things or cannot find feed and water, with a grey, pearl-coloured iris and a small irregular pupil.
Severe wasting, dehydration and starvation because the bird cannot reach feed and water.
Difficult breathing, gasping or a swollen crop if nerves to the chest or crop are affected.
Pullets that never start laying or layers whose egg production drops, sometimes with sudden deaths and tumours found later in the liver, spleen or ovary.
Lumps or tumours in the skin in the skin form, which may lead to carcasses being rejected at slaughter.
Steady deaths in the flock over several weeks rather than one sudden wave.

lookalikes.name: Newcastle disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Newcastle also causes paralysis and a twisted neck, but it usually spreads very fast through birds of all ages, with coughing, gasping, greenish watery diarrhoea, swollen heads and many deaths within days. Marek's spreads slowly, affects mainly growing birds, and the leg-forward-leg-back posture with grey eyes is typical. Newcastle is notifiable in Kenya, so if many birds of all ages are sick at once, call the vet urgently.

lookalikes.name: Lymphoid leukosis (avian leukosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: This is another virus that causes tumours in organs, but it usually affects birds older than about 16 weeks and does not cause paralysis or enlarged nerves. On post-mortem, leukosis tumours involve the bursa (a small organ near the vent), while Marek's usually does not. A lab test is often needed to tell them apart.

lookalikes.name: Vitamin deficiencies (vitamin B2, vitamin E, vitamin D)
lookalikes.howToTell: Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) deficiency causes curled toes and walking on the hocks in young chicks; vitamin E deficiency causes trembling and head pulling in chicks of about 2 to 4 weeks; vitamin D and calcium shortage causes soft beaks and bones and lameness. These usually affect younger chicks and many birds at once, often improve with corrected feed, and do not cause grey eyes or tumours.

lookalikes.name: Leg injuries and joint infections
lookalikes.howToTell: Injuries, bumblefoot and bacterial or mycoplasma joint infections cause swollen, hot or painful joints or footpads that you can feel. The bird still tries to use the leg. In Marek's the leg is weak or limp with no swelling of the joint, and the bird often holds it stretched forward or back.

detail.diagnosis: A vet first looks at the flock history and signs: the age of affected birds, the leg-forward-leg-back posture, grey eyes, wasting, and whether chicks were vaccinated. The surest way to confirm Marek's is a post-mortem (opening up a dead or culled bird). The vet compares the large nerves of both legs and wings; in Marek's one nerve is often thick, swollen, greyish or yellowish, and has lost its normal fine stripes, while the other side looks normal. The vet also looks for tumours in the liver, spleen, kidneys, heart, ovary, lungs and skin. Because other diseases such as lymphoid leukosis can look similar, the vet may send tissue samples to a laboratory, for example the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete, a regional veterinary investigation laboratory, a university veterinary lab or a private diagnostic lab, for histopathology (looking at tissue under a microscope) or PCR (a test that detects the virus's genetic material). To help, keep a record of how many birds are sick and dead, their ages, when signs started, where the chicks came from, the hatchery vaccination record, and other vaccines given. Take two or three typical sick birds to the vet alive, or keep freshly dead birds in a sealed bag in a cool place or fridge (not frozen) and deliver them within a day.
firstSteps: Separate any lame, paralysed or blind bird from the rest of the flock into a clean, quiet, dry pen so it is not trampled or pecked.
Place shallow feed and water dishes right next to the bird so it can eat and drink without standing; birds with Marek's often die of hunger and thirst rather than the tumours.
Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer and describe the signs, the age of the birds and their vaccination history; do not start any drug without the vet's advice.
Find and keep the chick purchase receipt and hatchery vaccination certificate, and write down the dates and numbers of sick and dead birds.
Keep freshly dead birds whole in a sealed bag in a cool place or fridge, not frozen, so the vet can do a post-mortem.
Stop moving birds off or onto the farm, and do not sell sick or culled birds at the market, where they would spread the virus.
Reduce dust and stress in the house: improve ventilation without creating cold draughts, avoid crowding, and do not add new chicks to this house.
Wear a dust mask and separate shoes or overalls in the house, wash hands afterwards, and look after the youngest birds before the sick ones, never the other way round.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no treatment that cures Marek's disease. It is caused by a virus, so antibiotics do not kill it, and herbal or other remedies have not been shown to reverse the nerve damage or tumours. Once a bird is paralysed, blind or wasting, it rarely recovers, and the vet will usually advise culling it humanely to end its suffering and reduce the amount of virus it sheds. The vet's main job is to confirm the diagnosis, rule out notifiable diseases such as Newcastle disease, and plan how to protect the rest of the flock and future batches. Sometimes affected birds also have secondary bacterial infections or coccidiosis because their immunity is weak, and a vet may prescribe treatment for those. Any antibiotic or other drug must be prescribed by a vet, used exactly as directed, and only when there is a real bacterial infection, because careless antibiotic use breeds antimicrobial resistance (germs that drugs no longer kill), which harms animal and human health. Respect the egg and meat withdrawal periods on the label or given by your vet, meaning the time you must wait after treatment before eating or selling eggs or meat. Vaccinating birds that are already sick or already several weeks old will not help them, because they have already met the virus. Expect the vet to focus on prevention: checking your chick source, vaccine handling, brooding practices and cleaning.
prevention: Vaccinate every chick against Marek's at day old or in the egg at the hatchery; this is the single most important step. The vaccine does not stop infection or shedding, but it greatly reduces paralysis, tumours and deaths.
Buy chicks only from registered, reputable hatcheries, ask for a written Marek's vaccination record, and avoid buying unvaccinated chicks or birds of unknown history from markets.

If you hatch your own kienyeji chicks, talk to your vet or agrovet about vaccinating them at day old; the vaccine usually comes in large vials that must be used within a short time after mixing, so farmer groups often arrange vaccination together through a vet.

Make sure the vaccine is handled correctly: it must be kept in the right cold chain (some types in liquid nitrogen), mixed with its own diluent, and used quickly. Poorly stored vaccine is a common cause of failure.

Protect chicks from the virus for their first two to three weeks while vaccine immunity builds: brood them in a separate, thoroughly cleaned house, far from older birds, and look after them first each day.
Practise all-in, all-out: raise one age group at a time per house, then remove all litter, sweep away dust and cobwebs, wash and disinfect, and rest the house before the next batch.
Control dust: good ventilation, dry litter and regular cleaning of walls, rafters and equipment reduce the virus load in the house.
Prevent other immune-weakening problems: vaccinate against Gumboro (infectious bursal disease) as advised, control coccidiosis, and avoid mouldy feed, since aflatoxins weaken immunity.
Feed a balanced ration with correct vitamins and minerals, and limit stress from crowding, heat, rough handling and long transport.
Apply basic biosecurity: a footbath or dedicated shoes at the house door, limited visitors, no birds returned from the market into the flock, and clean crates and egg trays.
detail.impact: Marek's disease hits Kenyan farmers at the worst time. Birds usually fall sick between 6 and 20 weeks, after the farmer has already spent heavily on chicks, feed, vaccines and labour but before pullets begin to lay or kienyeji birds reach selling weight. In unvaccinated flocks, losses can be heavy and continue for weeks. Survivors may grow poorly, start laying late or lay fewer eggs. Because the virus weakens immunity, the flock may suffer more from other diseases such as coccidiosis, respiratory infections or Gumboro, and other vaccines may work less well, adding treatment costs. Carcasses with tumours can be rejected at slaughter. Because the virus stays in dust and litter for months, the problem can return with the next batch unless vaccination and cleaning improve, which hurts confidence and income for small-scale layer and improved kienyeji farmers in particular.
detail.outlook: For an individual bird with clear signs such as paralysis, blindness or wasting, the outlook is very poor; almost all such birds die or need to be culled. A rare form causes temporary paralysis from which a bird may seem to recover, but it often relapses or develops tumours later. For the flock, the outlook depends on vaccination status, how early the chicks were exposed, the strength of the virus on the farm, the breed, and other stresses and diseases. Well-vaccinated flocks raised in clean, single-age housing usually have few or no cases. Unvaccinated flocks, or flocks where vaccine was mishandled, can keep losing birds over many weeks. The best outlook comes from fixing prevention for the next batch: correct day-old vaccination, clean separate brooding and all-in, all-out management.

faqs.q: Can I cure my paralysed chickens with antibiotics or herbal medicine?
faqs.a: No. Marek's is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not kill viruses. No medicine or herbal product is known to reverse the nerve damage and tumours. A vet may treat a secondary bacterial infection, but a paralysed bird with Marek's rarely recovers. The kindest and safest choice is usually humane culling, then putting your effort into protecting the rest of the flock and future batches.

faqs.q: My chicks were vaccinated at the hatchery. Why did they still get Marek's?
faqs.a: Vaccination greatly reduces disease but does not give 100% protection. Common reasons for failure include vaccine that was poorly stored or mixed, chicks being exposed to heavy virus in dusty or old houses before immunity developed in the first two to three weeks, mixing chicks with older birds, very strong virus strains, and other immune-weakening problems such as Gumboro or mouldy feed. Discuss your hatchery source and brooding practices with your vet.

faqs.q: Can I vaccinate my older birds now that Marek's is in the flock?
faqs.a: Generally no. The vaccine works only when given to day-old chicks or in the egg, before they meet the field virus. Birds that are several weeks old have usually already been infected, so vaccinating them will not protect them. Focus on vaccinating every new batch of chicks at day old and brooding them away from older birds.

faqs.q: Is it safe to eat eggs or meat from a flock with Marek's?
faqs.a: Marek's virus is not known to infect people. However, sick, thin or paralysed birds and carcasses with tumours should not be eaten or sold; meat inspection rejects carcasses with tumours. If any bird has been treated with antibiotics or other drugs, follow the withdrawal period given by your vet before using its eggs or meat. Always cook eggs and chicken well and wash your hands after handling birds.

faqs.q: How long does the virus stay in my poultry house?
faqs.a: The virus can survive in dry dust, feather dander and old litter for many months. That is why new chicks placed in a poorly cleaned house often get infected. After a batch with Marek's, remove all litter, sweep away dust from walls, rafters and equipment, wash and disinfect, and rest the house before bringing in new, vaccinated chicks.

faqs.q: Can Marek's pass from the hen to the chick through the egg?
faqs.a: No. Marek's is not passed through the egg, so chicks hatch free of the virus. They pick it up from dust in their surroundings, often within their first days of life. This is why day-old vaccination and clean, separate brooding are so important, especially for chicks hatched under kienyeji hens that live among older birds.

products.role: Aflatoxins from mouldy feed weaken a bird's immune system, which can make Marek's vaccination less effective and the flock more vulnerable. Adding this mycotoxin binder to feed helps reduce that extra immune stress in growing chicks and pullets. It does not prevent or treat Marek's itself and is only an aid alongside day-old vaccination, clean brooding and good feed storage.

Stress helps Marek's appear in infected flocks. This vitamin and mineral supplement can support the healthy birds in an affected flock as they recover from the stress of disease, handling and culling. It does not cure or prevent Marek's and does not replace vaccination or vet advice.

mareks-disease.imagePrompt: A young brown kienyeji pullet lying on clean wood-shaving litter in a simple Kenyan poultry house, one leg stretched straight forward and the other stretched straight back, alert but unable to stand, in soft natural daylight.
mareks-disease.seoDescription: Marek's disease in chickens: spot leg paralysis, grey eyes and tumours, and prevent it with day-old vaccination. Practical guide for Kenyan farmers.

card.headline: Wart-like scabs on comb and wattles
card.look: Small pale or yellowish bumps appear on the comb, wattles, face and around the eyes, then grow into brown or black crusty scabs like warts. Some birds also have yellow-white cheesy patches inside the mouth or throat and struggle to eat or breathe.
card.action: Separate birds with scabs or mouth lesions, make sure they can reach soft feed and clean water, and call your vet or agrovet to confirm the cause and plan vaccination for the rest of the flock.

aka: Chicken pox of poultry (not the human disease)
Wet pox or diphtheritic pox (mouth and throat form)
detail.summary: Fowl pox is a slow-spreading viral disease of chickens, turkeys and other birds. It causes wart-like scabs on the bare skin of the head (dry form) and, in some birds, yellow cheesy patches in the mouth, throat and windpipe (wet form). Most birds with only the dry form recover in a few weeks, but the wet form can block breathing and feeding and kill birds. The disease cuts egg production and growth, yet it is easy to prevent with a cheap vaccine and good mosquito control.
detail.cause: Fowl pox is caused by fowlpox virus, a member of the Avipoxvirus group. It is a large, very tough virus that can survive for months in dried scabs, dust and poultry house litter. The virus cannot pass through healthy, unbroken skin. It enters through small breaks in the skin, such as mosquito bites, pecking wounds, fighting injuries or scratches, or through the lining of the mouth, eyes and upper airway. Once inside, it multiplies in the skin cells, making them swell and pile up into raised nodules. These nodules dry out and turn into dark scabs, which is the dry form. When the virus infects the moist lining of the mouth, throat, windpipe (trachea) or eyes, it forms thick yellow-white membranes stuck to the tissue, which is the wet or diphtheritic form (diphtheritic means a tough false membrane forms on a moist surface). These membranes can make swallowing painful and can partly block the airway, so birds may starve or suffocate. Damaged skin and membranes also let bacteria in, which can make the illness worse.
spread: Mosquitoes are the main way fowl pox spreads between birds and between farms: a mosquito that bites an infected bird can carry the virus on its mouthparts for weeks and pass it to every bird it bites afterwards.
Other biting insects and mites, such as red mites and some flies, can also carry the virus mechanically from bird to bird.
Direct contact spreads the virus when birds peck at each other's scabs or fight, especially in crowded houses where pecking and injuries are common.
Scabs drop off infected birds into litter, dust and soil, where the virus can stay infectious for many months and infect birds through small wounds or by being breathed in.
Contaminated feeders, drinkers, crates, egg trays, clothing and footwear can carry the virus from an infected house to a clean one.
Buying in new or recovered birds from markets or other farms without quarantine can bring the virus onto a farm, because some birds may be carrying it without obvious signs.
Wild birds and free-roaming village chickens that mix with your flock can share the virus, mainly through the mosquitoes that bite all of them.
detail.atRisk: Birds of any age can catch fowl pox, but unvaccinated growers and young layers are most commonly affected, and chicks from vaccinated or recovered parents may be protected for only a short time. Chickens and turkeys are the main poultry species affected; pigeons, quails and other birds have their own pox viruses that may or may not cross over. In Kenya and East Africa, cases rise during and just after the long and short rains, when standing water lets mosquitoes breed in large numbers. Free-range and semi-free-range kienyeji chickens are at high risk because they are exposed to mosquitoes at dusk and mix with other village birds, and they are often not vaccinated. Overcrowded houses with feather pecking, poor ventilation and old litter also have more cases. Birds weakened by poor nutrition, especially low vitamin A, by parasites or by other diseases such as Gumboro (infectious bursal disease) or Marek's disease tend to suffer more severe pox, including the wet form.

early: Small white, grey or yellowish raised spots appear on bare skin, mainly the comb, wattles, earlobes, face and eyelids, and sometimes on the legs or under the wings.
The spots grow over a few days into larger lumps that look like warts and change colour to brown or black as they dry.
Some birds have watery or swollen eyes, and the eyelids may start to stick together if scabs form at the eye edge.
Birds may look slightly dull, eat a little less and stand apart, although many birds with mild dry pox carry on eating almost normally.
In laying flocks, the first sign the farmer notices may be a slow drop in the number of eggs collected each day.
Inside the mouth, small white or yellow raised spots may be seen on the tongue, corners of the beak or roof of the mouth if you gently open the beak in good light.
advanced: Thick crusty scabs cover large parts of the comb, wattles and face, and may join together into rough masses that crack or bleed slightly.
Scabs around the eyes can close one or both eyes, so the bird cannot see to find feed and water and loses weight quickly.
In the wet form, yellow-white cheesy patches stick firmly to the mouth, tongue, throat and sometimes the windpipe, and they leave a raw surface if pulled off.
Birds with the wet form breathe with an open beak, gasp, make rattling or wheezing sounds and stretch their necks to get air.
Affected birds have a bad smell from the mouth, drool, shake their heads and pick at feed but cannot swallow it, so they become thin and weak.
Egg production can fall sharply in laying flocks, and growth in young birds slows clearly.
Some birds with severe wet pox die from suffocation or starvation, and deaths are higher when other infections are present at the same time.

lookalikes.name: Infectious laryngotracheitis (ILT)
lookalikes.howToTell: ILT also causes gasping, coughing and cheesy material in the windpipe, and wet pox in the throat can look very similar. In ILT, birds often cough up blood-stained mucus and there are usually no wart-like scabs on the comb and wattles. If the same flock has scabs on the head as well as breathing problems, fowl pox is more likely, but a vet and laboratory are needed to be sure.

lookalikes.name: Vitamin A deficiency
lookalikes.howToTell: Lack of vitamin A causes small white pimple-like spots in the mouth, throat and gullet, dull feathers and sticky eyes, and can look like early wet pox. These spots are usually many tiny pustules that are not firmly stuck down, there are no scabs on the comb, and the problem builds up slowly across birds on the same poor diet rather than spreading during the rainy season.

lookalikes.name: Wounds from pecking or fighting
lookalikes.howToTell: Cocks fighting and feather pecking leave scabs on the comb and wattles too. These are usually cuts or scratches in lines or patches, they appear quickly after fights, and they heal without new spots forming. Pox lesions start as raised bumps, grow over days, and appear on many birds, including ones that do not fight.

lookalikes.name: Mouth canker (candidiasis or trichomoniasis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Fungal thrush (candidiasis) and trichomoniasis cause whitish or cheesy growths in the mouth and crop. Thrush often follows long antibiotic use and affects the crop with a thick white 'towel-like' lining; trichomoniasis is common in pigeons and can spread to chickens through shared water. Neither causes scabs on the comb, and a vet can tell them apart by examining samples under a microscope.

detail.diagnosis: A vet can usually recognise fowl pox from the typical scabs on the comb, wattles and face, especially when several birds are affected during the rainy season. The wet form is harder, because cheesy throat lesions can be caused by other diseases such as infectious laryngotracheitis or vitamin A deficiency. To confirm, the vet may take scabs or pieces of the mouth lesions and send them to a veterinary laboratory, such as a county or regional veterinary investigation laboratory or the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete. There the tissue can be examined under a microscope for the large inclusion bodies typical of pox virus (clumps of virus inside infected cells), tested by PCR (a test that detects the virus's genetic material) or grown in fertile eggs. A post-mortem on a bird that has died or been culled lets the vet look at the throat, windpipe and other organs and check for other diseases at the same time. Before the vet arrives, write down how many birds are affected and when signs started, the age and number of birds, vaccination history including the date and batch of any pox vaccine, recent new birds, egg production records and any deaths. Keep a sick or freshly dead bird cool (not frozen) in a sealed bag if the vet asks for one.
firstSteps: Separate birds with scabs or mouth lesions into a clean, dry pen away from the main flock, so other birds cannot peck at their scabs.
Provide fresh clean water and soft, moist feed such as wet mash in shallow containers so that birds with sore mouths or closed eyes can still eat and drink.
Keep sick birds in a quiet, shaded, well-ventilated place, protected from cold, rain and strong sun, so they use their energy to recover.
Do not pick, peel or scrape scabs or the yellow mouth patches yourself, because this causes bleeding and pain and releases more virus into the house.
Reduce mosquitoes at once by draining standing water around the house, clearing long grass, and using mosquito netting on windows of the poultry house, especially at dusk.
Collect fallen scabs, old litter and feathers carefully and burn or bury them, and wash and disinfect feeders and drinkers.
Stop selling, buying or moving birds to and from the farm until the vet has assessed the flock, and wash hands and change footwear after handling sick birds.
Call your vet, County Veterinary Officer or a trusted agrovet to confirm the diagnosis and ask whether the healthy birds in the flock should be vaccinated now.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no medicine that kills the fowl pox virus, and antibiotics do not cure it. Treatment is about helping birds through the illness, stopping spread and protecting the rest of the flock. A vet will usually advise good supportive care: soft feed, clean water, vitamins (especially vitamin A, which helps skin and mouth lining heal) and a calm, clean environment. The vet may recommend a mild antiseptic for skin scabs on selected birds, or may carefully treat mouth lesions in valuable birds; this should be done or shown by the vet, because rough removal causes bleeding and more harm. If bacteria have infected the scabs or airway, the vet may prescribe an antibiotic for a limited time. Use antibiotics only when a vet prescribes them, use the exact product and course given, and never use them 'just in case', because misuse breeds antimicrobial resistance (germs that no longer respond to medicines), which harms animal and human health. When any drug is used, follow the egg and meat withdrawal periods on the label and from the vet, and do not sell or eat eggs or meat from treated birds until that time has passed. In an outbreak, the vet will often recommend vaccinating birds that are not yet showing signs with live fowl pox vaccine, given by the wing-web stab method; this can slow the outbreak in the flock. Birds with severe wet pox that cannot breathe or eat may be humanely culled on the vet's advice to prevent suffering. Expect skin scabs to take a few weeks to dry and fall off.
prevention: Vaccinate every flock with live fowl pox vaccine, available from agrovets and produced locally, following the age and method advised by your vet or the vaccine label; it is usually given by pricking the wing web with a special two-pronged needle.

Check the vaccination site about a week after vaccinating: a small swelling or scab (called a 'take') shows the vaccine worked, and birds with no take may need to be re-vaccinated on your vet's advice.
Handle vaccine carefully: keep it cold, mix it just before use, use it all within the time on the label, and do not let vaccine splash onto the comb, face or eyes, where it can cause pox lesions.

Control mosquitoes, especially before and during the long and short rains, by draining puddles, clearing blocked drains and old tyres or containers, cutting long grass near the house and using netting on poultry house openings.
Bring free-range kienyeji chickens into a secure house before dusk, when mosquitoes are most active, and use clean, dry litter.
Prevent feather pecking and fighting by avoiding overcrowding, providing enough feeders and drinkers, separating aggressive cocks and giving birds perches and space.
Quarantine new birds for at least two weeks away from your flock, check them for scabs and mouth lesions, and buy from trusted, vaccinated sources where possible.
Feed a balanced ration with enough vitamin A and other vitamins, and control worms, mites and other diseases so birds' immune systems stay strong.
detail.impact: Fowl pox rarely wipes out a flock the way Newcastle disease can, but it quietly costs Kenyan farmers a lot. Layers often drop in egg production for several weeks, which directly cuts daily income on farms that sell trays of eggs. Growing birds and broilers eat less and grow more slowly, so they take longer to reach market weight and feed costs rise. The wet form can cause deaths, especially in unvaccinated kienyeji flocks and when birds also have other infections. Birds with scabby heads look sick and fetch lower prices at local markets, and some buyers will refuse them. Extra costs include labour for nursing sick birds, vitamins, vet visits, antibiotics for secondary infections and vaccination during the outbreak. Compared with these losses, routine fowl pox vaccination and mosquito control are very cheap.
detail.outlook: Most birds with only the dry skin form recover on their own, with scabs usually drying and falling off over about two to four weeks. Recovered birds normally develop strong, long-lasting immunity to fowl pox. The wet form is more serious: birds with large membranes in the throat or windpipe may die from suffocation or starvation, and recovery is slower. The outlook is better when birds are kept eating and drinking, when secondary bacterial infections are controlled, and when the rest of the flock is vaccinated early in the outbreak. It is worse in birds that are young, poorly fed, low in vitamin A, infested with parasites or suffering from other diseases at the same time. The virus stays in scabs and litter for months, so new unvaccinated birds placed on the same farm can catch it unless the house is cleaned and vaccination is kept up.

faqs.q: Can I eat eggs or meat from chickens with fowl pox?
faqs.a: Fowl pox does not infect people, so the disease itself is not a danger to humans. However, very sick birds should not be slaughtered for food, and any bird or egg from a bird treated with antibiotics or other drugs must not be sold or eaten until the withdrawal period given by your vet or the label has passed. Always cook poultry and eggs well as normal good practice.

faqs.q: My birds already have fowl pox. Is it too late to vaccinate?
faqs.a: It is not too late for the healthy birds. Vets often recommend vaccinating birds that do not yet show signs during an outbreak, because this can protect many of them before the virus reaches them. Vaccination will not cure birds that are already sick, and some vaccinated birds may still develop mild disease. Ask your vet to check the flock and advise which birds to vaccinate.

faqs.q: Should I remove the scabs or yellow patches in the mouth?
faqs.a: No, not by yourself. Pulling off scabs or mouth patches causes bleeding, pain and raw areas that bacteria can infect, and it spreads virus into the house. Scabs will dry and fall off on their own. If a valuable bird has mouth or throat lesions that stop it eating or breathing, ask your vet to examine it and advise what is safe.

faqs.q: Why do my chickens get fowl pox mostly during the rains?
faqs.a: The rains create puddles and standing water where mosquitoes breed. Mosquitoes are the main carriers of fowl pox, picking up the virus from one bird and passing it on to others for weeks. This is why outbreaks are common during and after the long and short rains, especially in free-range flocks. Vaccinating before the rains and controlling mosquitoes around the house greatly lowers the risk.

faqs.q: Will antibiotics cure fowl pox?
faqs.a: No. Fowl pox is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not kill viruses. A vet may sometimes prescribe an antibiotic if bacteria have infected the scabs or throat, but using antibiotics without good reason wastes money, leaves residues in eggs and meat, and helps create germs that medicines can no longer treat. Focus on nursing, vaccination and mosquito control.

faqs.q: Can a bird get fowl pox again after it recovers?
faqs.a: Birds that recover from fowl pox usually have strong, long-lasting immunity to it, so a second bout is uncommon. Vaccinated birds are also well protected when the vaccine 'takes' properly. The bigger risk is to new, unvaccinated birds you bring onto the farm, because the virus can remain in old scabs and litter for months. Vaccinate each new batch and clean the house well between flocks.

products.role: Liquid vitamin and mineral supplement that can be added to drinking water to support birds recovering from the stress of fowl pox, helping appetite, condition and laying performance while scabs heal; vitamins such as vitamin A support healthy skin and mouth lining. Use alongside vaccination, mosquito control and your vet's advice, not as a cure for the virus.

Oral rehydration solution to help keep sick birds drinking and hydrated when sore mouths, closed eyes or fever reduce their intake of feed and water, supporting recovery while the flock is nursed and assessed by a vet.

fowl-pox.imagePrompt: Close-up photo of a brown kienyeji hen in a simple Kenyan poultry house, showing dark brown wart-like scabs and raised yellowish bumps on her red comb, wattles and around one eye, in natural daylight.
fowl-pox.seoDescription: Fowl pox in chickens: spot wart-like scabs on comb and yellow mouth plaques, act before the vet comes, and prevent it with vaccination and mosquito control.

card.headline: Bloody droppings and hunched, ruffled chicks
card.look: Young birds stand hunched with ruffled feathers and half-closed eyes, with blood-stained, watery or mucus-filled droppings on wet litter. Combs and wattles look pale and the birds eat less and grow slowly.
card.action: Separate sick birds, replace wet litter with dry bedding, and call your vet or agrovet animal health officer quickly so treatment starts before more birds die.

aka: Caecal coccidiosis (when the caeca are affected)
detail.summary: Coccidiosis is a gut disease of poultry caused by tiny single-celled parasites called Eimeria. It damages the lining of the intestines, so birds bleed into the gut, cannot absorb feed well, grow poorly and may die. It is one of the most common and costly poultry diseases in Kenya, especially in broilers, layer chicks and kienyeji chicks kept on damp litter or wet ground. Fast action and good litter management save birds and money.
detail.cause: Coccidiosis is caused by protozoa, which are microscopic single-celled parasites, of the genus Eimeria. Several species infect chickens, and each attacks a different part of the gut. Eimeria tenella attacks the caeca, the two blind pouches near the end of the gut, and causes the classic bright red, bloody droppings. Eimeria necatrix attacks the middle of the small intestine and can kill older growers. Others, such as Eimeria acervulina, Eimeria maxima and Eimeria brunetti, cause watery, mucus-filled or orange-tinged droppings, poor growth and poor feed conversion, sometimes without obvious blood. A bird becomes infected when it swallows oocysts, the tough egg-like stage of the parasite, from litter, soil, feed or water. Inside the gut the parasite invades the cells lining the intestine and multiplies many times over, bursting those cells. This destroys the gut lining, causing bleeding, fluid loss and poor absorption of nutrients. Within about a week the bird passes huge numbers of new oocysts in its droppings, which then become infective in warm, moist litter within a day or two. The damaged gut also lets harmful bacteria, especially Clostridium perfringens, take hold, which can lead to a second disease called necrotic enteritis. Chicken Eimeria species are host-specific, meaning they infect chickens but not turkeys, ducks or other livestock, and those birds have their own Eimeria species.
spread: Birds swallow oocysts when they peck at contaminated litter, soil or droppings, which is how almost all infections start.
Wet, caked litter is the main trigger, because warmth and moisture let oocysts mature and become infective within one to two days.
Leaking drinkers, spilt water, rain coming through the roof or walls, and overcrowding all make litter wet and raise the infection pressure in the house.
Oocysts are carried between houses and farms on boots, crates, feed bags, equipment, wheelbarrows, wild birds, rodents and insects such as darkling beetles.

Oocysts are very hardy and can survive in soil and old litter for months, and many common disinfectants do not kill them, so reusing old litter or a poorly cleaned house carries infection to the next flock.
Stress from poor ventilation, heat, sudden feed changes, vaccination, moving birds, or other diseases such as Gumboro lowers immunity and lets an outbreak break out.
Kienyeji and free-range birds pick up oocysts from wet ground around the homestead, especially near drinkers, under roosting trees and in muddy runs during the rains.
detail.atRisk: Young birds are most at risk, especially chicks and growers between about three and six weeks of age, although outbreaks can happen from around two weeks old up to point-of-lay if birds have not built immunity. Broilers on deep litter, layer and kienyeji chicks being raised for replacement, and improved kienyeji birds kept in confined houses are commonly affected. Birds moved from cages or slatted floors onto litter or the ground for the first time can also fall sick because they have no immunity. Outbreaks peak during the long and short rains, when humidity is high, roofs leak and litter stays wet. Overstocked houses, poorly ventilated structures, flocks fed without an anticoccidial or coccidiosis vaccine programme, and farms that reuse litter or do not rest houses between batches face higher risk. Birds weakened by Gumboro (infectious bursal disease), mycotoxins in mouldy feed, poor nutrition or worms are more likely to get severe coccidiosis.

early: Birds look dull, sleepy and stand hunched with ruffled feathers and drooping wings.
Feed and water intake drop, and birds crowd near the heat source or stand still in corners.
Droppings become watery, mucus-filled, frothy or orange-tinged, and may show streaks of blood.
Litter around drinkers and feeders becomes wet and smelly more quickly than usual.
Uneven growth appears in the flock, with some birds clearly smaller than their batch mates.
Vent feathers become soiled and pasted with droppings.
advanced: Droppings turn bright red or dark, tarry and bloody, often with clots or mucus.
Combs, wattles, face and legs become very pale because of blood loss and anaemia.
Birds become weak, lie down, stop eating completely and may shiver or appear dehydrated with sunken eyes.
Growth stops, birds lose weight and feathers look rough, and layer pullets may be delayed in coming into lay.
Sudden deaths rise over a few days, sometimes with many birds dying in a short time in an unprotected flock.
Birds that survive may stay stunted and convert feed poorly for weeks because the gut lining has been damaged.

lookalikes.name: Necrotic enteritis
lookalikes.howToTell: This bacterial disease often follows coccidiosis. Birds die very suddenly, droppings are dark and foul-smelling, and at post-mortem the small intestine is swollen with a rough, yellow-brown, towel-like lining. A vet can tell the two apart, and both may be present together.

lookalikes.name: Gumboro (infectious bursal disease)
lookalikes.howToTell: Gumboro also hits birds of around three to six weeks, but droppings are usually whitish and watery rather than bloody, birds peck at their vents, and deaths rise and fall within about a week. At post-mortem the bursa, a small organ near the vent, is swollen, yellow or bloody, and there may be bleeding in the thigh and breast muscles.

lookalikes.name: Newcastle disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Newcastle disease affects birds of all ages, not only young growers, and usually causes greenish watery droppings, breathing problems, twisted necks, paralysis and a sharp drop in eggs. It spreads very fast and kills many birds. It is notifiable, so if you see nervous or breathing signs, report to your County Veterinary Officer.

lookalikes.name: Pullorum and other salmonella infections
lookalikes.howToTell: These mainly affect very young chicks in the first two to three weeks, with white, chalky, pasted vents, huddling and deaths soon after hatching. Droppings are white rather than bloody, and a lab test is needed to confirm.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or animal health officer usually suspects coccidiosis from the age of the birds, the bloody or mucoid droppings, wet litter and the pattern of deaths. The most reliable confirmation is a post-mortem examination of freshly dead or sick birds, where the vet opens the gut and looks for typical damage: swollen caeca filled with blood and clots, or a thickened, spotted, bloody or ballooned small intestine, depending on the Eimeria species. The vet may scrape the gut lining and look under a microscope for parasite stages. Faecal tests to count oocysts can help, but the number of oocysts does not always match how sick the birds are, so lesions and signs matter more. County veterinary laboratories and Kenya's regional veterinary investigation laboratories can help where a local vet lacks equipment. To help, keep two or three freshly dead or very sick birds cool, not frozen, in a sealed bag, and write down the age of the flock, number of birds, daily deaths, feed type and whether it contains an anticoccidial, vaccines given, and when signs started.
firstSteps: Separate visibly sick, hunched or bleeding birds into a clean, dry, warm pen so they are not trampled and are less exposed to oocysts.
Remove wet, caked litter, especially around drinkers and feeders, and replace it with fresh, dry wood shavings or other dry bedding.
Fix leaking drinkers, raise drinkers slightly, and repair roofs or walls letting rain in so the litter stays dry.
Make sure all birds have clean, fresh drinking water at all times, because sick birds lose a lot of fluid and dehydrate quickly.
Improve ventilation without creating cold draughts, and keep chicks warm, because chilled birds huddle and get sicker.
Reduce crowding if the house is overstocked by spreading birds out or moving some to another clean space.
Wear boots and clothes used only in that house, wash hands after handling birds or litter, and stop visitors and equipment moving between poultry houses.
Record the number of sick and dead birds each day, keep a few fresh carcasses cool for the vet, and call your vet or animal health officer promptly. Do not start drugs before speaking to them.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be prescribed by a vet, who will choose a drug based on the flock's age, type of production and what has been used before. Common anticoccidial drugs used in Kenya include amprolium, toltrazuril, diclazuril and sulfonamides such as sulfadimidine or sulfaquinoxaline, usually given through the drinking water so that the whole flock is treated, because many birds are infected before they show signs. Sulfonamides are antimicrobials, so use them only when prescribed and for the full course, because misuse adds to antimicrobial resistance, where drugs stop working for animals and people. The vet may also advise treating secondary bacterial infection such as necrotic enteritis if it is confirmed. Supportive care is important: clean water, dry litter, good feed and vitamin support, especially vitamins A and K, which help repair the gut and blood clotting. Ask your vet about the timing of vitamin supplements, because some, such as high doses of vitamin B1 (thiamine), can reduce how well amprolium works. Every drug has a withdrawal period, the time you must wait after the last treatment before selling or eating meat or eggs, and many anticoccidials are not allowed at all in laying hens producing eggs for eating. Follow the vet's and label's withdrawal instructions strictly. With early treatment, deaths usually slow within a few days, but damaged birds may take a week or more to start growing well again, and some stay stunted. Parasites can become resistant to anticoccidials when the same drug is used repeatedly, so your vet may rotate products between flocks.
prevention: Keep litter dry at all times by using enough clean bedding, fixing leaking drinkers, adjusting drinker height as birds grow, turning litter regularly and removing wet patches immediately.

Clean out all old litter after each flock, scrub and wash the house, let it dry fully and rest it before new chicks arrive, because oocysts survive many disinfectants and need thorough cleaning, drying and time to reduce their numbers.

Use either an anticoccidial programme in the feed (broiler and chick feeds from reputable millers often contain one; check the label) or a live coccidiosis vaccine given to chicks, as advised by your vet. Do not combine a vaccine with in-feed anticoccidials unless your vet says so, because the drug can stop the vaccine working.
Avoid overcrowding and follow recommended stocking density for your house size and bird type, with good ventilation that removes moisture and ammonia without chilling chicks.
Vaccinate against Gumboro and Newcastle disease on schedule, because these diseases weaken immunity and make coccidiosis far worse.
Feed a balanced, fresh, mould-free feed with adequate vitamins and minerals, and store feed off the floor in a dry place to avoid mycotoxins.
Practise biosecurity with house-specific footwear or a foot dip, limited visitors, control of rodents and wild birds, and raising one age group per house where possible, ideally all-in, all-out.

For kienyeji and free-range birds, keep chicks in a dry brooder for the first weeks, move drinkers often so the ground around them does not stay muddy, and keep chicks away from muddy runs during the rains.
detail.impact: Coccidiosis is one of the biggest causes of losses on Kenyan poultry farms. Deaths can be heavy in unprotected broiler or chick flocks, and the survivors often grow slowly and eat more feed for every kilogram of weight gained, which hits profit on broilers sold by weight. Uneven flocks fetch lower prices from buyers and hotels. Layer and kienyeji pullets damaged as growers may start laying late and produce fewer eggs. Farmers also pay for drugs, extra litter, vet visits and labour, and may have to delay sales because of drug withdrawal periods. Even mild, unseen coccidiosis quietly reduces weight gain across the flock, so the true cost is often higher than the number of dead birds suggests.
detail.humanHealth: Chicken coccidiosis does not infect people, because chicken Eimeria parasites only infect chickens. The main human risk is drug residues: meat or eggs from birds treated with anticoccidials or sulfonamides must not be eaten or sold until the full withdrawal period has passed, and many of these drugs are not permitted in hens laying eggs for human consumption. Always wash hands after handling sick birds, droppings or litter, as poultry droppings can carry other germs such as Salmonella.
detail.outlook: The outlook is generally good when coccidiosis is spotted early, the vet confirms it and the whole flock is treated while litter and housing problems are corrected. Deaths usually slow within a few days of starting correct treatment. The outlook is poorer when bloody droppings have been present for several days, many birds are already pale and weak, the flock also has Gumboro, necrotic enteritis or mycotoxin problems, or the litter stays wet. Birds that recover develop immunity to the Eimeria species they met, but they may remain stunted. Outbreaks are likely to return in the next batch unless litter management, cleaning and a prevention programme are improved.

faqs.q: Why do my chicks keep getting coccidiosis every rainy season?
faqs.a: During the long and short rains, humidity rises, roofs and walls often leak and litter stays damp. Wet, warm litter is exactly what coccidiosis oocysts need to become infective, so infection pressure jumps. Before the rains, repair roofs, raise and fix drinkers, add extra dry bedding and plan a vaccine or anticoccidial feed programme with your vet.

faqs.q: Can I treat coccidiosis with antibiotics from the agrovet without seeing a vet?
faqs.a: It is not wise. Several different diseases cause similar signs, and the wrong drug wastes money while birds keep dying. Some anticoccidials, such as sulfonamides, are also antimicrobials, and using them without proper diagnosis drives drug resistance. Withdrawal periods and rules for layers also matter. Call a vet or animal health officer so they can confirm the problem and prescribe the right product for your birds.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell eggs and meat from birds during treatment?
faqs.a: Not until the withdrawal period on the product label, or given by your vet, has passed. Many anticoccidial drugs are not allowed in laying hens producing eggs for eating at all, so tell your vet if your birds are laying. Eating or selling products too early can leave drug residues that may harm consumers.

faqs.q: Will my older birds or my ducks catch it from the sick chicks?
faqs.a: Chicken coccidiosis only infects chickens, so ducks, turkeys, goats and cattle will not catch it from your chicks, though they have their own types. Older chickens usually have some immunity from earlier exposure, but they can still carry and shed oocysts, which is a reason to raise chicks away from adult birds.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine for coccidiosis?
faqs.a: Yes, live coccidiosis vaccines exist and are usually given to young chicks in water, feed or by spray, so they build immunity gradually. They are mainly used for layer and breeder replacement birds. Availability in Kenya varies, so ask your vet or a large agrovet. Vaccines need correct handling and should not be used together with in-feed anticoccidials unless your vet advises it.

faqs.q: Does starter feed with a coccidiostat mean I don't need to worry?
faqs.a: It helps a lot, but it is not a guarantee. A coccidiostat is a drug in the feed that controls the parasite. It can be overwhelmed if litter is very wet or the house is overcrowded, and parasites can become resistant. Keep litter dry, avoid overcrowding, and still watch droppings daily, calling the vet early if you see blood.

products.role: A probiotic that supports a healthy balance of gut bacteria. Used as part of a prevention plan, alongside dry litter, good hygiene and the vaccine or anticoccidial programme your vet recommends, it can help the gut cope with coccidial challenge. During recovery it can help the gut return to normal. It is a support, not a treatment for an active outbreak, which needs a vet-prescribed anticoccidial.

A liquid vitamin and mineral supplement that can support appetite and stress recovery once the vet's treatment is under way, helping weakened birds regain condition after gut damage and blood loss. Ask your vet about timing, as some vitamins, especially vitamin B1, can interfere with amprolium if given at the same time.

coccidiosis.imagePrompt: A realistic close-up photo of a hunched, ruffled young broiler chick with a pale comb standing on damp wood-shaving litter beside a few blood-streaked droppings inside a simple Kenyan poultry house.
coccidiosis.seoDescription: Coccidiosis in chickens: spot bloody droppings, hunched birds and wet litter early. Learn causes, first steps, vet treatment and prevention for Kenyan farms.

card.headline: Foamy eyes and rattling, wet breathing
card.look: Birds sneeze, cough and make a gurgling or rattling sound when breathing, often loudest at night. You may see bubbly froth in the corner of the eye, a sticky nose and a puffy swelling of the face below the eye.
card.action: Separate the sick birds, improve ventilation and cut ammonia and dust in the house, and call your vet or County Veterinary Officer before giving any medicine.

aka: Air sac disease (when complicated by E. coli)
Mafua ya kuku (a general Swahili term for poultry colds)
detail.summary: Chronic respiratory disease (CRD) is a long-lasting infection of the airways in chickens, turkeys and other birds, caused by a tiny bacterium called Mycoplasma gallisepticum (MG). It rarely kills many birds on its own, but it spreads slowly through the flock, lowers egg production, slows broiler growth and wastes feed. Infected birds usually stay carriers for life, and hens can pass the infection to chicks through the egg. This makes CRD one of the most costly and stubborn poultry problems on Kenyan farms.
detail.cause: CRD is caused by Mycoplasma gallisepticum, a very small bacterium that has no cell wall. Because it has no cell wall, some common antibiotics such as penicillin and amoxicillin cannot kill it. The organism attaches to the lining of the nose, sinuses (the air spaces in the face around the eyes), windpipe and air sacs (thin balloon-like bags in the body that help birds breathe). There it damages the tiny hairs that normally sweep dust and germs out of the airways. The airways become inflamed and fill with mucus, which causes sneezing, rattling and swelling of the face. Once the natural cleaning system is damaged, other germs move in easily, especially E. coli bacteria and viruses such as infectious bronchitis and Newcastle disease. This mixed infection is called 'complicated CRD' and is far more serious. Cheesy yellow pus can build up in the air sacs and over the heart and liver, and birds may die. Infected birds rarely clear the organism completely. They become carriers that look healthy but shed the germ again whenever they are stressed.
spread: Through the egg: infected hens can pass MG into the egg, so chicks hatch already infected. This is why buying chicks from an MG-free hatchery matters so much.
Through the air: sick and carrier birds release the germ in droplets when they sneeze and cough, and nearby birds breathe it in.
By direct contact: birds sharing drinkers, feeders and perches pass the germ to each other through nasal discharge.

On people, equipment and crates: the germ can survive for a short time, often a few days, on feathers, clothing, egg trays, crates and dust. Visitors, traders and shared equipment can carry it between farms.
By bringing in new birds: buying birds from markets, or mixing kienyeji birds of unknown health with your flock, is a very common way the disease enters a farm.

Through stress that 'wakes up' carriers: cold nights, poor ventilation, high ammonia, dusty litter, overcrowding, transport, onset of lay and live respiratory vaccines can make carrier birds sick and start shedding again.
Wild birds and other poultry such as turkeys, ducks and guinea fowl kept with chickens may carry the infection, although the role of wild birds varies.
detail.atRisk: All ages of chickens and turkeys can be infected, but signs are usually worst in growing birds of about 4 to 12 weeks, in broilers, and in layers around the start of lay. Turkeys often develop very swollen sinuses. Disease is more common in the cold months of June to August and during the long and short rains, when houses are closed up, damp and full of ammonia. Farms that mix birds from many sources, keep different ages together, buy from markets or keep chickens with turkeys and ducks face higher risk. Commercial layer and broiler houses with poor ventilation are at risk, and so are free-range kienyeji flocks where many villagers' birds mix. Birds with other infections, worms, poor nutrition or mycotoxins (poisons from mouldy feed) get sicker.

early: Occasional sneezing and head shaking, often heard first at night when the house is quiet.
Wet, rattling or gurgling breathing sounds (called 'rales'), which you hear best by holding a bird close to your ear.
Clear, watery discharge from the nostrils, with feed or dust sticking around the nose.
Watery or slightly foamy eyes, with small bubbles in the corner of the eye.
A slight drop in feed intake and water intake in part of the flock.
A gradual fall in egg numbers in layers, or broilers growing more slowly than expected.
Only a few birds affected at first, with more birds slowly showing signs over several weeks.
advanced: Puffy swelling of the face below and in front of the eye from swollen sinuses, sometimes making the eye look half closed. This is very marked in turkeys.
Thick, sticky or cheesy discharge from the nose and eyes, with eyelids stuck together.
Open-mouth breathing, gasping and stretching the neck to breathe.
Birds sitting hunched with ruffled feathers, losing weight and with a pale comb.
A clear fall in egg production, and more small or poor-quality eggs.
Uneven, stunted broilers and more birds condemned or downgraded at slaughter.
Deaths rising when E. coli or a virus joins in, with cheesy yellow pus in the air sacs and over the heart and liver at post-mortem.

lookalikes.name: Infectious coryza
lookalikes.howToTell: Coryza spreads much faster, often through a whole house within a few days. The face and wattles swell quickly, and the nasal discharge often has a strong, foul smell. CRD spreads slowly over weeks and the discharge usually does not smell bad. Both diseases can occur together, so a lab test helps.

lookalikes.name: Infectious bronchitis (IB)
lookalikes.howToTell: IB is a virus that sweeps through the whole flock within a few days, with coughing and rattling. In layers it causes thin, soft, wrinkled or misshapen eggshells and watery egg whites. CRD spreads more slowly, lasts longer and is more likely to cause swollen sinuses. IB often triggers CRD in carrier flocks.

lookalikes.name: Newcastle disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Newcastle usually causes sudden, heavy deaths, greenish watery diarrhoea, and nervous signs such as twisted necks, circling or paralysis, along with breathing problems. CRD on its own causes few deaths and no nervous signs. Suspected Newcastle needs a vet urgently.

lookalikes.name: Vitamin A deficiency
lookalikes.howToTell: Birds may have sticky eyes and nasal discharge, but you also see small white spots or pimples in the mouth and throat, and the problem links to poor or old feed rather than a spreading infection. It does not cause rattling breathing passing from bird to bird.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will look at the flock history, the slow spread, the breathing sounds and the facial swelling. Signs alone cannot confirm CRD because several diseases look alike. The vet will usually open one or two sick or recently dead birds (a post-mortem) to look for thickened, cloudy or foamy air sacs, mucus in the windpipe and sinuses, and in complicated cases cheesy pus over the heart and liver. To confirm MG, the vet can take blood samples for antibody tests such as the rapid plate agglutination test or ELISA. They may also take swabs from the windpipe or cleft in the roof of the mouth for PCR, a test that detects the germ's genetic material, or for culture. Labs such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete and county or university labs can help. Results take time, and blood tests can be affected by recent vaccination, so the vet will interpret them.
