You can help by preparing: the age and breed of the birds, where and when you bought them, vaccination records, feed and water intake, daily egg records, number of deaths per day, and any medicines already given. Keep two or three typical sick birds alive and separated, or chill (do not freeze) fresh carcasses for the vet.
firstSteps: Move the clearly sick birds to a separate, clean, dry pen away from the main flock, and handle them last each day.
Improve ventilation without creating cold draughts at bird level. Open upper vents or curtains in the day and reduce crowding.
Remove wet, caked litter and add fresh dry litter to cut ammonia, the sharp smell that burns the eyes and damages the airways.
Make sure all birds have clean, fresh water and fresh feed within easy reach, as sick birds eat and drink less.
Keep chicks and young birds warm at night, as cold stress makes CRD much worse.
Stop buying, selling, mixing or moving birds, and do not share crates, egg trays or equipment with neighbours until the vet has advised you.
Record how many birds are sick, how many have died each day, feed and water use and daily egg numbers, so the vet can judge how fast it is moving.

Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer, and do not give antibiotics or other drugs from the agrovet without a vet's advice, because many common antibiotics do not work on Mycoplasma and wrong use leaves residues in eggs and meat.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be prescribed by a vet. Because Mycoplasma has no cell wall, the vet will choose antibiotic groups that work against it. Commonly used options include macrolides such as tylosin and tilmicosin, pleuromutilins such as tiamulin, and tetracyclines such as doxycycline or oxytetracycline, usually given in drinking water or feed for the whole flock. Some fluoroquinolones also act against Mycoplasma, but vets reserve these important drugs carefully. Where E. coli has joined in, the vet may pick a drug that covers both. Treatment can reduce signs, deaths and egg losses, but it usually does not remove the germ completely. Treated birds often stay carriers and the disease may come back with stress. Every drug has a withdrawal period, which is the time after the last dose during which eggs and meat must not be sold or eaten. Some products are not allowed at all in layers producing eggs for people, so ask the vet and read the label. Use antibiotics only when needed, at the full course the vet prescribes, and never as a routine 'just in case' treatment. Misuse breeds antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to drugs that people and animals depend on. Alongside drugs, the vet will advise on ventilation, litter, controlling other infections and whether vaccination or replacing the flock makes sense.
prevention: Buy day-old chicks and point-of-lay birds only from reputable hatcheries and breeders that test their parent flocks for MG and can show this. This is the single most important step because the disease passes through the egg.
Run an 'all-in, all-out' system where possible. Keep one age group per house, and clean, disinfect and rest the house between flocks.
Do not mix birds of different ages or sources, and keep chickens apart from turkeys, ducks and guinea fowl.
Quarantine any new or returning birds for at least two to three weeks in a separate pen, and watch them closely before mixing.
Keep houses well ventilated but free of draughts, with dry litter, low dust and low ammonia. Avoid overcrowding.
Control other diseases that trigger CRD by following a vet-advised vaccination programme for Newcastle disease, infectious bronchitis and Gumboro, and keep worms and coccidiosis under control.
Feed a balanced ration with enough vitamins and minerals, store feed dry, and avoid mouldy feed, because mycotoxins weaken immunity.
Practise biosecurity: a footbath at the door, dedicated boots and clothes, limited visitors, clean crates and egg trays, and wild birds kept out of the house.

Ask your vet about MG vaccines. Live and inactivated vaccines exist for layer and breeder flocks on farms where MG is a known problem, but availability in Kenya varies and they must be used as part of a vet's plan.
Do not hatch eggs from a flock known to have CRD unless a vet advises it, and consider replacing a chronically infected flock with clean birds after thorough cleaning.
detail.impact: CRD rarely wipes out a flock, but it drains money slowly and steadily. Layers lay fewer eggs, and the drop can last for weeks. Broilers grow unevenly, take longer to reach market weight and eat more feed for each kilo gained. More birds may be downgraded or condemned at slaughter because of damaged air sacs. When E. coli or viruses join in, deaths can rise sharply. Farmers also spend on medicines, vet visits and lab tests, and lose sales during drug withdrawal periods when eggs and meat cannot be sold. Because birds stay carriers, the problem returns with each cold season or stress, and a farm known for CRD may struggle to sell breeding stock, fertile eggs or chicks.
detail.humanHealth: Mycoplasma gallisepticum does not infect people. It is not known to cause illness in humans, and properly cooked eggs and meat from infected flocks are not a disease risk in themselves. The main human risk comes from antibiotic residues. If eggs or meat are sold or eaten during the drug withdrawal period, drug residues can reach people, cause allergic reactions in sensitive people and add to antimicrobial resistance. Always follow the withdrawal period your vet gives and the one on the label, keep treatment records, and do not sell eggs or birds early. Wear a mask when cleaning dusty, ammonia-heavy houses, and wash your hands after handling birds, because poultry dust irritates human lungs.
detail.outlook: Most birds survive CRD, especially when it is not complicated by other infections and when housing is improved quickly. Breathing signs often settle after vet-prescribed treatment and better ventilation. However, egg production may not return fully to previous levels, and affected broilers may stay smaller. Infected birds usually remain carriers for life, so the disease can flare up again with cold, crowding, vaccination or other stress. The outlook is worse in young birds, in poorly ventilated houses, and when E. coli, infectious bronchitis or Newcastle disease join in. Long-term control depends on clean chick sources, good management and biosecurity rather than repeated medication.

faqs.q: Why does CRD keep coming back even after I treat my birds?
faqs.a: Antibiotics usually reduce the signs but rarely remove Mycoplasma completely from the flock. Treated birds become carriers that look healthy, and whenever they are stressed by cold, ammonia, crowding, vaccination or the start of lay, the germ multiplies again. Repeating antibiotics without fixing ventilation, litter and biosecurity only builds resistance. Talk to your vet about a long-term plan, which may include vaccination or replacing the flock with clean birds.

faqs.q: Can I use amoxicillin or penicillin from the agrovet?
faqs.a: These drugs do not work against Mycoplasma because they attack the bacterial cell wall, and Mycoplasma does not have one. Using them wastes money, leaves residues in eggs and meat, and adds to antimicrobial resistance. Only a vet should choose the antibiotic, after confirming that CRD is the problem.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell eggs from a flock with CRD?
faqs.a: The disease itself does not infect people, so eggs from untreated birds are safe to eat when properly cooked. The problem comes when birds are on antibiotics. You must not eat or sell eggs or meat until the withdrawal period has passed. Some antibiotics are not permitted in laying hens at all. Ask your vet and follow the label.

faqs.q: Can I hatch eggs from my own hens if some have CRD?
faqs.a: It is risky. MG passes from the hen into the egg, so chicks can hatch already infected and carry the disease into the next generation. If CRD is confirmed in your flock, ask your vet before hatching. It is usually better to buy chicks from a hatchery whose parent flocks are tested free of MG.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine for CRD in Kenya?
faqs.a: Vaccines against Mycoplasma gallisepticum do exist, both live and inactivated types. They are mainly used in layer and breeder flocks on farms where the disease is a known problem. Availability in Kenya varies, and they are not a replacement for clean chicks and good housing. Your vet can advise whether vaccination makes sense for your farm and how it fits with your Newcastle and bronchitis programme.

faqs.q: How do I know it is CRD and not Newcastle or coryza?
faqs.a: CRD spreads slowly over weeks and causes few deaths on its own. Coryza spreads within days and often has a foul-smelling discharge. Newcastle disease usually kills many birds quickly and may cause green diarrhoea and twisted necks. Because these can look alike and can occur together, your vet should examine birds and may send samples to a lab to be sure.

products.role: MIX5's plant extracts are labelled to relieve respiratory problems. It can be used in drinking water as a supportive aid to help birds breathe more comfortably and cope with stress during a CRD outbreak or after vaccination. It does not kill Mycoplasma, and it does not replace vet-prescribed treatment, better ventilation or clean chick sources.

AGRIVITAM supplies vitamins and minerals for stress recovery and layer productivity. It can help birds that are eating less during CRD keep up their nutrient intake, and it supports the flock's recovery and return to lay alongside vet care and good management. It is not a treatment for the infection itself.

crd.imagePrompt: Close-up photo of a brown layer hen in a simple Kenyan wooden poultry house, with a puffy swollen face below one eye, small foamy bubbles in the corner of the eye and a slightly wet nostril, soft natural daylight.
crd.seoDescription: Chronic respiratory disease (CRD) in chickens: recognise sneezing, rattling breath and foamy eyes, act early, work with your vet and prevent Mycoplasma.

card.headline: Swollen face with eyes stuck shut
card.look: One or both sides of the face puff up around the eye, the wattles may swell, and a sticky, bad-smelling discharge runs from the nostrils and glues the eyelids together. Many birds sneeze, eat less, and egg collection drops within days.
card.action: Separate the sick birds from the rest of the flock right away, stop buying, selling or mixing birds, and call your vet or County Veterinary Officer to confirm the cause.

aka: Roup (old name, also used loosely for other eye and sinus problems)
Haemophilus infection (old name for the bacterium)
Mafua ya kuku (general Swahili term for chicken colds, used for several respiratory diseases)
detail.summary: Infectious coryza is a fast-spreading bacterial infection of the nose, sinuses and eyes of chickens. It rarely kills many birds on its own, but it spreads through a flock within days, causes swollen faces and smelly discharge, and can sharply cut egg production and growth. Recovered birds often stay carriers for life, so once it enters a farm it tends to return with every new batch unless the farm is managed carefully. It is common in Kenya, especially where birds of different ages are kept together.
detail.cause: Infectious coryza is caused by a bacterium called Avibacterium paragallinarum (it used to be called Haemophilus paragallinarum). The bacterium enters through the nostrils and eyes and settles in the lining of the nasal passages and the sinuses, which are the air spaces under the skin of the face, below and in front of the eyes. There it causes inflammation: the lining swells and produces large amounts of mucus and pus. Because the sinuses cannot drain well, the pus builds up, so the face swells and the discharge turns thick, yellow and foul-smelling. The eyelids become inflamed (conjunctivitis) and stick shut, so birds struggle to find feed and water. Sick birds eat and drink less, which is why growth slows and egg-laying drops. Signs usually appear within one to three days of infection. On its own the disease usually runs for about two to three weeks, but it often becomes worse and longer-lasting when other infections join in, especially Mycoplasma (chronic respiratory disease), other bacteria, or viruses such as infectious bronchitis. After recovery, many birds keep the bacterium in their noses and sinuses without looking sick. These carrier birds are the main reason the disease keeps coming back on a farm.
spread: The main source is carrier birds: recovered or healthy-looking chickens that still carry the bacterium in their nose and sinuses and shed it to others.
Bringing new birds onto the farm, especially point-of-lay pullets or kienyeji birds bought from markets, is one of the most common ways the disease arrives.
Birds pass it to each other through direct contact and through droplets sneezed or coughed into the air over short distances in the same house.
Shared drinkers and feeders spread it quickly, because sick birds drip nasal discharge into the water and feed.
Keeping several age groups on one farm lets older carrier birds infect each new batch of younger birds.
People, crates, egg trays, sacks and equipment carried between houses or farms can move the bacterium, though it does not survive long outside the bird.
Stress makes outbreaks worse: overcrowding, poor ventilation, ammonia from wet litter, cold draughts during the rains, transport, vaccination stress and poor nutrition.
It is not passed from hen to chick through the egg, so the problem starts after chicks meet infected birds.
detail.atRisk: Chickens are the main species affected; guinea fowl and some game birds can occasionally be infected, while ducks, turkeys and pigeons are generally considered resistant. Growing birds from a few weeks old and adult birds are affected, and the disease tends to be more severe in older birds and in layers. Pullets coming into lay and laying hens suffer the biggest losses because of the egg drop. Farms with multiple ages on one site, such as layer farms that add new batches without emptying, are at highest risk. Free-range and kienyeji flocks that mix at markets, with neighbours' birds or with newly bought birds are also at high risk. Outbreaks are often worse during the cold, wet long and short rains, when houses are closed up, litter gets wet and ammonia builds up. Crowded, poorly ventilated houses and birds stressed by poor feeding or other diseases are more likely to have severe outbreaks.

early: Sneezing and head shaking, often in several birds at once.
Watery discharge from the nostrils that soon becomes thick and sticky.
Wet, foamy or watery eyes, with birds partly closing their eyes.
Mild swelling under one or both eyes, which may be easier to feel than see at first.
A slightly sour or unpleasant smell in the house, especially near the birds.
Birds eating and drinking a little less than normal, and a small drop in egg collection.
Feed and dust stuck to the nostrils and the sides of the beak.
advanced: Clear swelling of the face on one or both sides, sometimes so large the eye is hidden.
Swollen wattles, which are often more obvious in cocks.
Eyelids glued shut with dried discharge, and yellow cheesy material in or around the eye.
Thick, yellow, foul-smelling nasal discharge and crusts around the nostrils.
A sharp fall in egg production, and pullets that delay starting to lay.
Birds standing hunched, losing weight, and not reaching feed and water because they cannot see.
Rattling or gurgling breathing sounds, mouth breathing, and some diarrhoea when the lower airways or other infections are involved.
Higher deaths than usual, which suggests other diseases have joined in and needs urgent vet attention.

lookalikes.name: Mycoplasma (chronic respiratory disease, CRD)
lookalikes.howToTell: Mycoplasma spreads more slowly through a flock and lasts for weeks or months. Birds often have foamy eyes, a gentle rattling cough and swollen sinuses, but the discharge is usually less foul-smelling. Coryza appears within days, spreads fast and has a strong bad smell. The two often occur together, so only lab tests can be sure.

lookalikes.name: Fowl cholera (Pasteurella multocida)
lookalikes.howToTell: The chronic form of fowl cholera also causes swollen wattles and faces, but it often comes with swollen joints, lameness, greenish diarrhoea and more deaths. The acute form can kill birds suddenly with few signs. Coryza mainly affects the face and nose and usually kills few birds on its own.

lookalikes.name: Newcastle disease or infectious laryngotracheitis (ILT)
lookalikes.howToTell: Newcastle disease usually causes many deaths, greenish diarrhoea and nervous signs such as twisted necks or paralysis. Suspected Newcastle disease must be reported to the County Veterinary Officer. ILT causes gasping with neck stretched and sometimes bloody mucus. Coryza causes mainly face swelling and nasal discharge, with far fewer deaths.

lookalikes.name: Vitamin A deficiency
lookalikes.howToTell: Lack of vitamin A causes whitish cheesy material in the eyes and nostrils and small white spots in the mouth and throat. It develops slowly over weeks and is linked to poor or old feed or no green feed. It does not spread suddenly from bird to bird like coryza, and there is little face swelling or bad smell.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will usually suspect coryza from the history and signs: a sudden outbreak of swollen faces, smelly nasal discharge and egg drop spreading through the flock within days, often after new birds were introduced. To confirm it, the vet may take swabs from the sinuses of sick birds or send live sick birds to a laboratory. In Kenya this may be the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete, a regional veterinary investigation laboratory, or a university veterinary laboratory. The bacterium is hard to grow, so labs use special culture methods or a DNA test (PCR). A post-mortem (examining a dead or put-down bird) shows sticky mucus and yellow cheesy pus in the nasal passages and sinuses. The lab may also check for other infections, such as Mycoplasma, infectious bronchitis or fowl cholera, because mixed infections are common and change the treatment plan. A sensitivity test may be done to show which antibiotics will still work. To help, the farmer should pick two or three birds in the early stage of illness that have not yet been given any medicine. Keep records of when signs started, how many birds are sick or dead, daily egg numbers, feed and water intake, vaccination history, and any birds recently bought or brought back from market.
firstSteps: Separate visibly sick birds into a clean, dry, draught-free pen away from the main flock, and care for them last each day.
Stop all movement: do not buy, sell, give away or mix birds until the vet has seen the flock, because selling infected birds spreads the disease to other farms.
Make sure every bird can reach clean, fresh water easily; place extra drinkers close to birds that cannot see well, and clean and refill drinkers at least daily.
Gently wipe dried crusts from the eyes and nostrils with clean cotton wool dipped in clean, warm water so birds can see to eat and drink, using a fresh piece for each bird.
Improve ventilation without creating cold draughts, remove wet and caked litter, and add fresh dry litter to reduce ammonia, which irritates the airways.
Reduce crowding and stress where possible, and keep feed fresh and easy to reach.
Wash your hands and change or clean your boots after handling sick birds, and keep visitors out of the poultry houses.
Record the number of sick and dead birds, egg collection and feed use each day, then call your vet or County Veterinary Officer. Do not start antibiotics on your own.
detail.vetTreatment: Once the vet has confirmed or strongly suspects coryza, treatment is usually an antibiotic given in the drinking water or feed for the whole affected house. Many cases are treated with medicines from groups such as sulfonamides (sometimes combined with trimethoprim), tetracyclines, or macrolides like erythromycin or tylosin. The vet chooses the drug based on the lab results, local resistance patterns, whether birds are laying, and what is approved for poultry in Kenya. Treatment usually reduces signs and losses, but it rarely clears the bacterium from every bird, so relapses after treatment stops and carrier birds are common. Badly affected birds that do not respond may need to be culled humanely. If other infections such as Mycoplasma are present, the treatment plan changes. Every antibiotic has a withdrawal period, the time after the last treatment during which eggs and meat must not be sold or eaten. Some antibiotics are not allowed at all in laying hens whose eggs are eaten. Follow the vet's instructions and the product label exactly. Use antibiotics only when a vet prescribes them, complete the full course, and never use leftover or human medicines. Wrong or repeated use breeds antimicrobial resistance, where the bacteria stop responding to drugs, and this harms both animal and human health.
prevention: Keep a closed flock where possible: buy birds only from trusted, well-managed hatcheries or farms with no history of coryza, and avoid restocking from open markets.
Quarantine any new or returning birds in a separate place for at least two to three weeks and watch them for sneezing, face swelling or eye discharge before mixing.
Use the all-in, all-out system: raise one age group per house or site, sell or cull the whole batch, then clean, disinfect and rest the house before new birds arrive.

On farms where coryza is known, vaccinate replacement pullets with an inactivated coryza vaccine before they begin laying, usually two injections some weeks apart, following your vet's programme. The vaccine should match the strains (serovars) found in the area.
Never keep recovered birds from an outbreak to mix with a new batch; plan to sell or cull the affected flock at the end of its productive life rather than carrying it over.
Provide good ventilation, dry litter and enough space per bird, and protect houses from cold draughts and rain during the long and short rains.
Clean and disinfect drinkers and feeders regularly, and raise or cover drinkers to keep litter and droppings out of the water.
Feed a balanced ration with enough vitamins, especially vitamin A, and control other diseases such as Newcastle disease, infectious bronchitis, Mycoplasma and worms, which make coryza worse.
Limit visitors, use dedicated boots or footbaths at each house, and do not share crates, egg trays or equipment with other farms without cleaning them.
detail.impact: Coryza hits Kenyan poultry farmers mainly through lost production rather than deaths. In layer flocks, egg collection can fall sharply within days, and pullets may start laying weeks late, directly cutting income from egg sales. Broilers and growing birds eat less and grow slowly, so they take longer to reach market weight and use more feed per kilogram gained. Swollen, sick-looking birds fetch lower prices, and kienyeji birds with swollen faces are hard to sell at market. Farmers also pay for vet visits, lab tests and antibiotics. During and after treatment, eggs and meat cannot be sold until the withdrawal period ends. Because recovered birds remain carriers, the disease tends to return with each new batch on multi-age farms, so losses repeat year after year unless the farm changes its management. When other infections join in, deaths and costs rise much more.
detail.humanHealth: Infectious coryza is not known to infect people, so handling sick birds does not give you the disease. The main human-health concern is drug residues: antibiotics used to treat the flock can remain in eggs and meat for a period after treatment. Do not eat or sell eggs or meat from treated birds until the vet's or label's withdrawal period has passed. Never use antibiotics in laying hens unless the vet confirms the product is allowed for layers. Always wash your hands after handling sick birds and their discharge, as good hygiene protects against other poultry germs.
detail.outlook: Most birds with uncomplicated coryza recover within about two to three weeks, and deaths are usually low. Recovery is slower and losses higher when other infections such as Mycoplasma, infectious bronchitis or fowl cholera are present. Poor ventilation, wet litter, overcrowding, cold weather and poor nutrition also make it worse. Early vet involvement, good nursing and better housing improve the outlook. Egg production usually returns as birds recover, but it may not fully reach the level it was before the outbreak. The biggest long-term problem is that many recovered birds stay carriers, so the flock remains a source of infection for new birds. Lasting control depends on all-in, all-out management, careful restocking and vaccination rather than on treatment alone.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell eggs from hens with coryza?
faqs.a: The disease itself does not infect people, so eggs from sick but untreated hens are not a coryza risk to humans, though sick hens lay fewer and sometimes poorer-quality eggs. The real concern comes once you treat: many antibiotics leave residues in eggs, and some are not allowed in laying hens at all. After any treatment, do not eat or sell eggs until the withdrawal period given by your vet or the product label has passed.

faqs.q: Why does coryza keep coming back on my farm?
faqs.a: The most common reason is carrier birds. Hens that recovered from an earlier outbreak look healthy but still carry the bacterium in their sinuses, and they infect each new batch of younger birds you bring in. Antibiotics reduce signs but rarely clear every carrier. To break the cycle, avoid keeping different ages together, empty and clean houses between batches, do not carry old birds over to mix with new ones, and talk to your vet about vaccinating pullets before lay.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine for coryza in Kenya, and does it work?
faqs.a: Yes, inactivated coryza vaccines are available through vets and some agrovets, usually given by injection to pullets before they start laying. They reduce how sick birds get and protect egg production, but they do not give complete protection. They work best when the vaccine contains the strains found in your area. Ask your vet or County Veterinary Officer whether vaccination is worthwhile for your farm and how to fit it into your programme.

faqs.q: Can I just buy an antibiotic from the agrovet and treat the birds myself?
faqs.a: It is better not to. Several diseases look like coryza, including Mycoplasma, fowl cholera and even Newcastle disease, and they need different handling. Newcastle disease is viral, so antibiotics will not help, and it must be reported. The wrong drug, dose or course length wastes money, leaves residues in eggs and meat, and helps bacteria become resistant. Let a vet confirm the cause and prescribe the right treatment and withdrawal period.

faqs.q: Should I cull the birds that had coryza?
faqs.a: Not always straight away. Many birds recover and lay again, and culling a whole laying flock can be costly. However, birds that stay badly swollen, blind or thin after treatment are best culled humanely. Recovered birds should not be mixed with new stock because they can carry the disease. Many farmers keep the recovered flock until the end of its laying life, then sell it, clean the house thoroughly and restock with clean birds.

faqs.q: Will coryza spread to my ducks, turkeys or other animals?
faqs.a: Coryza mainly affects chickens; guinea fowl and some game birds can occasionally be infected. Ducks, turkeys and pigeons are generally considered resistant, and it does not affect cattle, goats, dogs or people. Other birds and people can still carry contaminated dirt between houses, so keep good hygiene and limit movement between poultry pens during an outbreak.

products.role: Its plant extracts are labelled to relieve respiratory problems, so it can be used in the drinking water as supportive care to help birds cope with nasal and airway irritation during recovery. It does not kill the coryza bacterium or replace vet-prescribed treatment, vaccination or good ventilation.

A vitamin and mineral supplement labelled for stress recovery and layer productivity. It can help sick birds that are eating less to keep up their vitamin intake, including vitamin A for the lining of the airways, and support the return of egg production after the vet's treatment. It supports recovery but does not treat the infection.

infectious-coryza.imagePrompt: Close-up realistic photo of a brown laying hen in a Kenyan poultry house with one side of her face visibly swollen, the eye on that side closed and crusted, and a little yellowish discharge at the nostril, with other hens softly blurred in the background on dry litter.

card.headline: Pasted vents and dying young chicks
card.look: Chicks huddle under the heat source, chirp loudly and have white or creamy droppings stuck around the vent, with many deaths in the first two to three weeks. Older birds look dull and droopy, with pale, shrunken combs and watery yellow-green droppings.
card.action: Separate sick birds at once, stop selling or hatching eggs from the flock, and call your vet to confirm the cause before any treatment is given.

aka: Kuhara cheupe kwa vifaranga (white diarrhoea in chicks, descriptive Swahili)
detail.summary: Fowl typhoid and pullorum are two closely related bacterial diseases of chickens, caused by Salmonella bacteria that are adapted to poultry. Pullorum mainly kills young chicks in their first weeks of life, while fowl typhoid strikes growing and adult birds, causing anaemia, diarrhoea, egg drop and deaths. Both matter because birds that survive often stay infected for life and pass the bacteria into their eggs, so one infected hen or hatchery can spread the disease to many farms. They remain an important cause of losses in Kenyan layer, broiler breeder and improved kienyeji flocks.
detail.cause: Both diseases are caused by one type of bacteria, Salmonella enterica serovar Gallinarum, which comes in two forms (called biovars): Gallinarum, which causes fowl typhoid, and Pullorum, which causes pullorum disease. Unlike the Salmonella that cause food poisoning in people, these forms are host-adapted, meaning they mainly live in and harm poultry. After a bird swallows the bacteria, or a chick hatches already infected from the egg, the bacteria pass through the gut wall into the blood. They settle in the liver, spleen, heart, lungs, ovary and other organs, where they cause inflammation and small areas of dead tissue. In fowl typhoid the bacteria destroy red blood cells, which is why combs and wattles turn pale and the liver often becomes swollen with a bronze or greenish tinge. In chicks, the unabsorbed yolk sac becomes infected and the gut stops working properly, leading to white pasty diarrhoea and dehydration. In hens that survive, the bacteria can hide in the ovary for months or years, so the hen looks healthy but lays infected eggs. This 'carrier' state is the main reason the disease keeps coming back.
spread: Through the egg: infected carrier hens pass the bacteria inside their eggs, so chicks can hatch already infected. This is the most important route for pullorum.
In the hatchery and incubator: one infected egg can contaminate incubators, hatchers and chick boxes, spreading the bacteria to many chicks hatched in the same batch.
Through droppings: sick and carrier birds shed bacteria in their droppings, contaminating litter, feed, water drinkers and the ground around free-range runs.
By pecking and eating dead birds: chickens that peck at carcasses or infected eggs swallow large numbers of bacteria, so leaving dead birds in the house spreads the disease fast.
On people, equipment and vehicles: boots, clothes, egg trays, crates, feeders and vehicles moving between farms or markets carry contaminated droppings.

Through rodents, wild birds, flies and red mites: rats, mice and wild birds can carry the bacteria, and poultry red mites (small blood-sucking mites that hide in cracks of the house) have been linked to keeping fowl typhoid going on infected farms.
Buying in birds of unknown history: introducing chicks, pullets or cocks from untested sources or open markets is a common way infection reaches a new farm.
detail.atRisk: Pullorum mostly affects chicks in the first two to three weeks of life, with the heaviest losses usually seen in the first week or two. Fowl typhoid can affect birds of any age but is most often seen in growing and adult birds, especially laying hens and breeder flocks. Brown-egg layer breeds are commonly reported to be more susceptible to fowl typhoid than many lighter breeds, though all chickens can be infected. Turkeys, guinea fowl, quails and some game birds can also be affected; ducks and pigeons are generally more resistant. Farms that buy chicks from untested hatcheries, hatch their own eggs from untested hens, or run mixed-age flocks are at higher risk. Stress makes outbreaks worse: chilling or overheating in the brooder, overcrowding, poor ventilation, wet litter during the long and short rains, transport, and heavy egg production in layers. Free-range and kienyeji flocks that mix with neighbours' birds, scavenge near markets or share cocks for breeding can pick up and spread the infection easily.

early: In chicks: birds huddle together under the brooder or near the heat, look sleepy and droopy, and chirp loudly or shrilly.
In chicks: white or creamy, pasty droppings that stick to the feathers around the vent, sometimes so badly that the vent is blocked.
In chicks: poor appetite, drooping wings, ruffled fluff and chicks that look smaller and weaker than their batch-mates.
Dead-in-shell embryos and chicks that die soon after hatching, if the eggs came from infected hens.
In older birds: dullness, ruffled feathers, reduced feeding and birds standing with eyes half-closed.
In older birds: pale, shrunken or bluish combs and wattles caused by anaemia (loss of red blood cells).
In layers: a fall in egg production and sometimes more misshapen or poor-quality eggs.
advanced: In chicks: gasping or laboured breathing, lameness and swollen joints (hock joints) in some survivors.
In chicks: heavy daily deaths over the first two to three weeks, with survivors growing poorly and often uneven in size.
In older birds: watery yellow, yellow-green or greenish diarrhoea, soiled vent feathers and increased thirst.
In older birds: marked weakness, birds sitting down and unable to keep up with the flock, and steady or sudden deaths.
In layers: egg production may stop in badly affected birds, and deaths continue over days to weeks.
Survivors that look recovered but stay thin, pale or poor layers, which may be carriers that keep spreading infection.

lookalikes.name: Newcastle disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Newcastle also causes green diarrhoea, dullness and deaths, but usually brings breathing problems (coughing, gasping, rattling) and nervous signs such as twisted necks, circling or paralysis, and it often spreads very fast through the flock. Pale combs and a bronze, swollen liver at post-mortem point more to fowl typhoid. Because Newcastle is serious and spreads widely, any doubt needs a vet and lab check.

lookalikes.name: Coccidiosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Coccidiosis usually affects birds from about three to six weeks old, especially on wet litter, and often causes blood-stained or brown watery droppings. At post-mortem the gut or caeca (blind gut pouches) are swollen, often with blood. Pullorum is mostly seen in the first two to three weeks with white pasty droppings, and the problem lies in the liver, yolk and organs rather than mainly the gut lining.

lookalikes.name: Navel and yolk sac infection (omphalitis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Omphalitis is caused by various bacteria entering through a poorly healed navel, usually in the first week after hatching. Chicks have a wet, swollen, dark or scabby navel and a bloated belly, often with a bad smell. Pullorum can also leave an infected yolk sac, so the two can look similar; lab culture is needed to tell which bacteria are involved.

lookalikes.name: Fowl cholera
lookalikes.howToTell: Fowl cholera, caused by Pasteurella bacteria, also causes sudden deaths and greenish diarrhoea in adult birds, but affected birds often have purple, dark combs and swollen, hot wattles or joints rather than pale, shrunken combs. Post-mortem and lab tests are needed to confirm which disease it is.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will look at the flock history (age of birds, where chicks or eggs came from, pattern of deaths), examine live birds and usually open fresh dead birds (post-mortem). In chicks, typical findings include unabsorbed yolk, small white nodules in the heart, lungs, liver or gizzard, and cheesy cores in the caeca. In older birds, the vet often finds a swollen liver with a bronze or greenish colour, an enlarged spleen, small pale spots on organs, and misshapen or discoloured ovarian follicles in hens. These findings are strongly suggestive but not proof, so samples such as liver, spleen, ovary or yolk are sent to a laboratory to grow and identify the bacteria (culture). The lab can also run a sensitivity test to show which antibiotics will work. To find hidden carriers in a flock, especially breeders, vets use blood tests such as the rapid plate agglutination test or ELISA, and some labs use PCR, a test that detects the bacteria's genetic material. In Kenya samples can go to the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete, regional veterinary investigation laboratories, or university and private labs. To help, keep two or three freshly dead or very sick birds cool (not frozen) in a sealed bag, record the number of deaths each day, ages of birds, egg production, the hatchery or seller's name and batch, feed source, and any vaccines or medicines already given.
firstSteps: Remove sick and weak birds to a separate pen away from the main flock, with their own feeder, drinker and footwear if possible.
Collect dead birds quickly every day so other birds cannot peck them, keep one or two fresh ones cool for the vet, and bury the rest deeply or burn them away from water sources.
Keep birds warm and comfortable: chicks need a steady, correct brooder temperature without draughts, while adult birds need shade, good ventilation and dry litter.
Make sure clean, fresh drinking water is always available, change it at least daily, and clean drinkers so droppings do not build up in them.
Stop selling, giving away or hatching eggs and birds from the flock until the vet has given advice, to avoid spreading the disease to other farms.
Limit visitors, use a footbath or dedicated boots at the house entrance, and wash hands with soap after handling birds, droppings or dead birds.
Write down when signs started, how many birds are sick and dead each day, their ages, egg numbers, and where the chicks or eggs came from.
Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer and do not start antibiotics on your own; the wrong drug wastes money, may not work and can leave residues in eggs and meat.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be prescribed by a vet, ideally after the lab has confirmed the bacteria and run a sensitivity test. Vets may use antibiotics given in drinking water or feed, chosen from classes such as sulphonamides, trimethoprim-sulphonamide combinations, tetracyclines or amoxicillin, depending on what the test shows works locally. Some drug classes, such as fluoroquinolones, are important for human medicine and responsible vets avoid or reserve them. Treatment can reduce deaths and calm an outbreak, but it is important to know that antibiotics do not reliably clear the infection: many treated birds remain carriers and can keep laying infected eggs. For this reason, especially in breeder flocks and hatchery supply flocks, vets often advise testing and removing positive birds, or culling and replacing the whole flock, followed by thorough cleaning. Supportive care alongside treatment includes warmth, clean water, good feed and reducing stress. Every antibiotic has a withdrawal period, meaning a time after the last dose when eggs and meat must not be eaten or sold, and some antibiotics must not be used at all in hens laying eggs for people. Follow the vet's instructions exactly, finish the full course, and never use leftover or borrowed drugs. Misuse of antibiotics in poultry is a major driver of antimicrobial resistance, where bacteria stop responding to medicines in both animals and people.
prevention: Buy chicks only from hatcheries that test their parent flocks for pullorum and fowl typhoid and can show a clean health record; ask the agrovet or hatchery directly.
If you hatch your own eggs, only set clean, uncracked eggs from healthy hens that your vet has blood-tested, and never hatch eggs from a flock that has had an outbreak.

Ask your vet about vaccination: live vaccines (such as the 9R strain) and inactivated vaccines are used in some countries for layers and breeders against fowl typhoid, but availability in Kenya varies and vaccinated birds can test positive on blood tests, so it must be planned with a vet.
Practise all-in, all-out where possible: raise one age group at a time, then empty, clean, disinfect and rest the house before the next batch arrives.
Clean and disinfect incubators, hatchers, chick boxes, egg trays, feeders and drinkers regularly, and remove all old litter between batches.
Control rats, mice, wild birds, flies and poultry red mites by sealing feed stores, using rodent bait stations safely, and treating cracks and perches as your vet advises.
Keep good brooding conditions: correct temperature, dry litter, good ventilation and enough space to avoid chilling, overheating and overcrowding, especially in the rainy seasons.
Feed a balanced ration with the right vitamins and minerals, store feed dry to prevent mould, and provide clean water every day to keep the birds' natural defences strong.
Quarantine any new birds for at least two weeks before mixing them with your flock, and avoid bringing in birds from open markets or sharing cocks with neighbours' flocks.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan farm, pullorum can wipe out a large part of a batch of day-old chicks in the first weeks, which means losing the money paid for chicks, feed, brooding fuel and vaccines. Surviving chicks often grow unevenly and slowly, so broilers take longer to reach market weight and layers come into lay late. Fowl typhoid in layers causes ongoing deaths and a drop in egg numbers, hitting daily income from egg sales. Because survivors may remain carriers, a farmer may face the hard choice of culling a flock that still looks productive, plus the costs of cleaning and restocking. Treatment costs, lab fees and lost sales add up. For farmers who sell fertile eggs or chicks, including improved kienyeji breeders, an outbreak can damage their reputation and customer trust, and spread the problem to many other farms in the area.
detail.humanHealth: The forms of Salmonella that cause fowl typhoid and pullorum are adapted to poultry and are generally considered to pose little risk of illness to people, unlike other Salmonella types that cause food poisoning. However, sick flocks can carry other harmful bacteria at the same time, so always wash hands with soap after handling birds, eggs, droppings or carcasses, keep children away from sick birds, and cook eggs and meat thoroughly. The bigger human-health concern is antibiotic residues: eggs and meat from treated birds must not be eaten or sold until the full withdrawal period given by the vet has passed, and careless antibiotic use helps create resistant bacteria that can affect people.
detail.outlook: For an individual chick with pullorum, the outlook is poor once it is clearly sick, and many die despite care. In older birds with fowl typhoid, early vet-guided treatment and good nursing can reduce deaths, but recovery varies with the age of the birds, how quickly action was taken, the strain of bacteria, and how resistant it is to common antibiotics. The main problem is that recovered birds often remain carriers, so 'recovery' of the flock does not mean the infection has gone. Long-term success depends on finding and removing carriers, getting clean chicks from tested sources, and strict hygiene and rodent control. Farms that do this can become free of the disease, while farms that keep and hatch from survivors usually see it return.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell eggs from a flock with fowl typhoid?
faqs.a: These particular Salmonella types rarely make people sick, but you should not sell or hatch eggs from an affected flock until your vet advises. If the birds are being given antibiotics, eggs must be thrown away for the whole withdrawal period the vet gives you, and some antibiotics cannot be used in laying hens at all. Always cook eggs well and keep good hygiene.

faqs.q: My birds recovered after treatment. Can I keep them for breeding?
faqs.a: It is not wise to hatch eggs from birds that have had pullorum or fowl typhoid. Many survivors carry the bacteria in their ovaries and pass it into their eggs, so their chicks may hatch already infected. Your vet may suggest blood-testing the flock and removing positive birds, or keeping them only for egg or meat sale and buying clean chicks from a tested hatchery for breeding.

faqs.q: Will antibiotics from the agrovet cure the disease?
faqs.a: Antibiotics prescribed by a vet can reduce deaths, but they often do not clear the bacteria completely, and many treated birds stay carriers. Buying antibiotics without a diagnosis may mean using a drug that does not work against your strain, wasting money and adding to antibiotic resistance. Ask your vet to confirm the disease and, if possible, run a sensitivity test first.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine for fowl typhoid in Kenya?
faqs.a: Vaccines for fowl typhoid, including a live vaccine known as 9R and some inactivated vaccines, are used in various countries, mainly for layers and breeders. Availability in Kenya can change, so ask your vet or a trusted agrovet. There is no widely used vaccine for pullorum in chicks; prevention depends mostly on buying chicks from tested, clean parent flocks and good hatchery hygiene.

faqs.q: How do I know if the problem came from the hatchery?
faqs.a: If many chicks from the same batch fall sick or die in the first week or two with white pasty droppings, and your house was properly cleaned before they arrived, the infection may have come with the chicks. Keep the batch number, delivery date and receipt, and report the losses to the hatchery and your vet quickly. Lab tests on dead chicks can help confirm the cause.

faqs.q: How long should I wait before bringing in new birds after an outbreak?
faqs.a: There is no single answer, so follow your vet's advice. In general, remove all birds, old litter and droppings, scrub and disinfect the house and equipment, control rodents and mites, and leave the house empty and dry for a period before restocking. The bacteria can survive for weeks or longer in droppings and dirty litter, so thorough cleaning matters more than the exact number of days.

products.role: An oral rehydration solution that can help sick, droopy birds with diarrhoea replace lost fluids and salts while they are under vet care. It supports comfort and hydration only; it does not kill Salmonella or replace the treatment and flock decisions your vet recommends.

A probiotic that supports healthy gut bacteria, which can be useful once a vet-prescribed antibiotic course is finished, to help restore normal gut balance in recovering birds. Ask your vet about timing, as probiotics are usually given after rather than together with antibiotics. It is a gut-health aid, not a cure or a substitute for clean chicks, hygiene and vet care.

fowl-typhoid.imagePrompt: Close-up photo of a small group of droopy, fluffed-up day-old chicks huddled under a warm brooder lamp on wood-shaving litter, one chick in front showing creamy white droppings pasted around its vent feathers.
fowl-typhoid.seoDescription: Fowl typhoid and pullorum in chickens: spot pale combs, yellow-green diarrhoea and pasted vents in chicks, act early and prevent egg-borne spread on your farm.

card.headline: Sudden deaths with purple combs
card.look: Healthy-looking adult hens are found dead on the perch or nest with dark purple-blue combs and wattles, while others sit fluffed up with green, watery droppings. In slower cases, wattles, faces or leg joints become hot and swollen.
card.action: Separate sick birds at once, remove dead birds safely, and call a vet or the County Veterinary Officer today so a post-mortem can confirm the cause.

aka: Kipindupindu cha kuku (sometimes used loosely for any sudden mass deaths in chickens)
detail.summary: Fowl cholera is a bacterial infection of chickens, turkeys, ducks, geese and other birds. It can strike suddenly and kill many adult birds in a few days, or settle into a slow, long-lasting form with swollen wattles, lame joints and falling egg production. Birds that survive often stay infected for life and keep spreading the germ to new stock, so one outbreak can haunt a farm for years. Because it looks like other killer diseases such as Newcastle disease and fowl typhoid, a vet must confirm it quickly.
detail.cause: Fowl cholera is caused by a bacterium called Pasteurella multocida. It enters the bird mainly through the mouth, nostrils and eyes, or through wounds such as pecks, bites and scratches. Once inside, it multiplies quickly and can move into the bloodstream, causing septicaemia (blood poisoning). The bacteria and the toxins they release damage the small blood vessels, which is why the comb and wattles turn purple, the internal organs show tiny bleeding spots, and the liver develops small white dead patches. In birds that fight off the bloodstream stage, the germ hides in particular places such as the wattles, sinuses of the face, middle ear, joints, foot pads and the oviduct (egg canal), causing swelling, pus-like cheesy material and long-term illness. Strains differ a lot in how dangerous they are, so one farm may see mass deaths while another sees only a few sick birds.
spread: Carrier birds are the main source: chickens that recovered from fowl cholera, or that never showed signs, can carry the germ in their throat and nose for life and shed it to new birds.
Bringing in new birds from markets, neighbours or traders without quarantine is a very common way the disease enters a Kenyan flock.
Sick birds contaminate drinking water, feed and litter with discharge from the beak, nose and droppings, and healthy birds pick it up when they drink or peck.
Dead birds left lying in the house or thrown in the bush spread infection, because flock mates, dogs and wild birds peck or carry the carcasses.
Rats, mice, wild birds, and other animals such as pigs, cats and dogs can carry Pasteurella and bring it to the flock; cat bites and scratches are a known route of infection.
People, crates, egg trays, sacks and bicycles or motorbikes moving between farms and markets can carry contaminated droppings on boots, hands and surfaces.

Stress triggers outbreaks in carrier flocks: crowding, sudden weather changes during the long and short rains, wet litter, poor ventilation, the start of egg laying, moving birds, and other diseases or worm burdens.
The germ does not usually pass through the egg to the chick, but dirty eggshells and hatchery equipment can still spread it.
detail.atRisk: Fowl cholera mainly affects older birds: laying hens, breeding cocks and growers from a few months of age, while young chicks are less often affected. Turkeys, ducks and geese are very susceptible, and mixed flocks of chickens, ducks and turkeys raise the risk. Layers around the start of lay and at peak production are especially vulnerable, as are heavy, well-fed birds that can die suddenly. In Kenya, risk is high in free-range and semi-intensive kienyeji systems where birds mix with neighbours' flocks, wild birds and rodents, and in deep-litter houses that are crowded, damp and poorly ventilated. Farms that buy birds from open markets, keep birds of many ages together, and never fully empty and clean their houses are at greatest risk. Outbreaks often follow wet, cold periods during the rains or other stressful events.

early: Sudden deaths of one or more adult birds that looked normal the evening before, often found under the perch or in nest boxes.
Dark red, purple or bluish comb and wattles, especially in birds that are about to die.
Birds sitting fluffed up, sleepy and unwilling to move, with ruffled feathers and drooping wings.
Loss of appetite, but sometimes increased drinking because of fever; birds may feel hot to touch.
Watery diarrhoea that is often green or yellow-green, sometimes with mucus, soiling the vent feathers.
Mucus or frothy discharge from the beak and nostrils, and faster breathing.
A sudden drop in egg production and more soft-shelled or misshapen eggs.
advanced: Several or many birds dying over a few days, with high losses in the worst outbreaks.
Swollen, hot and later hard wattles, sometimes on one side only, filled with cheesy yellow material.
Swollen face and sinuses around the eyes, with eye discharge and crusting.
Swollen, painful hock joints, foot pads or wing joints causing lameness and birds that refuse to stand.
Twisted neck or loss of balance in some birds when the infection reaches the middle ear or skull.
Weight loss, pale or shrunken comb and a long, slow decline in chronic cases.
Noisy, rattling breathing in birds with chronic infection of the airways.

lookalikes.name: Newcastle disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Newcastle disease affects birds of all ages, including young chicks, and usually shows marked breathing signs such as gasping and coughing, plus nervous signs like twisted necks, paralysis and circling in many birds. Green diarrhoea and sudden deaths occur in both diseases, so a post-mortem and lab test are needed. Suspected Newcastle disease should be reported to the County Veterinary Officer.

lookalikes.name: Fowl typhoid (Salmonella Gallinarum)
lookalikes.howToTell: Fowl typhoid also kills adult birds and causes yellow-green diarrhoea, but sick birds usually have pale, shrunken combs from anaemia rather than purple ones. At post-mortem the liver is often enlarged with a bronze or greenish colour. Only a lab can reliably separate the two.

lookalikes.name: Highly pathogenic avian influenza
lookalikes.howToTell: Bird flu can cause very sudden mass deaths with purple, swollen combs and wattles, swelling of the head and bleeding under the skin of the legs, looking very much like acute fowl cholera. Any sudden heavy losses, especially where wild water birds are around, must be reported immediately to the County Veterinary Officer so it can be ruled out.

lookalikes.name: Infectious coryza
lookalikes.howToTell: Coryza causes a swollen face, foul-smelling nasal discharge and swollen wattles like chronic fowl cholera, but it spreads fast through the flock with many sick birds and few deaths. It does not usually cause sudden deaths, purple combs or swollen joints.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will start by asking about the flock: when deaths started, how many birds, their ages, recent purchases, vaccinations, and what the droppings look like. They will examine live sick birds and usually open one or more freshly dead birds (post-mortem). Typical findings in acute fowl cholera include small bleeding spots on the heart fat and gizzard, a swollen liver with many tiny white or grey spots, inflamed intestines and, in layers, soft, broken or 'cooked-looking' egg yolks in the belly. Chronic cases show cheesy pus in the wattles, joints, sinuses or oviduct. Because these findings overlap with other diseases, the vet will often send samples (liver, heart blood, bone marrow or swabs from swellings) to a laboratory such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete or a regional Veterinary Investigation Laboratory. The lab can grow and identify Pasteurella multocida and, importantly, run a sensitivity test to show which antibiotics will actually work. To help, keep two or three freshly dead birds cool (not frozen, and not left in the sun) in a sealed bag, write down the daily number of deaths and sick birds, note vaccines and drugs already used, and do not give antibiotics before samples are taken, as this can hide the cause.
firstSteps: Move sick and weak birds into a separate pen away from the main flock, with their own feeder and drinker, and handle them last each day.
Collect dead birds immediately using gloves or a plastic bag over your hand, keep the freshest ones cool for the vet, and burn or deeply bury the rest with lime, far from water sources.

Call your vet, agrovet-linked animal health officer or the County Veterinary Officer the same day, because acute fowl cholera can kill many birds within days and must be told apart from Newcastle disease and bird flu.
Give plenty of clean, fresh drinking water, wash and refill drinkers daily, and place them where weak birds can reach them easily.
Keep the house dry, well ventilated but draught-free, and shaded; remove wet, caked litter and add fresh dry litter.
Stop all movement of birds and eggs on and off the farm: do not sell, give away, or take birds to market, and do not bring in new birds until the vet advises.
Keep visitors out, use a footbath or change boots at the house entrance, and wash hands with soap after handling birds.
Keep a written record of daily deaths, sick birds, egg numbers and feed and water intake to help the vet judge the outbreak and the response to treatment.
detail.vetTreatment: Fowl cholera is a bacterial disease, so a vet may prescribe antibiotics to reduce deaths in the flock. Drug groups commonly used include sulphonamides, tetracyclines and some others chosen according to local availability and, ideally, a lab sensitivity test; treatment is usually given through the drinking water or feed for the whole flock, and sometimes by injection for valuable birds. All treatment, including the choice of drug, dose and length of course, must be prescribed by a vet. Treatment often reduces deaths, but the disease can return once the drug is stopped, and treated birds may remain lifelong carriers. Badly affected birds with swollen joints, heads or wattles often respond poorly and the vet may advise culling them. Every antibiotic has a withdrawal period, meaning eggs and meat must not be eaten or sold for a set number of days after the last dose; your vet and the product label will tell you the period, and some drugs are not allowed at all in laying hens producing eggs for people. Misusing antibiotics, such as using the wrong drug, stopping early, or buying drugs without advice, breeds antimicrobial resistance (germs that no longer respond to medicine), which harms your flock and public health. Because carriers keep the disease on the farm, the vet will often recommend that after an outbreak the flock is sold for slaughter or culled once withdrawal periods are over, followed by full cleaning, disinfection and a rest period before restocking with clean birds.
prevention: Buy chicks and birds only from trusted hatcheries and breeders, and avoid buying adult birds from open markets where carriers are common.
Quarantine any new or returning birds in a separate pen for at least two to three weeks and watch them closely before mixing them with your flock.
Practise all-in, all-out where possible: keep one age group per house, sell or remove the whole batch, then clean, disinfect and rest the house before restocking.

Ask your vet whether a fowl cholera vaccine (killed vaccines called bacterins, or live vaccines) is available and suitable in your area; vaccines are usually given to growers before lay, protection is strongest against matching strains, and they do not replace good hygiene.
Control rats and mice, keep wild birds out with wire mesh, and keep cats, dogs and pigs away from poultry houses and feed stores.
Keep chickens separate from ducks, geese and turkeys, which can carry and spread the germ.
Provide clean, safe drinking water, wash drinkers daily, and keep litter dry by fixing leaking roofs and drinkers, especially before the long and short rains.
Avoid overcrowding, ensure good ventilation, and feed a balanced ration so birds are less stressed and better able to resist infection.
Dispose of dead birds promptly by burning or deep burial, never by throwing them in the bush or feeding them to dogs or pigs.
Control worms, mites and other diseases, and vaccinate against Newcastle disease and others as advised, because weakened birds are more likely to develop fowl cholera.
detail.impact: Fowl cholera can be one of the most costly diseases on a Kenyan poultry farm. In an acute outbreak, a farmer may lose a large share of layers or breeding kienyeji hens within days, just when they are most valuable. Egg production falls sharply and may not fully recover in survivors. Chronic cases cause lame, thin birds with swollen heads that eat feed but produce little. Antibiotic treatment, lab tests and vet visits add costs, and eggs and meat must be withheld during withdrawal periods, cutting income further. Because survivors remain carriers, many farmers must sell or cull the whole flock and pay for cleaning, disinfection and an empty period before restocking. A farm known to have repeated outbreaks may also lose the trust of buyers and neighbours who buy breeding stock.
detail.humanHealth: The bacterium that causes fowl cholera, Pasteurella multocida, can infect people, but infection from chickens is uncommon. Most human cases come from cat and dog bites or scratches, causing painful, swollen wounds. To stay safe, wear gloves when handling sick or dead birds, cover any cuts on your hands, wash hands well with soap afterwards, and keep children away from sick birds. Seek medical care if a wound becomes red, swollen and painful after contact with animals. Eggs and meat from birds treated with antibiotics must not be eaten or sold until the withdrawal period is over, because drug residues can harm people and add to antimicrobial resistance. Do not eat birds that died of disease.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends on the strain of the germ, how quickly the vet confirms the disease, and how well the flock is managed. In acute outbreaks many birds may die before treatment takes effect, but prompt, vet-guided treatment usually reduces further deaths. Birds with chronic swellings of the wattles, face or joints rarely return to full health or production. The biggest long-term challenge is that recovered birds stay carriers, so outbreaks often come back under stress. Farms that remove the infected flock, clean and rest the premises, restock with clean birds and follow strict biosecurity and vaccination where available have the best chance of staying free of the disease.

faqs.q: My hens are dying suddenly but they were eating well yesterday. Is it definitely fowl cholera?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Sudden deaths in adult birds with purple combs and green droppings are typical of fowl cholera, but Newcastle disease, fowl typhoid and bird flu can look very similar. Only a vet with a post-mortem and lab test can confirm it. Call a vet the same day and keep fresh dead birds cool for examination; if deaths are heavy and sudden, also inform the County Veterinary Officer so bird flu can be ruled out.

faqs.q: Can I just buy antibiotics from the agrovet and treat the flock myself?
faqs.a: It is best not to. Antibiotics should be prescribed by a vet, who chooses a drug that works against the local strain, sets the correct dose and length of treatment, and tells you the withdrawal period for eggs and meat. Guessing often fails, wastes money, leaves drug residues in food and creates resistant germs. Giving drugs before the vet takes samples can also hide the true cause.

faqs.q: After treatment my birds look healthy again. Can I keep them and add new chicks?
faqs.a: Recovered birds usually remain carriers for life and can infect any new birds you bring in, even if they look well. Many vets advise keeping the old flock separate, then selling them for slaughter once withdrawal periods are over, cleaning and disinfecting the house, and resting it before bringing in new birds. Mixing new chicks or pullets with survivors is a common cause of repeated outbreaks.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine for fowl cholera in Kenya?
faqs.a: Fowl cholera vaccines exist, both killed (bacterin) and live types, but availability in Kenya varies and they protect best against matching strains. Ask your vet or County Veterinary Officer whether a suitable vaccine is available and whether your farm's risk justifies it. Vaccination works best alongside quarantine, rodent control, clean water and all-in, all-out management, not instead of them.

faqs.q: Are the eggs from my flock safe to eat during an outbreak?
faqs.a: Eggs from apparently healthy birds that are not on medicine are generally not a major risk to people, but collect them often, discard dirty or cracked eggs and wash hands after handling. If the flock is being treated with antibiotics, do not eat or sell eggs until the withdrawal period given by your vet is over. Never eat birds that died or were very sick.

faqs.q: Why does the disease keep coming back on my farm every rainy season?
faqs.a: Repeat outbreaks usually mean carrier birds, rats or wild birds are keeping the germ on the farm, and stress from cold, damp weather and wet litter allows it to flare up. Breaking the cycle means removing carrier flocks, cleaning and resting houses, controlling rodents, keeping litter dry and buying only from clean sources. Talk to your vet about a farm plan, including whether vaccination makes sense.

products.role: An oral rehydration solution added to drinking water to help weak, feverish birds stay hydrated and keep drinking while they receive vet-prescribed treatment; it supports comfort and recovery but does not kill the fowl cholera bacteria. Ask your vet about timing if medicine is also being given in the water.

A vitamin and mineral supplement that can help survivors cope with the stress of illness and treatment and support the return of appetite and egg production during recovery, used alongside vet care, culling decisions and strict hygiene, never as a treatment for the infection.

fowl-cholera.imagePrompt: A close-up realistic photo of an adult brown laying hen standing in a rural Kenyan chicken house with dry litter, her comb and swollen wattles a dark purple-blue colour, feathers slightly ruffled, soft natural daylight.
fowl-cholera.seoDescription: Fowl cholera in chickens: spot sudden deaths, purple combs, swollen wattles and green diarrhoea, act fast, and prevent outbreaks on Kenyan poultry farms.

card.headline: Dull, fluffed-up birds breathing hard
card.look: Birds stand hunched with ruffled feathers and half-closed eyes, eat little and may breathe with open beaks or a rattling sound. Young chicks may have wet, swollen navels and bloated bellies, and older birds may limp on hot, swollen joints.
card.action: Separate sick birds, clean out wet litter and open up ventilation, then call your vet before buying any antibiotic.

detail.summary: Colibacillosis is a group of infections in chickens and other poultry caused by harmful strains of the bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli). It is one of the most common causes of sickness and death in Kenyan broiler, layer and kienyeji flocks. It usually strikes when birds are already weakened by dirty housing, ammonia, poor brooding, or another disease such as Newcastle disease, infectious bronchitis, Gumboro or Mycoplasma. Because the bacteria live in every poultry house, prevention through hygiene and good management matters more than treatment.
detail.cause: E. coli bacteria live normally in the gut of every chicken and in their droppings, so they are always present in litter, dust and water around birds. Most strains are harmless, but some, called avian pathogenic E. coli (APEC), can invade the body when the bird's defences are down. The most common route is through the breathing system: ammonia from wet litter and heavy dust damage the fine hairs that clean the windpipe, or a virus like infectious bronchitis or Newcastle disease (or a strong reaction to a live vaccine) damages the lining. E. coli carried on dust then reaches the air sacs, which are thin balloon-like bags that help the bird breathe. From there the bacteria spread through the blood (septicaemia, meaning blood infection) and cause a thick, yellowish, cheesy layer of pus over the heart, liver and air sacs. In chicks, bacteria enter through a navel that has not healed or through dirty, cracked eggs in the hatchery, infecting the yolk sac (the leftover yolk the chick lives on in its first days). In layers, bacteria can travel up the vent into the oviduct (egg tube), causing salpingitis and egg peritonitis, where egg material and infection collect in the belly. Bacteria can also settle in joints, causing arthritis, or under the skin, causing cellulitis.
spread: Contaminated droppings, litter and dust: birds breathe in dust carrying E. coli, especially in closed, poorly ventilated houses.
High ammonia from wet, caked litter damages the airways and lets bacteria in; if the house smell stings your eyes, ammonia is too high.
Dirty or cracked hatching eggs, poor hatchery hygiene and chicks with unhealed navels lead to yolk sac infections in the first week.
Contaminated drinking water, dirty drinkers and stagnant water in free-range compounds spread bacteria between birds.
Other diseases weaken birds first: Newcastle disease, infectious bronchitis, Gumboro (IBD), Mycoplasma, coccidiosis and worms often open the door to E. coli.
Stress from chilling or overheating during brooding, overcrowding, transport, sudden feed changes and poor nutrition lowers resistance.
Rodents, wild birds, flies and dirty boots, crates or equipment carry contaminated droppings between houses and farms.
Mycotoxins (poisons from mouldy feed) weaken the immune system and make outbreaks more likely.
detail.atRisk: All poultry can be affected, including chickens, turkeys, ducks and quails. Young chicks in their first one to two weeks are at high risk of yolk sac infection, especially those from poorly managed hatcheries or hatched from dirty eggs under hens. Broilers between about three and eight weeks are commonly hit by airsacculitis and blood infection, often a few days after a respiratory virus or vaccination. Laying hens, particularly at the start of lay and in peak production, are prone to egg peritonitis and salpingitis. Risk rises in deep-litter and closed houses with poor ventilation, wet litter and overcrowding, common in zero-grazing style urban and peri-urban units. During the long and short rains, litter gets wet and ammonia builds up, while in cold nights people close curtains tightly and trap gases. In the dry, dusty season, dust levels rise. Kienyeji flocks are often more hardy but suffer losses in chicks hatched in dirty nests and in birds weakened by Newcastle disease or worms.

early: Birds are dull, sleepy and stand hunched with ruffled feathers, often away from the feeder.
Reduced feed and water intake, and broilers stop gaining weight evenly so the flock looks uneven in size.
Sneezing, a wet rattling sound or gurgling when you listen to the flock quietly at night.
Chicks with wet, red, swollen or scabbed navels and a bloated, soft belly; they may huddle near the heat source.
A small rise in daily deaths, often a few birds each day rather than many at once.
Pasty or watery diarrhoea, sometimes greenish or yellowish, soiling the vent feathers.
advanced: Open-mouth breathing, gasping and tail bobbing with each breath as the air sacs fill with pus.
Lameness, with hot, swollen hocks or foot joints, and birds sitting down and unwilling to walk.
Swelling of the head and around the eyes in broilers (swollen head syndrome), sometimes with one eye cloudy or closed.
In layers, a sharp drop in egg production, birds standing upright like a penguin with a swollen, hanging belly, and hens that stop laying for good.
Rough, yellowish or thickened skin patches over the belly or thighs in broilers (cellulitis), often noticed at slaughter.
Steadily rising deaths, with dead chicks that smell foul, and birds that become thin and stunted if they survive.

lookalikes.name: Newcastle disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Newcastle disease usually spreads very fast with many deaths in a few days, plus nervous signs such as twisted necks, circling and paralysis, and greenish diarrhoea. E. coli is often slower with a steady trickle of deaths. The two often occur together, so a vet and post-mortem are needed; Newcastle disease must be reported to the County Veterinary Officer.

lookalikes.name: Chronic respiratory disease (Mycoplasma gallisepticum)
lookalikes.howToTell: Mycoplasma causes slow-building respiratory signs with foamy eyes, swollen sinuses under the eyes and nasal discharge over weeks. It very often comes together with E. coli, which then causes the cheesy pus on heart and liver seen at post-mortem. Only lab tests can confirm Mycoplasma.

lookalikes.name: Pullorum disease and fowl typhoid (Salmonella)
lookalikes.howToTell: Pullorum causes white, chalky diarrhoea that pastes the vents of young chicks, while fowl typhoid causes sudden deaths in growers and adults with a swollen, bronze-coloured liver. These look very similar to E. coli infections and need lab culture to tell apart; your vet will advise if reporting is needed.

lookalikes.name: Fowl cholera and infectious coryza
lookalikes.howToTell: Fowl cholera often causes sudden deaths in adult birds with swollen, purple wattles and combs. Infectious coryza causes a swollen face with a sticky, foul-smelling nasal discharge spreading quickly through older birds. E. coli swollen head syndrome is mainly in young broilers and usually follows a viral infection.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will look at the flock history, ventilation, litter and recent vaccinations or illness, then examine live birds. The most useful step is a post-mortem (opening up freshly dead or sick, humanely killed birds). Typical findings include a thick, white-to-yellow cheesy layer covering the heart (pericarditis), liver (perihepatitis) and cloudy, thickened air sacs; infected, foul-smelling yolk sacs in chicks; and yolk-like material in the belly of layers. Because these findings can also be caused by Salmonella, Mycoplasma or others, the vet will often send samples to a laboratory such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete, a regional or county veterinary lab, or a university or private lab. The lab grows the bacteria (culture) and runs an antibiotic sensitivity test, which shows which drugs will actually work, important because resistant E. coli are common. Tests for underlying viruses or Mycoplasma may also be done. To help, keep records of daily deaths, feed and water intake, egg numbers, vaccination dates and any drugs already given. Bring two to four freshly dead or sick birds, kept cool in a clean sealed bag, and do not give antibiotics before samples are taken if you can avoid it, because this can hide the bacteria.
firstSteps: Separate obviously sick, lame or gasping birds into a clean, dry, draught-free pen with easy access to feed and fresh water.
Remove wet, caked litter, especially around drinkers, and add fresh dry litter such as wood shavings; do not wait for the end of the batch.
Improve ventilation by opening curtains or windows on the side away from strong wind, so the ammonia smell clears while birds are not chilled.
Clean and disinfect drinkers and feeders daily, provide fresh clean water, and check that the water source is safe.
Keep chicks at the correct brooding temperature; watch their spread under the heat source and adjust so they are neither crowded nor gasping.
Collect dead birds promptly, wearing gloves, keep a few fresh ones cool for the vet, and bury deeply or burn the rest away from the house and water.
Write down the number of sick and dead birds each day, feed and water use, egg numbers, and recent vaccines or drugs.
Call your vet or County Veterinary Office and do not buy or give antibiotics from the agrovet until a vet has examined the flock and advised you.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on the form of disease and what the lab finds. Vets usually treat the whole flock through the drinking water with an antibiotic, ideally chosen using a sensitivity test. Drug classes commonly used for poultry E. coli include tetracyclines, penicillins such as amoxicillin, and sulphonamides combined with trimethoprim; some drugs such as fluoroquinolones (for example enrofloxacin) and colistin are considered critically important for human medicine and should only be used when a vet decides nothing else will work. Doses and length of treatment must be prescribed by a vet, and the full course must be completed. Every antibiotic has a withdrawal period, a set time after treatment when eggs and meat must not be eaten or sold; follow the label and the vet's instructions exactly, and remember some drugs are not allowed at all in laying hens. Misuse, such as under-dosing, stopping early or routinely adding antibiotics to water, is a major reason E. coli in Kenya has become resistant, which means future treatment fails. The vet will also tackle the underlying cause, for example reviewing Newcastle, infectious bronchitis and Gumboro vaccination, Mycoplasma control, coccidiosis and worms, and housing. Expect birds with mild airsacculitis to improve within a few days if conditions are fixed. Chicks with yolk sac infection, layers with egg peritonitis and birds with badly swollen joints usually respond poorly, and the vet may advise humane culling of these birds.
prevention: Buy day-old chicks only from reputable, licensed hatcheries and check on arrival for dry, healed navels, bright eyes and active chicks; for kienyeji, set only clean, uncracked eggs and keep nests clean and dry.
Prepare the brooder properly before chicks arrive: clean and disinfect, use dry litter, pre-heat, and keep a steady temperature with chick guards to stop chilling and crowding.
Keep litter dry and loose by fixing leaking drinkers and roofs, raising drinkers to the right height, turning litter regularly and replacing wet patches, especially in the rainy seasons.
Control ammonia and dust with good ventilation day and night; adjust curtains rather than sealing the house shut on cold nights.
Provide clean drinking water from a safe source, clean drinkers daily, and consider water sanitation as advised by your vet or extension officer.

Vaccinate on time against Newcastle disease, infectious bronchitis and Gumboro according to your vet's or hatchery's schedule, as these diseases open the door to E. coli; ask your vet whether an E. coli vaccine is suitable and available for your farm.
Avoid overcrowding, practise all-in-all-out with a full clean-out and rest period between batches, and keep birds of different ages apart.
Practise biosecurity: footbaths, dedicated boots and clothes, control of rodents, wild birds and flies, and limit visitors and shared crates.
Feed a balanced, fresh ration stored off the floor in a dry place, avoid mouldy feed, and control worms and coccidiosis to keep the gut and immune system strong.
