Collect eggs often from clean nest boxes so eggs are not soiled, and do not use dirty or cracked eggs for hatching.
detail.impact: Colibacillosis is one of the costliest poultry problems on Kenyan farms because it causes a steady flow of losses rather than one dramatic event. Chick deaths in the first week reduce the number of birds you can sell and waste money spent on chicks and brooding. Broilers that survive are often stunted and uneven, eat feed without gaining well, and may be condemned or downgraded at slaughter because of pus on the organs or skin cellulitis. In layers, egg peritonitis kills hens and causes others to stop laying permanently, and production drops can last weeks. Farmers also spend money on drugs, often more than once if the wrong antibiotic is chosen, and must throw away or not sell eggs and meat during withdrawal periods. Repeated use of antibiotics builds resistance on the farm, making each new outbreak harder and more expensive to control.
detail.humanHealth: The E. coli strains that cause disease in chickens are not usually a major direct threat to people, but some can be related to strains that cause urine or blood infections in humans, and chicken droppings can also carry other germs. Antibiotic-resistant E. coli from poultry can pass to farm workers and consumers through droppings, poor hand hygiene and undercooked meat. Wash hands with soap after handling birds, litter or dead chickens, wear gloves and boots when cleaning, keep children away from sick birds, and cook chicken and eggs thoroughly. Never eat or sell eggs or meat from treated birds before the withdrawal period is over, because drug residues can cause allergies in some people and add to antibiotic resistance.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends on how early the problem is caught and whether the underlying causes are fixed. Flocks with mild airsacculitis often recover well once ventilation, litter and water are improved and the correct antibiotic is used. Birds with advanced disease, chicks with yolk sac infection, layers with egg peritonitis and birds with chronically swollen joints rarely return to full production, and culling is often the kindest and most economical choice. If ammonia, poor hygiene or other diseases are not dealt with, the problem tends to come back in every batch, and treatment becomes less effective as resistance builds.

faqs.q: Can I just buy an antibiotic at the agrovet and put it in the water?
faqs.a: It is better not to. E. coli in Kenya is often resistant to commonly used antibiotics, so a drug chosen by guessing may not work, wastes money and builds more resistance on your farm. Many other diseases look similar, some of which antibiotics cannot help, such as Newcastle disease. A vet can examine the flock, do a post-mortem and, ideally, a sensitivity test to choose a drug that works, and tell you the correct withdrawal period for eggs and meat.

faqs.q: Why are my chicks dying in the first week with big, smelly bellies?
faqs.a: This is usually yolk sac infection, also called omphalitis. Bacteria enter through dirty or cracked eggs at hatching or through an unhealed navel. Chilling, overheating and dirty brooders make it worse. Treatment rarely saves badly affected chicks, so talk to your supplier about chick quality, check navels on arrival, and make sure your brooder is clean, dry and at the right temperature.

faqs.q: Is it safe to eat eggs or meat from a flock with E. coli?
faqs.a: Eggs and meat from healthy-looking birds are safe if cooked thoroughly and the birds have not been treated recently. If the flock has received antibiotics, you must wait for the full withdrawal period on the label or given by your vet before eating or selling. Do not eat or sell birds that were sick or died.

faqs.q: Does E. coli spread from one chicken to another like Newcastle disease?
faqs.a: Not in the same way. E. coli is already present in every flock. It causes disease mainly when birds are weakened by ammonia, dust, dirty water, poor brooding or another disease. That is why fixing housing and hygiene is the most important step, along with vaccinating against the viral diseases that open the door to it.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine for E. coli?
faqs.a: Some E. coli vaccines exist for poultry in other countries and may be available through some suppliers in Kenya, but they do not cover every strain and are not a replacement for hygiene. Ask your vet whether one is suitable for your farm. Much more important for most farmers is vaccinating on time against Newcastle disease, infectious bronchitis and Gumboro.

faqs.q: Why does the problem keep coming back in every batch?
faqs.a: Repeated outbreaks usually mean the root cause is still on the farm: wet litter, poor ventilation, a poor chick source, dirty water, crowding, mixing ages, or an underlying disease like Mycoplasma. A full clean-out and rest between batches, better ventilation, and a vet visit to review vaccination and management usually make the biggest difference.

products.role: A probiotic that supports healthy gut bacteria. It can help keep the gut balanced as part of good management and may help the gut recover after a vet-prescribed antibiotic course. Ask your vet about timing during treatment. It does not treat E. coli infection or replace hygiene, vaccination or vet care.

An oral rehydration solution that helps dull, feverish birds keep drinking and stay hydrated while they recover under vet treatment. It is also useful during hot weather or after transport, when stress can trigger outbreaks. It supports recovery but does not cure the infection.

colibacillosis.imagePrompt: A realistic photo inside a Kenyan deep-litter poultry house showing several young broiler chickens standing hunched with ruffled feathers and half-closed eyes, one breathing with its beak open, on damp, caked litter near a drinker.
colibacillosis.seoDescription: Colibacillosis (E. coli) in chickens: dull birds, yolk infections, swollen joints and airsacculitis. First steps, vet care and prevention in Kenya.

card.headline: Sudden deaths and dark sticky droppings
card.look: Well-grown broilers, often 2 to 5 weeks old, suddenly sit hunched with ruffled feathers and half-closed eyes. Some are found dead without warning. Droppings turn dark brown to black, sticky and foul-smelling, and the litter gets wet.
card.action: Remove dead birds at once, keep two or three fresh ones cool (not frozen) and call your vet today for a post-mortem and treatment plan.

detail.summary: Necrotic enteritis is a bacterial disease of the chicken's small intestine. It is caused by toxins from Clostridium perfringens, a germ that lives in most chicken guts at low levels. When the gut is damaged, often by coccidiosis or a sudden feed change, the bacteria multiply and kill the gut lining. It matters because it can kill many fast-growing broilers close to market age, and the milder hidden form quietly wastes feed and slows growth across the whole flock.
detail.cause: The cause is Clostridium perfringens, a bacterium found in soil, dust, litter, feed and the normal chicken gut. On its own, in small numbers, it does little harm. The problem starts when something upsets the gut. Coccidia (tiny parasites that cause coccidiosis) damage the gut wall and make it leak protein into the gut. That protein is perfect food for the clostridia, which multiply very fast. Disease-causing strains produce powerful toxins (poisons), especially one called NetB, that destroy the lining of the small intestine. The gut wall becomes thin, swollen with gas and covered in a yellow-brown, dead layer that vets describe as looking like a rough towel. A damaged gut cannot absorb food or water, and toxins can pass into the blood and liver. This is why birds become dull, stop eating and can die within hours. In the milder, hidden (subclinical) form, the gut is only partly damaged, so birds survive but grow slowly, convert feed poorly, and their livers may be rejected at slaughter.
spread: Clostridium perfringens is already present on almost every poultry farm, so the disease is mostly triggered by stress on the gut rather than brought in from outside.
Coccidiosis is the most common trigger, because the parasites damage the gut wall and open the door for the bacteria.
A sudden change of feed, for example switching from starter to grower overnight or changing feed brands, upsets gut bacteria and can set off an outbreak.
Diets very high in protein, especially fishmeal (including omena-based feeds) or rich animal protein, feed the clostridia.
Feeds with a lot of wheat, barley or bran fibre can make gut contents sticky and slow-moving, which favours bacterial overgrowth.
Wet, caked litter and dirty drinkers allow spores (tough, long-lasting resting forms of the bacteria) to build up, and birds pick them up by pecking.
Mouldy feed containing mycotoxins (poisons produced by fungi) and immune-damaging diseases such as Gumboro (IBD) weaken the bird's defences.
Spores survive for a long time in litter, soil and equipment, so a house with past outbreaks carries a higher risk for the next flock.
detail.atRisk: Broilers between about 2 and 6 weeks old are most at risk, with many outbreaks around 3 to 4 weeks, when growth is fastest and coccidia challenge is high. Layer pullets and kienyeji or improved kienyeji chickens on deep litter can also be affected, as can turkeys. Risk is highest in deep-litter houses with high stocking density, poor ventilation and wet bedding, which is common in the long and short rains when humidity rises and litter stays damp. Flocks that recently had coccidiosis, Gumboro or a feed change are at special risk. Farms that use high-fishmeal home-mixed rations, buy feed of uncertain quality, or reuse old litter without cleaning are also more exposed. Free-range birds are less often affected, but it can still happen where they share damp, crowded night shelters.

early: A sudden rise in deaths in birds that looked healthy the day before, sometimes the first and only sign.
Birds sitting hunched and quiet with ruffled feathers and half-closed eyes, reluctant to move when you walk through the house.
Reduced feed intake: feeders stay fuller than usual and birds crowd less at feeding time.
Droppings that are darker than normal, brown to black, sticky or tarry, sometimes with a reddish tint.
A stronger, rotten smell in the house than usual and patches of wet, caked litter.
In the hidden form, the flock simply grows slower and eats more feed per kilo of weight gained, with uneven bird sizes.
advanced: Many birds lying down, unable or unwilling to stand, with dull combs and dehydrated, shrunken appearance.
Diarrhoea that is very dark, watery or foamy and foul-smelling, staining the vent feathers.
Deaths rising quickly over a few days, with dead birds often still in good body condition.
Dead birds swelling and decomposing faster than normal because of gas-forming bacteria in the gut.
When a vet opens a bird, the small intestine is thin, ballooned with gas, fragile and lined with a yellow-green or brown crusty layer, with a very bad smell.
At slaughter, livers may be enlarged, pale or spotted and get condemned, even in birds that seemed to recover.

lookalikes.name: Coccidiosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Coccidiosis often causes fresh red blood or bloody, mucus-like droppings, especially caecal coccidiosis in young birds, and lesions are often in the caeca (blind gut pouches). Necrotic enteritis droppings are more dark, sticky and foul-smelling, and the small intestine is gassy with a crusty lining. The two often occur together, so a vet post-mortem and a smear test are needed.

lookalikes.name: Newcastle disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Newcastle usually shows breathing problems (gasping, coughing), nervous signs such as twisted necks and paralysis, greenish diarrhoea, and a sharp drop in eggs in layers. It spreads fast to birds of all ages, including free-range kienyeji flocks. Necrotic enteritis does not cause nervous or breathing signs and is mostly linked to gut stress in growing broilers. Newcastle is notifiable, so report any suspicion.

lookalikes.name: Fowl typhoid and other Salmonella infections
lookalikes.howToTell: Fowl typhoid often causes greenish-yellow diarrhoea, pale combs and deaths in older birds and layers, and the vet finds an enlarged, bronze-coloured liver. Necrotic enteritis mainly damages the small intestine and gives dark, sticky droppings. Lab culture separates them.

lookalikes.name: Gumboro disease (IBD)
lookalikes.howToTell: Gumboro usually hits 3 to 6-week-old birds with whitish watery droppings, pecking at the vent, and trembling. At post-mortem the bursa (a small gland near the vent) is swollen or bloody and leg muscles may show bleeding. Gumboro can also trigger necrotic enteritis by weakening immunity, so both may be present.

detail.diagnosis: A vet usually suspects necrotic enteritis from the flock history (age, recent coccidiosis or feed change, sudden deaths) and confirms it by post-mortem. Opening fresh birds shows the typical thin, gassy, fragile small intestine with a dead, crusty lining. The vet or lab may take a smear from the gut lining and see large numbers of rod-shaped bacteria under the microscope, grow the bacteria in culture, and check for coccidia at the same time. Liver samples may be examined, and feed may be tested for mycotoxins if mouldy feed is suspected. In Kenya, your private vet, County Veterinary Officer or a regional veterinary investigation laboratory can help, and the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete handle more detailed tests. To help, keep two to four birds that died within the last few hours, or sick live birds, in a cool box or plastic bag in a cool place, but do not freeze them because freezing spoils the gut lesions. Write down the bird age, number of deaths per day, feed type and any recent feed change, vaccination dates, any past coccidiosis treatment, and any drugs already given. Keep a sample of the current feed.
firstSteps: Collect dead birds immediately, at least twice a day, so healthy birds do not peck them and pick up more bacteria; keep a few fresh ones cool for the vet and dispose of the rest by deep burial or burning away from water sources.
Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer the same day, because this disease can move fast and the right treatment depends on a proper diagnosis.
Separate clearly sick, dull birds into a clean, dry pen with fresh bedding, clean water and feed close by so they do not have to walk far.
Remove wet, caked litter around drinkers and feeders, add fresh dry bedding, and fix leaking drinkers so the floor stays dry.
Give plenty of clean, fresh drinking water and wash drinkers daily, since sick birds lose fluid through diarrhoea.
Do not make any more sudden feed changes while waiting for the vet, and stop feeding any feed that smells musty or looks mouldy; keep a sample for testing.
Improve ventilation by opening curtains on the side away from the wind, while avoiding cold draughts on the birds.
Wear boots and overalls only for that house, wash hands well after handling birds, and keep visitors out to avoid carrying spores to other houses.
Record daily deaths, feed and water use and bird age, which will help the vet decide on treatment and withdrawal timing.
detail.vetTreatment: Necrotic enteritis is a bacterial disease, so a vet will usually prescribe an antibiotic that works against clostridia, given in the drinking water for a set number of days. Drug groups commonly used include penicillins such as amoxicillin, as well as tylosin, lincomycin or bacitracin, depending on what is registered and available in Kenya and on any lab sensitivity results. Because coccidiosis is often the trigger, the vet may also prescribe an anticoccidial drug such as amprolium or toltrazuril, or adjust the coccidiosis control programme. The vet will also look at feed, litter and water management, because drugs alone will not stop repeat outbreaks. Only a vet should choose the drug and the dose; never guess the amount or use leftover medicine. Birds that are badly affected may still die even with treatment, but deaths usually slow down within a few days if the cause is correct. Every antibiotic and anticoccidial has a withdrawal period, which is the time after the last dose before meat or eggs are safe to sell or eat. Broilers are often close to slaughter when this disease hits, so plan sale dates with your vet and never sell treated birds early. Use antibiotics only when prescribed and finish the full course. Overuse and underdosing help bacteria become resistant (antimicrobial resistance), which makes future treatment harder for animals and people.
prevention: Control coccidiosis well, using a coccidiosis vaccine for chicks or an anticoccidial programme in feed or water as advised by your vet, because preventing gut damage from coccidia is the single most important step.
Keep litter dry and loose: use enough wood shavings or rice husks, turn the litter regularly, fix leaking drinkers, and avoid overcrowding, especially during the long and short rains.
Change feeds gradually over three to five days by mixing the old and new feed, rather than switching from starter to grower or between brands overnight.

Buy balanced feed from trusted mills and avoid rations with too much fishmeal or poor-quality animal protein; if you mix your own feed, follow a proper formulation from an extension officer or nutritionist.
Store feed dry, off the floor and away from walls, and never feed mouldy or caked feed, since mycotoxins weaken the gut and immunity.
Vaccinate against Gumboro, Newcastle and other diseases according to your vet or hatchery schedule, because a healthy immune system resists clostridial overgrowth.
Between flocks, remove all old litter, clean and disinfect the house and equipment, and leave the house empty for at least two weeks to reduce the build-up of spores.
Support a healthy gut with good-quality water, clean drinkers, and gut-health aids such as probiotics or acidifiers used as advised, alongside good management rather than in place of it.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan broiler farm, necrotic enteritis can be costly because it usually strikes when birds have already eaten most of their feed and are only days or weeks from sale. Sudden deaths mean lost birds that were nearly ready for market. Survivors often grow unevenly and eat more feed for each kilo of weight, which cuts profit when feed is the biggest expense. The hidden form may never be noticed but steadily lowers weights and raises feed costs batch after batch. Treatment costs money, and withdrawal periods can delay sale, upsetting agreements with buyers, hotels or brokers. Livers may be condemned at slaughter, and wet litter raises ammonia and breast blisters, lowering carcass quality. Repeat outbreaks in the same house can make broiler keeping unprofitable until hygiene and coccidiosis control are improved.
detail.humanHealth: The necrotic enteritis strains of Clostridium perfringens mainly harm chickens, but other strains of the same bacterium are a well-known cause of food poisoning in people, usually from meat that is cooked and then left warm for hours. Never eat or sell birds that died or were sick, and dispose of carcasses safely. Cook chicken thoroughly, eat it soon after cooking, and refrigerate leftovers quickly. Wash hands with soap after handling birds, droppings or litter. The main human risk on farms is drug residues: if birds were treated with antibiotics or anticoccidials, strictly observe the meat and egg withdrawal periods given by your vet so that residues do not reach consumers.
detail.outlook: Outlook depends on how fast the problem is recognised and treated and whether the trigger is removed. With early vet diagnosis, correct antibiotic treatment and control of coccidiosis, deaths usually fall within a few days and most remaining birds recover. Birds that are already lying down and badly dehydrated often do not survive. Recovered birds may stay smaller and less efficient because the gut lining takes time to heal, and some may have liver damage. If litter stays wet, coccidiosis is not controlled or feed problems continue, outbreaks often return in the same or next flock. Good management between flocks greatly improves the chances of avoiding it next time.

faqs.q: My broilers looked fine yesterday and today several are dead. Could it be necrotic enteritis?
faqs.a: It could be. Sudden deaths in well-grown broilers, especially around 3 to 5 weeks, with dark sticky droppings and wet litter, are typical. But Newcastle, Gumboro, coccidiosis, heat stress and poisoning can also cause sudden deaths. Keep two or three fresh dead birds cool, not frozen, and get a vet to do a post-mortem the same day so you treat the right disease.

faqs.q: Can I just buy an antibiotic at the agrovet and put it in the water?
faqs.a: Please do not treat on guesswork. The wrong drug, wrong dose or a short course may not work, wastes money, leaves residues in meat and eggs, and helps germs become resistant. Many antibiotics also have withdrawal periods that may clash with your sale date. Let a vet confirm the cause and prescribe the drug, dose and length of treatment.

faqs.q: Why does necrotic enteritis keep coming back after coccidiosis?
faqs.a: Coccidia damage the gut wall and cause it to leak protein, which feeds Clostridium perfringens and lets it multiply. If coccidiosis is not well controlled, necrotic enteritis often follows within days. Work with your vet on a coccidiosis vaccine or anticoccidial programme and keep litter dry, because wet litter helps coccidia spread.

faqs.q: Is it safe to sell my broilers after they recover?
faqs.a: Only after the full withdrawal period of every drug they received has passed, as told by your vet or written on the drug label. Selling earlier risks drug residues in the meat, which is unsafe and illegal. Never sell or eat birds that are sick or died of the disease.

faqs.q: Can probiotics or herbal products replace antibiotics for this disease?
faqs.a: No. Once birds are sick and dying, they need a vet diagnosis and usually prescribed treatment. Probiotics, acidifiers and good nutrition can support gut health and help prevent future problems, but they do not cure an active outbreak. If the vet prescribes an antibiotic in the water, ask when to give a probiotic, because antibiotics can kill the helpful bacteria in the product.

faqs.q: Do I need to change my feed to stop this disease?
faqs.a: Not always, but feed matters. Avoid sudden changes, use balanced feed from a trusted supplier, and be careful with rations very high in fishmeal or poor-quality protein. Never feed mouldy feed. If outbreaks repeat, ask your vet or an extension officer to check your ration and keep a feed sample for testing.

products.role: A probiotic that helps build up beneficial gut bacteria and supports coccidiosis prevention, which reduces the gut damage that lets Clostridium perfringens take over. Use it as part of prevention and during recovery alongside vet treatment, coccidiosis control and dry litter, not as a cure; ask your vet about timing if antibiotics are being given in the water.

An oral rehydration solution that helps sick and recovering birds replace fluid and salts lost through diarrhoea and keeps them drinking. It supports comfort and recovery while the vet-prescribed treatment works, but it does not treat the infection itself.

necrotic-enteritis.imagePrompt: A realistic photo of a dull broiler chicken sitting hunched with ruffled feathers and half-closed eyes on damp wood-shaving litter in a poultry house, with dark brown sticky droppings visible on the litter beside it.
necrotic-enteritis.seoDescription: Necrotic enteritis in broilers: spot sudden deaths and dark sticky droppings, act before the vet arrives, and prevent it with coccidiosis and litter control.

card.headline: Wet, swollen navel and big belly
card.look: Day-old to week-old chicks with a red, wet or scabby navel and a soft, swollen, bluish belly. They huddle under the heat source, look sleepy, and some die each day in the first week.
card.action: Separate weak chicks, check that brooder heat, water and litter are right, and call your vet or agrovet animal health officer to examine chicks and open a dead one.

detail.summary: Navel and yolk sac infection is a bacterial infection of the navel and the leftover yolk inside the belly of newly hatched chicks. It is one of the most common causes of chick deaths in the first week of life. It is not usually a disease that sweeps from chick to chick. It is a sign that something went wrong with egg hygiene, incubation or the first hours after hatching. Fixing those causes protects every future batch.
detail.cause: When a chick hatches, it pulls the remaining egg yolk into its belly through the navel. That yolk is its packed lunch for the first two to three days. The navel should then close and dry within about a day. If bacteria get in, either through dirty eggshells during incubation or through a navel that has not closed properly, they multiply quickly in the warm, nutrient-rich yolk. The most common germ is E. coli, a gut bacterium found in droppings. Others include Staphylococcus, Streptococcus and Enterococcus, Pseudomonas, Proteus and sometimes Clostridium. The infected yolk is not absorbed. Instead it turns watery, greenish, brown or cheesy and often smells foul. The chick loses its first food supply, becomes weak and dehydrated, and bacteria can spread into the blood and cause inflammation of the belly lining. Many chicks die within the first few days. Survivors are often stunted. Poor incubation conditions make it worse: too high humidity, temperature swings or too-early hatching leave navels large, wet and open, so germs get in easily.
spread: Dirty, cracked or droppings-stained eggs set in the incubator or under a hen carry bacteria on the shell, and these germs can move through the shell pores into the egg, especially when a warm egg cools and 'sucks in' air and dirt.
Washing eggs with dirty or cold water, or wiping them with a wet cloth, can push bacteria through the shell instead of removing them.
A dirty incubator, hatcher, egg trays or chick boxes that were not cleaned and disinfected between batches pass germs from one hatch to the next.
Incubator problems common with small and locally made machines, such as power cuts, temperature swings and humidity that is too high, cause poorly healed, wet navels that infect easily.
Exploding rotten eggs in the incubator spray large numbers of bacteria over other eggs and newly hatched chicks.
Wet, dirty or reused litter in the brooder, and dirty drinkers and feeders, expose open navels to droppings in the first hours after placement.
Rough handling, long transport and chilling or overheating of day-old chicks lower their defences and make infection more likely to become serious.
Under kienyeji hens, dirty damp nests, nests shared with sick birds, and a hen that comes back with muddy or soiled feathers can contaminate eggs.
detail.atRisk: Chicks in the first 7 days of life are at risk, with most deaths in the first 3 to 5 days; a few may die up to about 2 to 3 weeks. Broilers, layers, improved kienyeji and indigenous chickens can all be affected, and the same problem occurs in ducklings, turkey poults and quail. Chicks from young or old parent flocks, from small or very large eggs, and from flocks with poor nutrition tend to be weaker. Risk is higher for chicks from small-scale or home incubators with unreliable power, from hatcheries with poor hygiene, and for chicks that travelled far before reaching the farm. Wet seasons such as the long and short rains bring more dirty eggs, damp nests and wet litter. Cold nights in highland areas make chilled chicks more likely to suffer.

early: Navel that looks red, swollen, wet, or has a dark scab or a small string of dried tissue still attached.
Belly that feels soft, swollen and mushy when gently held, and may look bluish or dark through the skin.
Chicks that are sleepy, droop their wings and stand with eyes half closed while others are active.
Chicks crowding tightly under the brooder heat or lamp even when the temperature is correct.
Weak chirping or constant distressed peeping, and chicks that are slow to go to feed and water.
Pasty or wet feathers around the vent and belly, and a sour or rotten smell from the chick or the chick box.
advanced: Chicks lying on their side or unable to stand, and being trampled by others.
Very swollen, tight or discoloured belly with dull, ruffled down.
Severe weakness, dehydration with shrivelled-looking legs, and no interest in food or water.
Rising daily deaths in the first week, often with a foul smell when dead chicks are handled.
Survivors that stay small, uneven and slow-growing compared with the rest of the batch.

lookalikes.name: Pullorum disease or other Salmonella infection
lookalikes.howToTell: Salmonella can also infect the yolk, but it is often passed from infected parent hens through the egg and tends to cause white, chalky droppings pasting the vent, gasping, and deaths that continue into the second and third week. Only lab testing of dead chicks can separate them, so let your vet send samples.

lookalikes.name: Brooder pneumonia (aspergillosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: This is a fungal infection from mouldy litter or feed. Chicks gasp, breathe with open mouths and may have watery eyes, while the navel looks normal. At post-mortem the vet finds yellow or green nodules in the lungs and air sacs rather than a rotten yolk.

lookalikes.name: Chilling, overheating or starve-out
lookalikes.howToTell: Chicks that are too cold pile up under the heat, and overheated chicks pant and spread away from it, but their navels are clean and dry. Starve-out chicks have empty crops and never found feed or water, and their yolk is usually absorbed or small rather than swollen and smelly.

lookalikes.name: Coccidiosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Coccidiosis is caused by gut parasites and is rare before about 10 days of age. It shows as bloody or watery droppings, ruffled birds and deaths usually from the third week onward, not swollen navels in the first days.

detail.diagnosis: Your vet will look at the history of the batch, including where the eggs or chicks came from, incubation conditions, transport, and the pattern of deaths. They will examine live chicks, feel the bellies and look at the navels. The most useful step is a post-mortem, which means opening a freshly dead chick. In yolk sac infection the yolk is large and not absorbed, its contents are watery, lumpy, greenish, brown or cheesy, and it often smells foul; the belly lining may be inflamed. The vet may send yolk samples or whole chicks to a laboratory, such as a County or regional veterinary lab, to grow the bacteria and test which antibiotics still work against them. This is called culture and sensitivity, and it also helps rule out Salmonella. To help, keep three to five freshly dead chicks cool in a clean, sealed bag in the fridge, not the freezer. Write down the hatch date, chick source, number placed, daily deaths, brooder temperature, and what feed, water additives or medicines have been given.
firstSteps: Move clearly weak, swollen-bellied chicks to a separate warm box so they are not trampled and so you can watch them closely.
Check the brooder temperature at chick level and watch the chicks' behaviour: comfortable chicks spread evenly, so adjust the heat source, draughts and ventilation until they do.
Make sure clean, fresh drinking water is available right away and placed close to the heat, and dip the beaks of weak chicks gently into the water to teach them to drink.
Replace wet or caked litter with clean, dry wood shavings, and wash and refill drinkers and feeders at least daily.
Wash your hands well after handling chicks and dead birds, and keep children from handling sick chicks.
Remove dead chicks promptly, keep a few fresh ones cool for the vet, and bury the rest deeply or burn them away from the house and water sources.
Record daily deaths and symptoms, and inform the hatchery or chick supplier quickly, since many will want to know and may help if the problem came from the hatchery.
Call your vet or a qualified animal health officer before giving any antibiotic or medicine, and do not mix random drugs into the water.
detail.vetTreatment: Yolk sac infection responds poorly to treatment once the yolk has rotted, because medicines cannot easily reach the dead yolk material. Badly affected chicks with a hard, swollen, discoloured belly rarely recover, and the vet will usually advise humane culling of these chicks to end their suffering and protect the batch. For the rest of the batch, especially if deaths are high, the vet may prescribe an antibiotic in the drinking water, chosen ideally after culture and sensitivity testing. Antibiotic classes sometimes used against E. coli and similar bacteria in poultry include some tetracyclines, sulphonamide combinations, amoxicillin and others, but resistance is common in Kenya and the right choice depends on the lab result. Only a vet should prescribe the drug, the dose and the length of treatment. Giving antibiotics 'just in case' to every batch of chicks speeds up antimicrobial resistance, which means these drugs stop working for animals and people. If broilers are treated, the withdrawal period on the label must be followed before birds are sold or eaten, which is especially important for short-cycle broilers. Alongside medicine, the vet will focus on supportive care: correct heat, water, feed and dry litter. Expect deaths to drop off after the first week as surviving chicks outgrow the risk, and expect the vet to help you trace the source so it does not happen again.
prevention: Collect eggs at least two to three times a day from clean, dry nests with fresh bedding, and use only clean, uncracked, normal-shaped eggs for hatching.

Do not set eggs heavily soiled with droppings; lightly soiled eggs can be dry-cleaned gently, and if washing is needed use clean water warmer than the egg and an approved egg sanitiser, then dry them well.
Store hatching eggs in a cool, clean place for no more than about a week before setting, and avoid sweating, which happens when cold eggs are moved into warm, humid air.
Clean and disinfect the incubator, hatcher, trays, chick boxes and brooder thoroughly between every batch, and remove any cracked, leaking or rotten eggs during candling.
Run the incubator at the temperature and humidity recommended for its model, use a reliable thermometer and hygrometer, and plan backup power such as a generator, battery or solar for power cuts.
Buy day-old chicks only from licensed, reputable hatcheries with good hygiene and reject chicks that arrive with wet, open or scabbed navels.

Prepare the brooder before chicks arrive: preheated, draught-free, with clean dry litter, clean drinkers and feeders, and the correct brooder temperature so chicks can drink and eat within the first hours.

Keep parent and breeder flocks healthy and well fed with correct vitamins and minerals, follow their vaccination and deworming programme, and test breeders for Salmonella where possible, because stronger parents give stronger chicks.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan farm, the losses come fast and early. Every chick that dies in the first week has already cost the price of the chick or the hatching egg, transport, brooding fuel or electricity, and starter feed. A batch with heavy yolk sac infection may lose a noticeable share of chicks, and survivors are often uneven and slower growing, which hurts broiler weights at market and delays the start of lay in layers. Farmers who sell day-old or week-old chicks, including improved kienyeji producers, can lose customers and reputation if chick quality is poor. Extra costs for vet visits, lab tests and medicines add up, and unnecessary antibiotic use raises the risk of residues and resistance.
detail.humanHealth: The bacteria involved, especially E. coli and any Salmonella, can live on chicks, eggs, litter and chick boxes, and some strains can cause stomach upsets or more serious illness in people. Young children, older people, pregnant women and anyone with a weak immune system are most at risk. Wash hands with soap and water after handling chicks, eggs, litter or dead birds, do not let children kiss or cuddle chicks, and keep chicks out of kitchens and eating areas. If birds have been treated with antibiotics, follow the vet's withdrawal period before selling or eating birds or eggs to avoid drug residues.
detail.outlook: Chicks with a clearly rotten, swollen yolk sac usually die or remain stunted, even with treatment. Chicks with only a mildly inflamed navel and a soft belly may recover with good warmth, water and feed. In most outbreaks deaths peak in the first few days and fall away after the first week. The long-term outlook for the farm is good if the cause is found and corrected: clean eggs, good incubator hygiene and settings, good chick sources and a well-prepared brooder usually bring the problem under control in the next batches.

faqs.q: Can this infection spread from sick chicks to my healthy ones?
faqs.a: It is not mainly a contagious disease. Most chicks are infected before or just after hatching, from dirty eggs, the incubator or the hatchery. However, sick and dead chicks shed large numbers of bacteria into the litter and water, so removing them quickly and keeping the brooder clean protects chicks whose navels are still healing.

faqs.q: Should I put antibiotics in the water for every new batch of chicks to prevent this?
faqs.a: No. Routine antibiotics for every batch do not fix the real causes, which are egg hygiene, incubation and brooding. They also cost money and drive antimicrobial resistance, so the drugs stop working when you really need them. If you have repeated losses, ask your vet to do a post-mortem and lab test, then follow their advice and fix the hygiene problems.

faqs.q: The chicks came from a hatchery. Is it my fault?
faqs.a: Often the problem starts at the hatchery or with the parent flock, especially when many chicks show wet navels on arrival and deaths start on day one or two. Poor transport and brooding can make it worse. Record the hatch date, arrival condition and daily deaths, keep some dead chicks for your vet, and contact the supplier quickly with this information.

faqs.q: My home incubator keeps giving chicks with big bellies and wet navels. What should I check?
faqs.a: Check that the thermometer and humidity reading are accurate, because high humidity and temperature swings are common causes of poorly healed navels. Clean and disinfect the machine fully between batches, set only clean eggs, remove rotten eggs at candling, and plan backup power for outages. Follow the manufacturer's settings for your model.

faqs.q: Can I treat the navel by applying something on it?
faqs.a: Painting navels does not usually help, because the infection is mostly inside, in the yolk. Handling chicks a lot can also spread germs and stress them. Focus on clean, dry litter, correct warmth and early water and feed, and ask your vet before using any product on the chicks.

faqs.q: How do kienyeji farmers using hens to hatch eggs prevent this?
faqs.a: Give the hen a clean, dry nest box with fresh bedding, away from damp corners and droppings. Change soiled bedding during sitting, do not add very dirty eggs under her, and keep the area free of rats and mites. After hatching, give chicks clean water and feed and keep them dry, especially during the rains.

products.role: An oral rehydration solution that can be added to clean drinking water to help weak or travel-stressed chicks take in fluids and electrolytes in the first days while you correct brooding conditions and get vet advice. It supports hydration only; it does not treat the infection, and brooder temperature must still be kept correct.

Vitamins A, D3 and E for parent or breeder hens can support good egg quality, hatchability and chick vigour when their diet is short of these vitamins, as one part of preventing weak chicks. It does not prevent or treat infection on its own and works only alongside clean eggs, incubator hygiene and good brooding.

omphalitis.imagePrompt: Close-up photo of a day-old yellow chick held gently upside down in a cupped hand, showing a red, wet, swollen navel and a soft, bulging bluish belly, with a brooder and wood-shaving litter softly blurred in the background.
omphalitis.seoDescription: Navel and yolk sac infection (omphalitis) in chicks: spot the wet swollen navel and big belly, act early, and stop early chick deaths with hatchery hygiene.

card.headline: Pale, slow-growing birds with bruising
card.look: Several birds in the flock look pale in the comb, wattles and legs, grow slowly or lay fewer eggs, and may show bruises under the skin. The problem often starts soon after a new batch of feed or grain, especially in damp weather.
card.action: Stop feeding the suspect feed straight away, keep a sample of it, and call your vet.

detail.summary: Mycotoxin poisoning happens when birds eat feed containing poisons made by moulds (fungi). The most important in Kenya is aflatoxin, which grows on damp or badly stored maize, groundnuts and oilseed cakes. It damages the liver, weakens the immune system and makes vaccines work poorly, so a flock can suffer slow growth, egg drop and repeated disease outbreaks without an obvious cause. Because the poison is invisible and the feed can look normal, many farmers lose money for weeks before they realise the feed is the problem.
detail.cause: Mycotoxins are poisons produced by certain moulds as they grow on grain and feed ingredients. Aflatoxins are made mainly by Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus, moulds that thrive in warm, humid conditions and on grain that was harvested wet, dried poorly or stored in damp, leaking stores. Maize, maize bran, groundnut cake, cottonseed cake and sunflower cake are common sources. Other mycotoxins also affect poultry: ochratoxin damages the kidneys, T-2 toxin (from Fusarium moulds) causes sores in the mouth and beak corners, and fumonisins and other toxins add to the harm. Feed is often contaminated with more than one toxin at once, and their effects can add up. Once eaten, aflatoxin is absorbed from the gut and carried to the liver, which is the organ that processes poisons. The liver becomes damaged, swollen, pale or yellow and fragile. A damaged liver cannot make enough protein, including the proteins that help blood clot, so birds bruise and bleed easily. Fat and the yellow pigments in feed are absorbed poorly, which is why combs, shanks and egg yolks turn pale. Aflatoxin also shrinks the bursa and thymus, the organs where young birds build their immune defences, so birds catch other diseases easily and respond weakly to vaccines. The damage depends on how much toxin is in the feed and how long birds eat it; low levels over weeks cause silent losses, while high levels can cause deaths.
spread: It is not contagious: birds do not catch it from each other, and every affected bird has eaten contaminated feed.
Grain that was harvested during or just after rain, or left on the ground or in heaps before drying, can carry mould into the feed.
Poor storage is a major trigger: feed bags stacked directly on the floor or against damp walls, leaking roofs, and hot, humid stores let mould grow after the feed leaves the mill.
Wet feeders and spilled feed that gets damp in the litter can grow mould inside the poultry house within days.
Buying cheap or poorly stored maize, maize bran, groundnut cake or sunflower cake from unknown sources raises the risk.
Keeping feed too long, especially in the long and short rains, gives mould more time to grow and produce toxin.
Insect and rodent damage to grain opens the kernels and lets mould enter more easily.
detail.atRisk: All poultry can be affected, but sensitivity varies. Ducks and ducklings are especially sensitive, turkeys and quails are also highly sensitive, and chickens are somewhat more tolerant, though they still suffer losses. Young birds such as chicks, poults and ducklings are hit harder than adults. Fast-growing broilers show poor growth and weight gain, while layers show egg drop and poor shells. Risk is highest during and after the long and short rains, in humid coastal and lake regions, and when harvests were wet. Farms that mix their own feed from locally bought maize and cakes, and zero-grazing or semi-intensive units that store large amounts of feed, are at higher risk. Kienyeji chickens that scavenge on mouldy grain, spoiled food scraps or brewer's waste can also be exposed.

early: Birds eat less, grow more slowly than expected and the flock looks uneven in size.
Combs, wattles, shanks and skin look pale, and broiler skin is less yellow than normal.
Layers produce fewer eggs, and eggs may be smaller with paler yolks.
Feed conversion worsens: birds eat the feed but do not gain weight well.
Birds look dull, ruffled and less active, especially young birds.
Vaccinated flocks still get diseases like Gumboro or Newcastle, or other infections seem to keep coming back.
Watery or pale droppings may be seen in some birds.
advanced: Bruises and small bleeding spots appear under the skin, on the legs, wings and breast, even with light handling.
Birds become weak, lame or reluctant to stand, and may sit with eyes half closed.
Egg shells become thin or soft and egg production can drop sharply.
In ducklings and young birds, deaths rise and some may have shaking or unsteady walking before dying.
If T-2 toxin is involved, yellowish crusty sores appear at the corners of the beak and inside the mouth.
If ochratoxin is involved, birds drink a lot, droppings are very wet and litter becomes soaked.
At post-mortem the liver is enlarged, pale or yellow and breaks easily, and the bursa may be small.

lookalikes.name: Gumboro (infectious bursal disease)
lookalikes.howToTell: Gumboro usually strikes chicks around 3 to 6 weeks old suddenly, with many birds sick within days, white watery droppings and deaths that peak and fall within about a week. Aflatoxin problems build up slowly, affect birds of any age, and follow a change of feed. The two often happen together, because aflatoxin weakens vaccine protection against Gumboro.

lookalikes.name: Newcastle disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Newcastle often causes coughing, gasping, greenish diarrhoea, twisted necks and rapid spread with high deaths across the flock. Aflatoxin poisoning has no breathing signs or twisted necks and does not spread from bird to bird or farm to farm.

lookalikes.name: Coccidiosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Coccidiosis causes bloody or reddish-brown droppings, huddled birds and is linked to wet litter, usually in young birds. Aflatoxin causes pale birds and bruising rather than bloody droppings, and a vet can check gut samples for coccidia to tell them apart.

lookalikes.name: Fatty liver haemorrhagic syndrome
lookalikes.howToTell: This affects overweight laying hens in high production, often with sudden deaths from liver bleeding while the rest of the flock looks well. Aflatoxin affects birds of all body conditions, causes pale combs and bruising across many birds, and is linked to the feed batch; a feed test settles the question.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will look at the flock history, the timing of signs and any recent change of feed, then examine live birds and open some dead or sick birds (post-mortem). An enlarged, pale or yellow, crumbly liver, a small bursa, bruising and bleeding in the muscles strongly suggest aflatoxin. The vet may send liver samples for laboratory tissue examination (histopathology). The most important test is analysis of the feed itself: laboratories at KALRO, the universities, the Government Chemist and some private and feed-company labs can measure aflatoxin and other mycotoxins, and some vets and agrovets use rapid test kits. Because mould grows in patches, a single handful can miss the toxin. To help, collect small amounts from many places in the bag or store (top, middle, bottom, several bags), mix them, and keep around one kilogram in a clean, dry, labelled bag in a cool place. Write down the feed brand, batch number, date bought and supplier, keep receipts, and record egg numbers, weights, feed intake and deaths day by day. Bring a few freshly dead or sick birds to the vet if asked.
firstSteps: Stop feeding the suspected feed immediately and replace it with fresh feed from a trusted source, ideally a different batch or supplier.
Keep a well-mixed sample of the old feed in a labelled bag, and keep the remaining bags aside rather than throwing them away, in case they need testing or you need to discuss them with the supplier.
Empty, scrub and dry all feeders, and remove caked, wet or mouldy feed and litter around feeders and drinkers.
Make sure every bird has plenty of clean, fresh water at all times, and place feed and water where weak birds can reach them easily.
Separate very weak, lame or badly bruised birds into a clean, quiet, dry pen so they are not trampled and can eat without competition.
Handle birds gently, because their skin and muscles bruise and bleed easily.
Wear a dust mask and gloves when handling mouldy feed or litter, and wash your hands afterwards.
Record dates, feed batches, egg numbers, weights and deaths, then call your vet or County Veterinary Officer before giving any medicines or vaccinating.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no antidote that removes aflatoxin or reverses the poison once it is inside the bird, so treatment focuses on stopping exposure and helping the liver recover. The vet's first step is confirming the feed source and switching to clean feed. They will usually advise adding a mycotoxin binder (an ingredient such as certain clays or yeast cell wall products that holds toxins in the gut so less is absorbed) to the new feed, and may raise the protein quality of the diet, since a damaged liver needs good protein and amino acids such as methionine to repair. Vitamin supplements, especially vitamins A, D3, E and K and selenium, are commonly used because aflatoxin increases the need for them and vitamin K helps blood clotting. If birds already have secondary bacterial infections, the vet may prescribe an antibiotic, but antibiotics do not treat the toxin itself, and using them without a clear need adds cost and drives antimicrobial resistance, where drugs stop working for animals and people. Only use medicines prescribed by a vet, follow the label, and observe egg and meat withdrawal periods, which is the time after treatment when eggs and meat must not be sold or eaten. Because vaccines may have failed, the vet may also review your vaccination programme and advise when and whether to revaccinate once birds recover. Most flocks start to improve within one to several weeks after clean feed is given, but badly damaged birds may never return to full production.
prevention: Buy feed only from reputable, licensed feed millers and agrovets, check the manufacture date and batch number, and avoid bags that are damp, lumpy, musty-smelling, discoloured or caked.
Buy only as much feed as your flock will finish in about two to three weeks, especially during the long and short rains, so feed does not sit long enough to grow mould.
Store feed bags on wooden pallets off the floor and away from walls, in a dry, cool, well-ventilated store with a sound roof, and keep rats and insects out.

If you mix your own feed, dry maize and other grain well, to the safe moisture level of around 13.5% or lower recommended for maize, sort out rotten, discoloured, shrivelled or insect-damaged kernels, and never use visibly mouldy grain or cakes.
Use a mycotoxin binder in the feed as a routine safeguard during high-risk seasons or when you cannot be sure of ingredient quality, while still prioritising clean feed.
Clean feeders regularly, fill them with only what birds will eat in a day, place drinkers so they do not wet the feed, and replace wet litter around feeders.
Never feed birds mouldy bread, spoiled food scraps, mouldy brewer's waste or rotten grain, including to free-range kienyeji chickens.
Give a well-balanced diet with adequate protein, vitamins and minerals, and keep your vaccination and parasite control programmes up to date so birds are better able to cope.
detail.impact: Aflatoxin often causes silent, ongoing losses that farmers blame on poor chicks or bad luck. Broilers take longer to reach market weight and eat more feed for each kilogram gained, eating into already thin margins. Layers lay fewer and smaller eggs with weaker shells, raising breakages and rejected trays. Bruised carcasses may be downgraded or rejected by buyers. The biggest hidden cost is immune suppression: vaccines against Newcastle, Gumboro and other diseases may fail, leading to disease outbreaks, extra vet bills, medicine costs and deaths. Ducklings and young birds can die in large numbers on highly contaminated feed. A farmer may also lose money on bags of feed that cannot be used. Because laying flocks that suffer severe liver damage may not fully return to peak lay, the losses can last for the rest of the flock's life.
detail.humanHealth: Aflatoxin does not spread from birds to people as an infection, but it is a serious human poison. It damages the liver and is a known cause of liver cancer with long-term exposure, and Kenya has experienced deadly human aflatoxin poisoning from contaminated maize. Small amounts of aflatoxin and its breakdown products can pass into eggs and especially into the liver of poisoned birds, so avoid eating the livers of affected birds and follow your vet's advice on when eggs and meat are safe to use again. Never give mouldy maize or feed meant for animals to people, and do not try to 'clean' mouldy grain for home use. Dust and spores from mouldy feed and litter can cause breathing problems and, rarely, lung infection with Aspergillus mould, especially in people with weak immunity, so wear a dust mask and gloves when handling mouldy material and wash afterwards. Observe withdrawal periods for any medicines your vet prescribes.
detail.outlook: The outlook is usually fair to good if the contaminated feed is found and removed early and the toxin levels were moderate. Most birds start eating better and growing again within days to a few weeks on clean feed, and egg numbers gradually recover. Recovery is slower and less complete when birds ate highly contaminated feed for a long time, when young birds or ducks were affected, or when secondary diseases took hold because of immune suppression. Some birds with severe liver damage may stay stunted or poor layers and may need to be culled after discussion with your vet. The key to a good outcome is acting quickly, preventing re-exposure and supporting the flock through recovery.

faqs.q: The feed looks fine and does not smell bad. Can it still have aflatoxin?
faqs.a: Yes. Aflatoxin itself has no colour or smell, and feed can be contaminated even when you cannot see mould, because the toxin stays after the mould has died or been ground up in the mill. Visible mould, musty smell, lumps or dampness are warning signs, but clean-looking feed is not proof of safety. Only a laboratory test or a reliable test kit can tell you the toxin level.

faqs.q: Can I dry mouldy feed in the sun and use it again?
faqs.a: No. Drying stops more mould growing, but it does not destroy the aflatoxin already made. Heating, cooking or sun drying do not make poisoned feed safe. Mouldy feed should not be fed to poultry, other livestock or people; ask your vet or County Veterinary Officer how to dispose of it safely.

faqs.q: My birds were vaccinated, so why did they get Gumboro or Newcastle?
faqs.a: Aflatoxin weakens the immune organs, so birds may not build strong protection after vaccination. Vaccine failure can also come from poor vaccine storage, wrong timing or poor water quality, so discuss all these with your vet. If aflatoxin is confirmed, your vet can advise how to plan revaccination once birds are on clean feed.

faqs.q: Is a toxin binder enough on its own?
faqs.a: No. A binder reduces how much toxin is absorbed, and it is a useful safety net, but it cannot make heavily contaminated feed safe and it does not repair liver damage that has already happened. Clean feed, good storage and buying from reliable suppliers always come first, with a binder as extra protection.

faqs.q: Are the eggs and meat safe to eat?
faqs.a: Only small amounts of aflatoxin pass into eggs and meat, with more ending up in the liver. Avoid eating livers from affected birds, and ask your vet when eggs and meat can safely be used again, especially if birds received any medicines with withdrawal periods. Once birds have been on clean feed for some time, residues fall away.

faqs.q: Can I complain to the feed supplier?
faqs.a: You can, and a tested sample makes your case much stronger. This is why you should keep a labelled sample, the bag with its batch number and your receipt. You can also report suspected poor-quality feed to the Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) or seek advice from your County Veterinary Officer.

products.role: A mycotoxin binder mixed into feed to help reduce how much aflatoxin and ochratoxin birds absorb from the gut. Useful as a routine safeguard in the rainy seasons and when changing to new feed after an outbreak. It cannot make mouldy feed safe or reverse liver damage, so always remove contaminated feed and follow your vet's advice.
Supports liver function and digestion while birds recover on clean feed after aflatoxin exposure. It is an aid alongside vet care, vitamins and good nutrition, not a cure for liver damage.

mycotoxicosis.imagePrompt: A realistic close-up photo of a pale, dull-looking young chicken in a Kenyan poultry house, with a pale comb and wattles and small purple bruises visible under the skin of its leg and wing, standing beside a feeder of feed with greenish mould patches.
mycotoxicosis.seoDescription: Aflatoxin poisoning in poultry: spot pale birds, poor growth, bruising and egg drop from mouldy feed. Learn first steps, vet diagnosis and prevention in Kenya.

card.headline: Open-mouthed panting with wings held out
card.look: Birds pant with beaks open, hold their wings away from the body and crowd near water, walls or fans. They eat less, drink much more, and heavy broilers may collapse or die suddenly in the hottest part of the day.
card.action: Cool the house right away: open all sides for airflow, give plenty of clean, cool drinking water, and stop handling or moving the birds until evening.

detail.summary: Heat stress happens when chickens take in or make more heat than they can get rid of. Chickens have no sweat glands and are covered in feathers, so they cool themselves mainly by panting and spreading their wings. In hot, humid weather this is not enough, and they lose appetite, growth, egg numbers and shell quality. Heavy broilers and high-producing layers can die within hours, so it is a real money problem on Kenyan farms, especially in hot lowland areas and in the hot dry months.
detail.cause: Chickens feel most comfortable at moderate temperatures, roughly the high teens to mid-twenties °C for grown birds. As the air gets hotter, the bird's body struggles to shed heat. Heat also builds up inside the bird from digesting feed and from growing or laying, so fast-growing broilers and busy layers make a lot of their own heat. The bird's main cooling method is panting. This loses water and also blows out too much carbon dioxide from the blood. That upsets the blood's acid balance, a state vets call respiratory alkalosis. One result is that less carbonate is available to build eggshells, so shells become thin and crack easily. The bird also drinks much more water and eats much less feed, so growth and laying drop. If body temperature keeps rising, the heart and circulation cannot keep up, blood thickens from water loss, and the bird becomes weak, collapses and can die. High humidity makes all of this worse, because panting cools far less well when the air is already wet. Crowding, poor ventilation and hot iron roofs push the inside of a house well above the temperature outside.
spread: Heat stress does not spread from bird to bird; it is caused by the environment and how birds are housed and managed.
Hot spells and the hot dry months, such as January to March and the weeks before the short rains, are common triggers in many parts of Kenya.
Hot, humid areas such as the Coast, the Lake Victoria basin and other lowlands carry a higher year-round risk than cool highland areas.
Houses with bare iron-sheet roofs, no ceiling, low walls, closed sides or poor airflow trap heat and can be much hotter inside than outside.
Overcrowding raises the heat in the house because every bird gives off body heat.
Shortage of drinking water, warm water from tanks or pipes in the sun, or too few drinkers quickly turns a hot day into a deadly one.
Handling, catching, vaccinating, weighing or transporting birds during the hottest hours greatly increases the risk of sudden deaths.
Feeding a full crop just before the hottest part of the day adds digestive heat at the worst moment.
detail.atRisk: Broilers close to market weight, usually from about four weeks of age onwards, are at the highest risk because they are heavy, grow fast and make a lot of body heat. High-producing commercial layers at peak lay are also very vulnerable, and heavy breeder birds too. Improved breeds suffer more than kienyeji (indigenous) chickens, which are smaller and generally handle heat better, although kienyeji birds can still suffer when confined in hot houses or kept without shade and water. Birds in deep-litter or cage systems under iron roofs, overcrowded flocks, and birds kept in hot humid lowland counties face the most danger. Risk peaks between late morning and late afternoon, and during the hot dry season and sudden hot spells. Birds already weakened by disease, worms or poor feed cope worse.

early: Birds breathe with their beaks open and pant quickly, and you may see the throat fluttering.
Wings are held out and away from the body to let heat escape.
Birds drink far more than usual and crowd around drinkers, and droppings become wetter and more watery.
Feed intake drops, especially at midday, and birds stop moving around and look dull.
Birds spread out, press against walls, lie on cool floors or move towards any breeze or shade.
Combs and wattles may look pale or, in some birds, darker and flushed.
Layers produce fewer eggs, and shells become thin, rough or easily cracked, with more soft-shelled eggs.
advanced: Birds become weak, wobble or cannot stand, and may lie flat with legs stretched out and wings drooped.
Panting becomes laboured, then slows down as the bird tires, which is a very bad sign.
Birds stop responding when you approach and may have their eyes half closed.
Heavy broilers die suddenly, often several at once in the afternoon or soon after, and the heaviest birds are usually the first to die.
Growth slows clearly across the flock and broilers miss their target market weight.
Egg production falls sharply and more eggs are small or misshapen.

lookalikes.name: Newcastle disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Newcastle disease also causes gasping and deaths, but it spreads through the flock regardless of the weather and often brings green watery diarrhoea, nasal discharge, swelling around the eyes, twisted necks, paralysis and a sudden stop in laying. Heat stress improves quickly once the house is cool, and deaths happen mainly in the hottest hours. If birds stay sick in the cool of the evening and morning, suspect disease and call the vet.

lookalikes.name: Infectious bronchitis and chronic respiratory disease (CRD)
lookalikes.howToTell: These respiratory infections cause sneezing, coughing, rattling or gurgling breath sounds, watery eyes and nasal discharge. Heat-stressed birds pant fast and open-mouthed but have clean nostrils and eyes and no rattling sounds. Infectious bronchitis also causes thin or wrinkled shells, so if shell problems continue in cool weather, ask the vet to check.

lookalikes.name: Acute fowl cholera or other bacterial infections
lookalikes.howToTell: Sudden deaths can look similar, but fowl cholera often shows purple or dark swollen combs and wattles, yellow-green diarrhoea, swollen joints and deaths at any time of day and in any weather. A post-mortem by a vet separates them.

lookalikes.name: Ascites (water belly) in broilers
lookalikes.howToTell: Ascites also causes heavy broilers to breathe hard and die, but these birds have a swollen, soft, fluid-filled belly and a bluish comb, and it is more common in cool highland areas and at altitude. Heat stress birds have normal bellies and recover when cooled.

detail.diagnosis: Heat stress is usually diagnosed from the history and the setting: hot weather, birds panting with wings out, more drinking, less eating and deaths clustered in the hottest hours, with birds improving once it cools. A vet or animal health officer will examine live birds to rule out infectious diseases such as Newcastle disease, infectious bronchitis or fowl cholera, which can look similar or happen at the same time. A post-mortem of freshly dead birds may show dehydration, congested (blood-filled) organs and lungs, and no signs of infection; the vet may send samples to a laboratory if disease is suspected. You can help a great deal by preparing: record the highest temperature inside the house each day (a simple maximum-minimum thermometer hung at bird height is very useful), the time and number of deaths, how much water and feed the flock used, egg numbers and shell problems, the age and breed of the birds, and recent vaccinations. Keep one or two freshly dead birds cool in a sealed bag, but do not freeze them, so the vet can open them.
firstSteps: Open all curtains, doors and windows straight away and remove anything that blocks airflow, so hot air can escape and a breeze can pass through the house.
Give plenty of clean, cool drinking water, add extra drinkers, and shade water tanks and pipes or replace warm water with fresh water several times a day.
Stop catching, vaccinating, weighing, moving or transporting birds during the hot hours, and do any necessary work only in the early morning or evening.
Remove feed for a few hours before and during the hottest part of the day, then feed in the cool early morning and evening, so birds are not digesting during peak heat.
Cool the house from outside: wet the roof or lay wet sacks or grass on the roof, plant or put up shade, and if you have fans, switch them on to move air over the birds.
Gently move collapsed birds to a shaded, airy, cooler spot with water within reach, and avoid dunking birds in cold water, which can shock them.
Reduce crowding by moving some birds to another house or a shaded run if you can, and spread out litter that is wet and smelly.

Remove dead birds quickly, record the number and time of deaths, and call your vet or animal health officer if deaths continue, or if birds are still sick in the cool of the evening, in case a disease is also present.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no medicine that cures heat stress; the real treatment is cooling the birds and fixing the housing and management. A vet or animal health officer will first make sure no infectious disease is involved, then advise on ventilation, stocking density, water supply and feeding times. They may recommend adding electrolytes (salts that replace those lost through panting and wet droppings) and vitamins, especially vitamin C and E, to the drinking water during hot spells. Some vets advise sodium bicarbonate or other additives to help the blood's acid balance and eggshell quality, and some anti-stress or fever-reducing products exist; these should only be used on a vet's advice because the wrong mix can upset salt balance and harm the birds. Antibiotics do not treat heat stress and should not be used unless the vet confirms a bacterial infection, because unnecessary antibiotic use builds antimicrobial resistance, which makes medicines fail for animals and people. If any medicine is prescribed, follow the label and the vet's instructions and respect the egg and meat withdrawal periods, the time you must wait before selling eggs or slaughtering birds. Once cooled, most birds start eating and drinking normally again within hours, though growth and laying may take days to weeks to recover.
prevention: Build or improve houses for airflow: face the long side across the main wind direction, keep side walls low with wire mesh above, raise the roof height, and add roof overhangs to keep out direct sun.
Insulate or cool the roof by adding a ceiling, painting iron sheets white or silver, putting a thatch or grass layer on top, or planting shade trees around the house.
Do not overcrowd; follow the space recommendations for your bird type and reduce numbers in the hot season, especially for broilers near market weight.
Make sure there is always enough clean, cool water, with extra drinkers in hot weather, shaded tanks and buried or shaded pipes, because birds may drink about twice as much in heat.
Feed in the cool early morning and evening, and plan to sell or slaughter broilers before the hottest months where possible.
Do all catching, vaccination, debeaking and transport in the early morning, late evening or at night, and never pack birds tightly in hot vehicles.
Use electrolytes, vitamins and anti-stress supplements in the water before and during expected hot spells and stressful events, as advised by your vet or agrovet.

Keep birds healthy with good vaccination, worm control and quality feed free of mould, because sick or weakened birds cope much worse with heat, and keep a thermometer in the house so you can act before birds start dying.
detail.impact: Heat stress costs Kenyan poultry farmers money in several ways. Broilers eat less, grow slower and take longer to reach market weight, which means more days of feed costs and lower selling weights, and sudden deaths of the heaviest birds just before sale hit profits hardest. Layers lay fewer eggs, eggs are smaller, and thin or cracked shells mean more broken eggs, more rejects at the market and lower prices. Feed is used less efficiently, so the cost of producing each kilogram of meat or tray of eggs rises. Heat-stressed birds also have weaker immunity, so outbreaks of other diseases and vaccination failures become more likely. For small-scale farmers with a few hundred birds, one hot afternoon with poor ventilation can wipe out a large part of the profit of the batch.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good when the problem is caught early. Most birds recover quickly once the house is cooled and they have water, often within a few hours. Birds that have collapsed, stopped panting strongly or cannot stand are much less likely to survive, and heavy broilers near market weight are the most likely to die. Growth and egg production usually recover over days to weeks, but a flock that suffers repeated hot spells may never reach its full potential. Long-term success depends mainly on better housing, ventilation, stocking and water supply rather than on any single product.

faqs.q: Why are my eggshells thin when the weather is hot?
faqs.a: When hens pant to cool down, they breathe out too much carbon dioxide, which upsets the acid balance of the blood. This leaves less material to build the shell, and hens also eat less feed, so they take in less calcium. The result is thin, rough or soft shells. Cooling the house, feeding in the cool hours, keeping good calcium in the layer feed and following your vet's advice on additives all help. If shell problems continue in cool weather, ask the vet to check for diseases such as infectious bronchitis.

faqs.q: Should I give my chickens ice-cold water or pour water on them?
faqs.a: Cool, fresh water is very helpful, but there is no need for ice. Changing warm water for fresh water several times a day is usually enough. Do not dunk birds in cold water or soak them heavily, as this can shock them, and in humid areas wet birds and wet litter make things worse. It is better to cool the roof, improve airflow and move collapsed birds to a shaded, breezy place.

faqs.q: Can I use antibiotics to stop the deaths?
faqs.a: No. Heat stress is caused by the environment, not by germs, so antibiotics will not help and waste money. Using antibiotics without need also builds antimicrobial resistance and can leave residues in eggs and meat. Only use antibiotics if a vet examines your birds and finds a bacterial infection, and then respect the withdrawal period.

faqs.q: When is the best time to feed during a heat wave?
faqs.a: Feed in the cool early morning and again in the evening, and remove feed for a few hours before and during the hottest part of the day. Digesting feed makes heat inside the bird, so a full crop at midday adds to the danger. Always keep water available, even when feed is removed.

faqs.q: Do kienyeji chickens get heat stress too?
faqs.a: Yes, though less often than broilers and commercial layers. Kienyeji chickens are smaller, grow more slowly and are adapted to local conditions, so they handle heat better. But if they are locked in hot houses, crowded, or left without shade and water on a hot day, they can still suffer and even die. Give them shade, water and space to move to cooler spots.

faqs.q: My house has an iron-sheet roof. What can I do without spending a lot?
faqs.a: Iron roofs get very hot. Cheap fixes include laying grass, thatch or wet sacks on the roof, painting it white, adding a simple ceiling of polythene or sacks with an air gap, planting shade trees, and raising curtains during the day to let air through. Reducing the number of birds in the house during the hot season also makes a big difference.

products.role: An oral rehydration and heat-stress relief solution for the drinking water that helps replace water and salts lost through panting and wet droppings during hot spells; use it alongside cooling, ventilation and plenty of clean water, not instead of them.

An osmolyte (a substance that helps cells hold water) added to feed that can help birds stay better hydrated and keep up performance in hot weather; it supports birds through the hot season as part of good housing and management, but does not replace cooling or treat collapsed birds.

heat-stress.imagePrompt: A realistic photo of a white broiler chicken standing on wood-shavings litter inside a warm poultry house, beak wide open while panting and both wings held slightly out and away from its body, with other birds crowded near a water drinker in the background.
heat-stress.seoDescription: Heat stress in chickens: spot panting, spread wings and thin eggshells early, cool birds fast and prevent sudden broiler deaths in Kenya's hot season.

card.headline: Fat hens dying suddenly, pale combs
card.look: Heavy, well-fed caged layers that looked healthy are found dead with no warning, often with very pale combs. Live hens in the same cages may have pale, scaly combs and egg numbers start to drop.
card.action: Take a freshly dead hen to a vet or veterinary laboratory for a post-mortem, and check how much and what feed the hens are getting.

detail.summary: Fatty liver haemorrhagic syndrome (FLHS) is a nutrition and management problem of laying hens. Too much fat builds up in the liver until it becomes soft and weak, and it can suddenly bleed inside the belly, killing the hen. It mostly hits overweight, high-producing hens in cages that eat high-energy feed and get little exercise. It is not an infection, but it quietly costs farmers their best layers and a lot of eggs.
detail.cause: A laying hen's liver works very hard. Under the influence of the female hormone oestrogen, it makes large amounts of fat and yolk material that are sent to the ovary to build eggs. When a hen eats more energy than she needs, especially from starchy grains like maize, the liver makes more fat than it can send out. The extra fat stays in the liver cells. Over weeks the liver becomes enlarged, yellow, greasy and very fragile, like overripe pawpaw. Small blood vessels in this weak liver tear easily. A small tear causes a small bleed and the hen may recover, but a bigger tear causes heavy bleeding into the belly and the hen dies within minutes to hours. Hens with many small bleeds lose blood slowly, which is why their combs turn pale. Other things make the damage worse: hot weather (hens need less energy but keep eating), lack of exercise in cages, too little calcium in the feed (hens eat more to find calcium), mouldy feed containing aflatoxin (a poison made by moulds that damages the liver), and shortages of nutrients that help the liver move fat out, such as choline, methionine, vitamin E and selenium. Experts agree the main driver is too much energy for too little work, but the exact mix of causes varies between farms.
spread: It does not spread from bird to bird. It is not caused by a germ, so it cannot be passed by contact, eggs, droppings or visitors.
The main trigger is feeding too much energy, for example giving layers mash freely all day or adding extra maize, maize bran or other starchy grain to a complete layer feed.
Home-mixed rations that are heavy on maize and light on protein, calcium and vitamins raise the risk, because the hen eats more to meet her needs and stores the extra energy as fat.
Hot weather is a known trigger, especially the hot dry months before the long rains, because hens need less energy to keep warm but often eat the same amount.
Lack of exercise in battery cages or crowded houses means the hens burn little energy and get fat more quickly.
Feed contaminated with moulds and aflatoxin, a common problem with damp-stored maize in Kenya, can damage the liver and make fatty liver worse.
Sudden stress such as rough handling, catching, chasing by rats or dogs, loud noise or vaccination can cause a fragile liver to tear and bleed in hens that are already affected.
detail.atRisk: Laying hens at or after peak production are most at risk, especially high-producing commercial layer breeds kept in cages. Hens that are heavier than the breed's target weight are the main victims, and the best layers are often the ones that die because their livers are working hardest. Commercial caged layer units in peri-urban areas such as Kiambu, Nakuru, Machakos and Kajiado are where most Kenyan cases are seen, along with deep-litter layers that are overfed. Flocks fed freely all day, or fed complete layer mash plus extra grain, are at high risk. Cases rise in hot months. Kienyeji and improved kienyeji chickens on free range rarely get it because they walk, scratch and forage, using up energy, though overfed confined indigenous birds can still be affected. Broilers and young pullets are rarely affected; males are not affected because it is linked to egg-laying hormones.

early: Hens look fat and heavy when lifted, with a large soft belly and thick fat that you can feel under the skin around the vent and abdomen.
Egg production drops slowly below what the flock was laying, even though the hens look well fed and are eating normally.
Some combs and wattles become pale, and may look dry or scaly, instead of being bright red.
The flock is eating a lot of feed, more than the bag or breed guide suggests for their age.
One or two good layers are found dead with no illness seen beforehand, often under or near the feeder.
