advanced: Sudden deaths continue, a few birds at a time, mostly among the heaviest and best-laying hens.
Dead birds have very pale combs, wattles and skin, because they bled internally.
Some live hens become dull, sit quietly and stop laying, and may have a swollen, heavy belly.
Eggs become fewer and the flock never returns to its expected laying level.
When a dead hen is opened, the belly contains a large blood clot, and the liver is big, yellow or orange, greasy and breaks apart easily when touched.
The belly and organs are surrounded by large amounts of yellow fat.

lookalikes.name: Newcastle disease (kideri)
lookalikes.howToTell: Newcastle usually kills many birds quickly across all ages, with coughing, gasping, twisted necks, paralysis and green watery droppings. FLHS kills a few fat hens at a time with no breathing or nervous signs, and the post-mortem shows a blood clot around a fatty liver.

lookalikes.name: Fowl typhoid and fowl cholera
lookalikes.howToTell: These bacterial diseases make birds visibly sick before death: drowsy, ruffled feathers, fever, yellow-green or watery diarrhoea, and often swollen wattles in cholera. Deaths are often higher and hit birds of all weights. At post-mortem the liver may be bronze-coloured or have white spots rather than being yellow, greasy and bleeding. Laboratory tests tell them apart.

lookalikes.name: Heat stroke
lookalikes.howToTell: Heat stroke deaths happen on very hot afternoons, with many birds panting, wings held out and lying flat before dying. Dead birds often have dark combs. FLHS deaths are scattered over days or weeks, can happen in cool weather, and show a clot in the belly.

lookalikes.name: Egg peritonitis and egg binding
lookalikes.howToTell: Egg peritonitis hens stand upright like a penguin, stop laying and slowly waste, and the belly contains yolk or smelly material rather than a blood clot. Egg-bound hens strain at the vent and an egg can be felt stuck. FLHS deaths are sudden with fresh blood in the belly.

detail.diagnosis: FLHS is confirmed mainly by post-mortem examination, which means opening a dead bird to look inside. A vet or veterinary laboratory will find a large blood clot in the belly, a swollen, yellow, greasy liver that crumbles easily, and lots of belly fat. They may look at a piece of liver under the microscope. Because sudden deaths in layers can also come from Newcastle disease, fowl typhoid, fowl cholera or poisoning, the vet may take samples to rule these out, and may test the feed for aflatoxin. You can help by bringing one or two birds that died within the last few hours, kept cool but not frozen, in a sealed bag. Also bring or write down: the age and breed of the flock, number of birds, how many have died and when, daily egg numbers, how much feed the flock eats per day, the feed brand or your home-mix recipe, any extra grain or kitchen waste given, and recent weather and housing changes. If you have a scale, weighing ten hens and comparing with the breed target weight is very useful.
firstSteps: Remove dead birds quickly and take one or two fresh ones to your vet, County Veterinary Officer or nearest veterinary laboratory for a post-mortem, because other serious diseases can also cause sudden deaths.
Stop adding any extra maize, maize bran, bread, ugali leftovers or other starchy foods on top of the layer feed, and feed only a good complete layer ration.

Check how much feed you are giving against the feed company or breed guide for the hens' age, and stop leaving feeders full all day if you have been overfeeding; do not starve the hens or cut feed sharply without advice, as this can crash egg production.
Look at your feed and stored grain for mould, caking, bad smell or damp, and stop using any feed that looks mouldy.
Handle hens calmly and as little as possible, avoid chasing and catching, and keep dogs, rats and noise away, because stress can cause fragile livers to bleed.
Keep the house cool and airy with open sides, shade on the roof, and plenty of clean, cool drinking water at all times.
Make sure the hens are getting enough calcium, for example from a good layer feed, and ask your vet or feed adviser before adding limestone or shell grit.
Record daily deaths, egg numbers and feed used so the vet can see the pattern and you can tell whether changes are working.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no medicine that cures a liver that has already bled badly, and hens with heavy internal bleeding usually die. Treatment is mainly about correcting the diet and management so that the rest of the flock stops getting worse. A vet or poultry nutritionist will typically review the ration and feeding method, reduce the total energy the hens eat (for example by controlled feeding rather than free access, or by changing the ration), and make sure protein, calcium and phosphorus are balanced. They may advise replacing part of the starchy energy with a small amount of fat or oil, which some references show can reduce liver fat production, and providing calcium partly in coarse particles such as limestone grit. They may recommend lipotropic supplements, meaning nutrients that help the liver move fat out, such as choline, methionine, vitamin E, selenium and B vitamins; these can help but results vary, and they do not replace diet correction. If aflatoxin is found or suspected, they will advise changing the feed and possibly using a mycotoxin binder. Antibiotics do not treat FLHS because it is not an infection, and using them without a proper diagnosis wastes money, may leave residues in eggs, and adds to antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to drugs. If the vet finds a bacterial infection as well and prescribes a drug, follow their instructions and respect the egg withdrawal period stated on the product before selling or eating eggs. Expect deaths to slow over several weeks once the diet is corrected, but already-damaged hens may keep dying for a while and egg numbers may not fully recover in older hens.
prevention: Control body weight from the start: rear pullets to the breed's target weight, weigh a sample of birds every two to four weeks, and adjust feed so hens stay on target rather than getting fat.
Feed a complete, balanced layer ration from a reputable miller or a home-mix formulated by a qualified nutritionist, and do not add extra maize, bran or kitchen leftovers on top of it.
Give the amount of feed recommended for the breed and age instead of filling feeders all day, and adjust down during hot weather when hens need less energy.
Make sure the ration has enough calcium and phosphorus, ideally with part of the calcium as coarse limestone or shell grit, so hens are not eating extra feed searching for calcium.
Ensure the feed contains adequate choline, methionine, vitamin E and selenium, which help the liver handle fat; ask your feed supplier what the ration provides.
Buy dry, clean feed and maize, store it off the floor on pallets in a dry, aired store, use it within a few weeks, and never feed mouldy feed, to reduce aflatoxin damage to the liver.
Keep houses cool with good ventilation, roof insulation or shade, and constant cool water, especially during the hot dry months.
Where possible, give hens room to move and scratch, for example deep litter with scattered grit, and avoid overcrowding.
Keep stress low by handling birds gently, controlling rats and predators, and planning vaccinations and moves carefully.
detail.impact: FLHS usually kills only a small number of birds at a time, but those are often the heaviest, best-laying hens, so each death is a real loss. Death rates vary from farm to farm and can add up over months if the cause is not fixed. Egg production in affected flocks drops below the expected level, which hurts daily income on a layer farm where eggs pay for feed and labour. At the same time the farmer is paying for extra feed that is turning into liver fat instead of eggs, so feed cost per tray goes up. Repeated unexplained deaths also push farmers to buy antibiotics and other drugs that do not help, adding cost and residue risks. On a Kenyan smallholder unit of a few hundred caged hens, the combination of lost hens, fewer eggs and wasted feed can turn a profitable flock into a loss-making one.
detail.outlook: Hens that suffer a large liver bleed usually die quickly, and there is no reliable way to save them. Hens with mild fatty liver can improve gradually once the diet and feeding are corrected, and the number of deaths in the flock usually falls over the following weeks. Recovery of egg production is often only partial, especially in older hens past peak, because the liver damage takes time to heal. The outlook is best when the problem is caught early, the post-mortem confirms the cause, feed energy and quantity are corrected, mouldy feed is removed and heat stress is controlled. Flocks where overfeeding or poor feed continues will keep losing birds.

faqs.q: My hens look fat and healthy. Why are they dying?
faqs.a: A fat hen is not always a healthy hen. In laying hens, extra fat collects in the liver and makes it weak and easy to tear. The hen looks fine until a blood vessel in the liver bursts and she bleeds inside, often dying within hours. That is why the heaviest, best layers are often the ones found dead.

faqs.q: Will giving more feed make my hens lay more eggs?
faqs.a: Only up to the point that meets their needs. Once a hen gets enough energy, protein, calcium and vitamins, extra feed does not make more eggs; it turns into fat, including in the liver. Feed the amount recommended for the breed and age, and check body weight regularly. Overfeeding costs money and can cause FLHS.

faqs.q: Should I give antibiotics to stop the deaths?
faqs.a: No, not unless a vet diagnoses an infection. FLHS is caused by diet and management, not germs, so antibiotics will not help. Using them without need wastes money, may leave residues in your eggs and helps create germs that resist treatment. Get a post-mortem done first so you know what you are dealing with.

faqs.q: Are eggs from my flock safe to eat or sell?
faqs.a: FLHS is not an infection and does not pass to people, so eggs from hens with fatty liver are not a health risk in themselves. However, if your vet prescribes any medicine for another problem, follow the egg withdrawal period on the product before selling or eating the eggs. Also avoid mouldy feed, because aflatoxin can harm both hens and, through residues, people.

faqs.q: Can I just cut the feed sharply to make them slimmer?
faqs.a: Do not suddenly starve layers. A sharp cut in feed can crash egg production and cause other problems. Changes should be gradual and guided by a vet or feed adviser, usually by moving to controlled daily feeding, removing extra grain, and balancing the ration, while keeping water always available.

faqs.q: Do kienyeji chickens get fatty liver?
faqs.a: It is uncommon in free-range kienyeji chickens because they walk and forage all day and are not usually overfed. Improved kienyeji or indigenous hens kept confined and fed large amounts of high-energy feed can still be affected, so the same rules on controlled feeding and exercise apply.

products.role: Choline helps the liver package and move fat out of liver cells. Used as a feed supplement under the advice of your vet or feed nutritionist, it can support liver function and help reduce fat build-up in layers at risk, alongside the essential steps of cutting excess energy, controlling body weight and correcting the ration. It cannot repair a liver that has already bled.

Mouldy maize and feed can contain aflatoxin, which damages the liver and can make fatty liver worse. This mycotoxin binder added to feed helps reduce the toxins hens absorb, as support alongside buying clean feed, storing it dry and throwing away mouldy feed. It does not treat fatty liver itself.

fatty-liver.imagePrompt: A heavy white commercial laying hen standing in a wire battery cage in a Kenyan poultry house, her comb and wattles noticeably pale pink instead of bright red, with healthy red-combed hens in neighbouring cages for contrast, soft natural daylight.
fatty-liver.seoDescription: Fatty liver haemorrhagic syndrome in layers: spot sudden deaths, pale combs and egg drop, learn first steps, diet fixes and prevention for Kenyan farms.

card.headline: Chicks with curled toes or rubbery legs
card.look: Young birds sit on their hocks with toes curled inward, have soft rubbery beaks and legs, throw the head back or fall over, or show crusty, watery eyes. Laying hens may lay thin-shelled eggs that hatch poorly.
card.action: Check the feed first: its age, storage and whether it has been diluted. Then call your vet or agrovet adviser to confirm the problem and correct the diet quickly.

detail.summary: Vitamin deficiencies happen when chickens do not get enough of one or more vitamins from their feed, or cannot absorb them. The most common problems involve vitamins A, D3, E, B2 (riboflavin) and B1 (thiamine). Each one causes its own pattern of signs, such as curled toes, soft bones, stargazing, eye discharge or poor hatching. They are not contagious, but they can hit a whole flock at once because all the birds eat the same feed, and they cause slow growth, deaths, low egg production and wasted money.
detail.cause: Vitamins are small nutrients the body needs to grow bones, nerves, eyes, skin and eggs. Chickens cannot make most of them, so they must come from feed. Problems start when the feed is poor, old, badly stored or diluted, or when the gut cannot absorb what is there. Vitamin A protects the lining of the eyes, mouth and airways; without it, the eyes water and crust, white spots form in the mouth and throat, and birds catch infections easily. Vitamin D3 lets the bird use calcium and phosphorus; without it, or when calcium and phosphorus are out of balance, chicks get rickets (soft, bendy bones and beaks) and hens lay thin or soft shells. Vitamin E, working together with the mineral selenium, protects cells from damage; shortage can cause crazy chick disease (softening of the brain, called encephalomalacia), fluid swelling under the skin, and white streaks in the muscle. Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) keeps nerves healthy; lack of it damages the leg nerves so chicks walk on their hocks with toes curled inward. Vitamin B1 (thiamine) is needed for nerve and brain function; shortage causes weakness and stargazing, where the head is drawn back over the body. Breeder hens short of these vitamins also put too little into the egg, so embryos die in the shell and hatched chicks start life already deficient. Vitamins break down with heat, light, moisture and time, and rancid fats in feed destroy vitamins A and E quickly.
spread: It does not spread from bird to bird; it comes from the diet, so many birds on the same feed can show signs at the same time.
Old feed, or feed stored in hot, damp or sunny places, loses its vitamins over time, even if it looked good when bought.
Diluting commercial feed with maize bran, maize germ or kitchen scraps to save money lowers the vitamin level below what birds need.
Home-mixed feeds made without a proper vitamin-mineral premix, or with the wrong amount, are a common cause.
Gut diseases such as coccidiosis and worms, and mycotoxins (poisons from moulds in feed), damage the gut and liver so vitamins are poorly absorbed or stored.
Rancid (stale-smelling) fats or oils in feed destroy vitamins A and E.
Some medicines can interfere with vitamins; for example, giving the coccidiosis drug amprolium for too long or too strongly can lead to thiamine (B1) shortage.
Breeder hens on a poor diet pass the shortage to their eggs, causing poor hatchability and weak chicks.
detail.atRisk: Young chicks and fast-growing broilers in their first few weeks are most at risk because they grow quickly and have small reserves; curled toes, rickets and crazy chick disease usually show within the first few weeks of life. Laying hens in peak production are at risk of vitamin D3 problems that show as thin shells and falling egg numbers. Breeder flocks, including improved kienyeji hens used for hatching, are at risk of poor hatchability when their feed is low in vitamins. Birds kept indoors all the time with no sunlight depend fully on feed for vitamin D3. Kienyeji chickens on free range usually find greens and sunshine, but those fed only on maize, kitchen leftovers or bran during the dry season can also become deficient. Risk rises when feed is bought in bulk and stored for long, in hot and humid weather, during the long and short rains when feed can get damp and mouldy, and on farms with ongoing coccidiosis or worm problems.

early: Chicks look dull, grow slowly and the flock becomes uneven in size even though they are eating.
Feathers look ruffled and rough, and birds seem weak or reluctant to move.
Watery eyes or a slight sticky discharge from the eyes and nostrils (often vitamin A).
Chicks walking stiffly or resting on their hocks more than normal; some toes beginning to curl inward (often vitamin B2).
Beaks and leg bones that feel softer or bend more easily than normal when gently pressed (often vitamin D3 or calcium/phosphorus imbalance).
In layers, a drop in egg numbers and more thin-shelled or shell-less eggs.
In breeders, more eggs failing to hatch, with chicks dying late in the shell.
advanced: Chicks unable to walk, sitting on their hocks with toes curled tightly inward and wings drooped to help balance (vitamin B2, curled toe paralysis).
Very soft, rubbery beaks and legs, bent bones, lameness and swellings along the ribs (rickets from vitamin D3 shortage).
Chicks staggering, falling on their side, paddling their legs or twisting the head, often at a few weeks old (vitamin E, crazy chick disease).
Greenish-blue, jelly-like swelling under the skin of the breast or belly (vitamin E and selenium shortage).
Head pulled back so the bird looks at the sky, followed by weakness and collapse (vitamin B1, stargazing).
Eyelids stuck together with thick, cheesy material and small white spots in the mouth and throat (vitamin A).
Hens sitting in a 'penguin' posture, unable to stand, with very soft-shelled eggs; increased deaths and secondary infections across the flock.

lookalikes.name: Newcastle disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Newcastle can also cause twisted necks and stargazing, but it usually comes with coughing, gasping, green watery diarrhoea, a sudden drop in eggs and many deaths spreading quickly through birds of all ages. Vitamin problems usually affect one age group on one feed and do not cause sudden mass deaths. Because Newcastle is serious and common in Kenya, always let a vet rule it out when birds show nervous signs.

lookalikes.name: Marek's disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Marek's also causes leg paralysis, but it usually appears from around six weeks of age or older, often with one leg stretched forward and one back, grey or irregular eyes, and tumours found at post-mortem. Curled toe paralysis from vitamin B2 shortage usually appears in young chicks with toes curled inward, and improves or stops in new birds when the feed is corrected.

lookalikes.name: Infectious coryza and other respiratory infections
lookalikes.howToTell: Coryza causes a swollen face, a bad-smelling nasal discharge and spreads quickly from bird to bird. Vitamin A shortage gives eye discharge and cheesy material in the eyes too, but without the strong smell, and often with white spots in the mouth and poor growth across the flock. Vitamin A shortage can also make birds more likely to catch these infections, so both can happen together.

lookalikes.name: Mycotoxin poisoning (mouldy feed)
lookalikes.howToTell: Mouldy feed can cause poor growth, leg weakness, pale birds, poor feathering and poor egg shells, and it also causes vitamin shortages by damaging the gut and liver. Look for caked, musty-smelling or discoloured feed. A vet may find a pale or enlarged liver at post-mortem. Often the answer is both: remove the bad feed and correct the vitamins.

detail.diagnosis: A vet usually starts with the history: the age of the birds, which signs appear, how many are affected, the type and brand of feed, its manufacture date, how it is stored and whether anything has been added to it. They will examine live birds, checking the legs, toes, beak, bones, eyes, mouth and nervous signs. A post-mortem (opening a dead or culled bird) is very useful. It can show swollen leg nerves in riboflavin shortage, soft bones and beaded ribs in rickets, softened brain tissue in vitamin E shortage, white spots in the throat and white urate deposits in vitamin A shortage, and it helps rule out Newcastle, Marek's and other infections. Samples can be sent to a county veterinary laboratory or the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete, and feed samples can be tested for nutrients and mycotoxins. Often the diagnosis is confirmed when birds improve after the diet is corrected. To help your vet, keep a sample of the feed in a clean labelled bag, keep the feed bag label with the batch number and date, note when signs started and how many birds are affected and dead, and keep one or two freshly dead or very sick birds cool (not frozen) for examination.
firstSteps: Separate birds that cannot walk or eat into a warm, clean, dry pen with feed and water placed right next to them, so stronger birds do not trample them.
Check the feed right away: look at the manufacture date, smell for rancid or musty odours, check for lumps, mould or dampness, and stop using any feed that looks or smells bad.
Stop diluting commercial feed with maize bran, scraps or other materials, and give a fresh, properly made complete feed suited to the birds' age.
Make sure clean, fresh drinking water is always available, and help weak birds to drink by dipping their beaks gently.
Give birds kept indoors safe access to some morning sunlight if possible, and give free-range or kienyeji birds fresh greens such as sukuma wiki or amaranth (terere) leaves.
Write down the age of the birds, the signs, the number affected and any deaths each day, and keep a sample of the feed and the bag label.
Call your vet or a trained agrovet adviser to confirm the cause before giving any medicine, because nervous signs can also be Newcastle disease.
Do not give antibiotics or other drugs on your own; they do not fix vitamin shortages and can cause residues in eggs and meat.
detail.vetTreatment: Once the vet has confirmed a vitamin problem and ruled out infectious diseases, treatment usually means two things together: giving the missing vitamins quickly and fixing the feed so the problem does not come back. The vet may recommend a water-soluble multivitamin, a vitamin A, D3 and E product, a vitamin B-complex, or a specific vitamin such as riboflavin or thiamine, given in the drinking water or feed for a set period. For valuable birds, such as breeders, the vet may give an individual injection. Calcium and phosphorus may also need to be corrected in rickets and shell problems. The vet will set the product and amount; do not guess, because too much vitamin A or D3 can itself harm birds and damage the kidneys. Birds with mild signs often improve within days, but those with severe curled toes, bent bones or brain damage may not recover, and the vet may advise humane culling to prevent suffering. Antibiotics do not treat vitamin shortages; they are only used if the vet confirms a secondary bacterial infection, and then the full course and the egg and meat withdrawal period (the time you must wait before selling or eating eggs or meat) must be followed. Using antibiotics without need encourages antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to drugs. If mycotoxins or coccidiosis are part of the problem, the vet will also advise on controlling those.
prevention: Buy feed from reputable feed millers and agrovets, check the manufacture date on every bag, and avoid feed that is old, torn, damp or smells bad.
Buy only what you will use within a few weeks and store bags in a cool, dry, shaded place, raised off the floor on pallets and away from walls, rain and direct sun.
Feed the correct complete feed for each stage: chick starter, grower, finisher or layer feed, and do not dilute it with maize bran, germ or kitchen scraps.
If you mix your own feed, use a proper poultry vitamin-mineral premix from a trusted supplier at the recommended rate, and follow a balanced formulation from an extension officer or nutritionist.
Feed breeder hens, including improved kienyeji breeders, a proper breeder or layer feed so their eggs carry enough vitamins for good hatching and strong chicks.
Control coccidiosis, worms and other gut problems, and use a mycotoxin binder where feed quality is uncertain, especially in the rainy seasons, so vitamins are properly absorbed.
Give free-range and kienyeji birds access to sunlight and fresh greens, and consider a vitamin supplement during the dry season when greens are scarce.

Provide extra vitamins during stress periods such as vaccination, transport, heat, disease outbreaks and peak lay, as advised by your vet, and avoid long or overly strong courses of amprolium without vet guidance.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan farm, vitamin shortages quietly eat into profit. Broilers grow slowly and unevenly, so they take longer to reach market weight and use more feed per kilo of meat. Chicks with curled toes, rickets or nervous signs often die or must be culled, and the survivors may stay stunted. Layers produce fewer eggs and more cracked, thin or soft-shelled eggs that cannot be sold. Breeders and farmers hatching kienyeji chicks in incubators or under hens see more eggs failing to hatch, which wastes eggs, time and incubator power. Deficient birds also have weaker immunity, so diseases like Newcastle, coryza and coccidiosis hit harder and vaccines may work less well. The good news is that prevention is usually cheap compared with these losses: good feed, good storage and a sensible supplement plan cost far less than a lost batch.
detail.outlook: The outlook is generally good when the problem is caught early and the feed is corrected quickly. Birds with mild signs, such as slow growth, early eye discharge or slight leg weakness, often recover well once they get the missing vitamins. Laying hens usually return to normal shell quality and egg numbers after their diet is fixed, though this can take a few weeks. Recovery is much less likely when damage is severe: chicks with tightly curled toes for a long time, badly bent bones, or brain damage from vitamin E shortage may stay disabled. Outcomes also depend on whether the true cause is removed, such as mouldy feed, coccidiosis or diluted rations; if not, the problem will come back with the next batch.

faqs.q: My chicks are walking on their hocks with curled toes. Is it a disease that will spread to my other birds?
faqs.a: Curled toes in young chicks are a classic sign of vitamin B2 (riboflavin) shortage, which is a feeding problem, not an infection, so it does not pass from bird to bird. However, many chicks on the same feed can show it at the same time. Check the feed age and storage, stop any dilution, and ask your vet to confirm. Leg paralysis can also come from Marek's disease or other conditions, so do not assume without a check.

faqs.q: I bought feed from the agrovet, so how can my birds still be short of vitamins?
faqs.a: Even good feed loses vitamins over time, and faster in heat, damp and sunlight. Feed that sat in a hot store, got rained on, or was kept for many weeks may no longer have enough. Feed that has picked up mould can also block vitamin absorption. Always check the manufacture date, buy in amounts you will finish within a few weeks, and store it raised, dry and shaded.

faqs.q: Can I just add a vitamin powder or liquid to the water and solve it?
faqs.a: A good vitamin supplement helps birds recover faster, but on its own it is not the full answer. You must also fix the cause: replace old or mouldy feed, stop dilution and control gut problems like coccidiosis. Use supplements according to the label or your vet's advice, because giving too much vitamin A or D3 can harm birds. Supplements support recovery; correct feed prevents the problem coming back.

faqs.q: My eggs are not hatching well. Could vitamins be the reason?
faqs.a: Yes, it is a common cause. When breeder hens lack vitamins such as A, D3, E and B2, embryos often die in the shell, especially late in incubation, and chicks that hatch can be weak. Other causes include old or dirty eggs, poor incubator temperature or humidity, too few cocks or old cocks, and disease. Feed breeders a proper breeder or layer ration, consider a vitamin supplement, and review your egg handling and incubation with an extension officer or vet.

faqs.q: Do free-range kienyeji chickens get vitamin deficiencies?
faqs.a: Less often than birds kept indoors, because they get sunshine and eat greens, insects and seeds. But kienyeji birds fed only maize, bran or kitchen leftovers, especially in the dry season when greens are scarce, can become deficient. Chicks raised in brooders without sunlight are also at risk. Giving fresh greens, some sunlight and a balanced feed or supplement, especially for growing chicks and laying hens, makes a big difference.

faqs.q: My birds are falling over and looking up at the sky. Is it vitamins or Newcastle?
faqs.a: It could be either, which is why you should call a vet quickly. Stargazing and falling over can come from vitamin B1 or vitamin E shortage, but Newcastle disease can cause very similar twisted necks. Newcastle usually brings breathing problems, green diarrhoea and many deaths spreading fast. Isolate affected birds, keep records, keep a sample of the feed and let the vet examine birds or do a post-mortem before deciding.

products.role: Supplies vitamins A, D3 and E, the vitamins most often behind eye problems, rickets, crazy chick disease and poor hatchability. Used as directed by the label or your vet, it can help top up these vitamins during recovery and for breeder and layer flocks, alongside correcting the feed itself.

A liquid vitamin and mineral supplement that can support recovery and productivity when birds have been on poor or old feed, or during stress such as vaccination, heat or peak lay. It helps fill gaps while you fix the diet, but does not replace a proper complete feed or a vet's diagnosis.

vitamin-deficiency.imagePrompt: A realistic close-up photo of a young broiler chick in clean wood-shavings litter, resting on its hocks with its toes clearly curled inward and wings slightly drooped, soft natural daylight in a simple Kenyan poultry house.
vitamin-deficiency.seoDescription: Vitamin deficiencies in poultry: spot curled toes, rickets, stargazing, eye discharge and poor hatchability early, and prevent them with good feed in Kenya.

card.headline: Birds sitting with twisted, bowed legs
card.look: Young birds, often fast-growing broilers, sit down a lot, walk on their hocks or limp, and one or both legs bend outwards at the hock joint. Some birds have a flattened, swollen hock where the big tendon has slipped off to the side.
card.action: Move lame birds to a small, dry pen with feed and water within easy reach, then check your feed source and call your vet or extension officer to review the ration.

aka: Rickets (when caused by vitamin D, calcium or phosphorus problems)
Tibial dyschondroplasia (one type of leg weakness)
detail.summary: Leg weakness is a group of problems in growing chickens where the bones, joints or tendons of the legs do not develop properly, so birds cannot stand or walk well. Perosis is one form, where the main tendon at the back of the hock slips sideways and the leg twists out. It is mostly a nutrition and management problem, not an infection, and it is most common in fast-growing broilers and chicks on poorly balanced or home-mixed feed. It matters because lame birds eat and drink less, grow poorly, get trampled and often have to be culled, which cuts the income from a flock.
detail.cause: Leg weakness happens when a bird's skeleton cannot keep up with its growth or cannot be built properly because nutrients are missing or out of balance. Modern broilers gain weight very fast, and their soft, young bones and growth plates (the zones of cartilage near the ends of long bones where new bone is made) are under heavy strain. Perosis is mainly linked to a shortage of manganese, and also of choline, biotin, folic acid or niacin. Without these, the long bones and the hock joint grow short, thick and slightly crooked, and the large gastrocnemius tendon (the thick cord at the back of the hock, similar to a person's heel tendon) slides off its groove, so the lower leg twists outward and the bird cannot straighten it. Rickets is a different but related problem caused by too little vitamin D3, calcium or phosphorus, or by the wrong ratio between calcium and phosphorus. The bones stay soft and rubbery, bend under the bird's weight, and the growth plates become wide and weak. Tibial dyschondroplasia is a third form, where a plug of soft cartilage stays in the top of the shank bone instead of turning into hard bone; it is linked to very fast growth and to calcium-phosphorus imbalance. Mouldy feed can make all of these worse, because mycotoxins (poisons made by moulds, such as aflatoxin) damage the liver and kidneys, which are needed to activate vitamin D and use minerals properly.
spread: It does not spread from bird to bird like an infection; many birds are affected at the same time because they all eat the same faulty feed.
Home-mixed rations made without a proper mineral and vitamin premix, or with wrong proportions of maize, bran and protein, are a common trigger in Kenya.
Diluting commercial broiler or chick feed with maize bran, maize germ or kitchen scraps to save money lowers the minerals and vitamins each bird gets.
Feeding layer mash to chicks or broilers gives far too much calcium, which upsets the calcium-phosphorus balance and can damage bones and kidneys.
Old feed, or feed stored in damp, hot stores, loses vitamins and can grow moulds that produce mycotoxins.
Very fast growth pushed by 24-hour lighting, with no dark rest period, makes heavy birds sit more and puts extra load on young legs.
Wet, caked or slippery floors, overcrowding and poor ventilation make birds less active and worsen leg problems.
Chicks from breeder hens fed a poor diet may hatch with low reserves of vitamins and minerals and show leg weakness in the first weeks.
detail.atRisk: Broiler chickens between about one and six weeks of age are most at risk, especially heavy, fast-growing males. Chicks and young growers of improved kienyeji types (such as KALRO Kienyeji, Kuroiler and Rainbow Rooster) can also be affected when fed cheap or home-made feeds. Turkeys and ducks can get perosis too. Indoor birds with no sunlight depend completely on vitamin D3 in the feed, so deep-litter and cage systems are more exposed than free-range birds that get sun. Farms that mix their own feed, buy from unknown or uncertified feed sellers, or store feed for long periods in hot, humid weather (common during the long and short rains) face the highest risk. Free-range kienyeji chickens that scavenge are less often affected, but chicks kept indoors in brooders during cold, wet weather can still develop rickets.

early: Birds sit down more than normal and get up slowly or unwillingly when you walk through the house.
A slight limp, unsteady or waddling walk, or birds resting on their hocks instead of standing on their feet.
Birds that stay near the feeder or drinker and do not move around the house like the rest of the flock.
Some birds look smaller and less even in size than the flock, because they reach feed and water less often.
In rickets, the beak and toes may feel soft and bend easily when pressed gently between your fingers.
Slight swelling or flattening of the hock joint on one or both legs.
advanced: The lower leg twists outwards at the hock, often only on one side, and the bird cannot straighten it; you may feel the thick tendon lying to the side of the joint instead of at the back.
Legs bowed outward or inward (valgus or varus deformity), giving a knock-kneed or bow-legged look.
Birds walk on their hocks or push themselves along with their wings, or cannot stand at all.
Beading or knobbly swellings along the ribs where they join the spine (a sign of rickets).
Weight loss, dull feathers, dirty or breast-blistered birds from lying on wet litter, and dehydration because they cannot reach drinkers.
Lame birds pecked or trampled by others, and rising numbers of culls and deaths.

lookalikes.name: Marek's disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Marek's is a viral disease mostly seen in unvaccinated layers and kienyeji birds from about 6 to 20 weeks old, and rarely in broilers. A typical bird lies with one leg stretched forward and the other backward, the eyes may turn grey, and there is weight loss. The legs are paralysed but not twisted at the hock, and the vet finds enlarged nerves or tumours at post-mortem.

lookalikes.name: Infectious arthritis or tenosynovitis (bacterial, Mycoplasma synoviae or viral reovirus)
lookalikes.howToTell: Infected joints and tendons are usually hot, swollen and sometimes contain pus or sticky fluid, and birds may also have breast blisters, fever or other illness. Nutritional leg weakness usually has no heat or pus, and affects many birds in an even way linked to feed. A vet needs to open joints or send samples to the lab to tell them apart.

lookalikes.name: Curled-toe paralysis (riboflavin or vitamin B2 deficiency)
lookalikes.howToTell: Chicks walk on their hocks with the toes curled inward like a fist, usually in the first two to three weeks. In perosis the toes are normal but the leg twists out at the hock. Both point to a poor feed premix, so the ration needs checking either way.

lookalikes.name: Newcastle disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Newcastle can cause leg paralysis, but it also brings twisted necks, coughing, green diarrhoea, a sudden drop in eggs and many sudden deaths across all ages. Nutritional leg weakness develops slowly in young growing birds with no breathing signs or diarrhoea. If you see nervous signs plus sudden deaths, call the vet urgently.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or animal health officer will first look at the flock: the age of affected birds, how many are lame, the type of housing and lighting, and above all the feed you are using. They will handle lame birds to check whether the tendon has slipped, whether the bones are soft or bent, and whether joints are hot or swollen, which would point to infection. A post-mortem on a few typical birds is very helpful. The vet can split the shank bone to look for the white cartilage plug of tibial dyschondroplasia, check for wide, soft growth plates and beaded ribs of rickets, and rule out infection or Marek's disease. Feed samples can be sent to a feed analysis laboratory (for example KALRO, a university laboratory or a private feed lab) to measure calcium, phosphorus and, where possible, mycotoxins. Bone ash tests are sometimes done to measure how well bones are mineralised. To prepare, keep a sample of about half a kilo of the current feed in a clean, labelled bag, note the feed brand, batch number and date bought, write down what you add if you mix your own feed, and record bird age, lighting hours, number of lame birds and daily deaths. Keep two or three live, typical lame birds ready for the vet to examine.
firstSteps: Walk through the house and count how many birds are lame or sitting, and write down their age, the feed in use and daily deaths so you can see if the problem is growing.
Move lame but alert birds to a small, dry, well-bedded pen where feed and water are at their level and they do not have to compete or walk far.
Lower drinkers and feeders, or add extra ones, so that weak birds in the main house can still eat and drink easily.
Stop diluting the feed with bran, maize or leftovers, and do not give layer mash to chicks or broilers.
Check your feed store and sacks for damp, caking, a musty smell or visible mould; stop using any spoiled feed and keep a sample for testing.
Keep litter dry and loose, fix leaking drinkers and improve ventilation so birds are not sitting on wet, ammonia-smelling litter.
If you run lights all night, give birds a dark rest period each night as your vet or feed supplier advises, which slows very fast growth and lets birds rest.
Call your vet, animal health officer or feed supplier's technical advisor to review the ration before you add any supplements; do not give drugs without a vet's advice.
Birds that cannot stand, cannot reach water or are badly twisted are suffering; ask your vet about humane culling rather than leaving them to slowly die.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no single drug that cures leg weakness, so treatment is mainly about correcting the feed and managing the flock. The vet or nutritionist will advise changing to a properly balanced, certified feed or fixing your home-mixed ration with the right mineral and vitamin premix. Depending on the cause found, they may recommend extra vitamin D3, a correctly balanced calcium and phosphorus source, manganese, choline or B vitamins such as biotin, usually given through feed or drinking water for a short period. The amounts must come from the vet or nutritionist, because too much calcium, phosphorus or vitamin D can itself damage bones and kidneys. Early rickets often improves within one to two weeks once the diet is corrected, and birds may recover well. A fully slipped tendon in perosis, or badly bent bones, usually does not return to normal even after the diet is fixed, so those birds are often culled humanely or marketed early if otherwise healthy. Antibiotics do not help nutritional leg problems and should only be used if the vet confirms a bacterial joint infection; unnecessary antibiotic use feeds antimicrobial resistance, meaning drugs stop working for animals and people. If any medicine is prescribed, follow the vet's instructions exactly and respect the meat and egg withdrawal period, which is the time you must wait after the last dose before selling or eating the birds or eggs.
prevention: Buy chick, broiler and grower feed from reputable, KEBS-certified feed millers, use the right feed for each stage, and do not mix it with extra bran, maize or scraps.

If you mix your own feed, follow a tested formula from KALRO, your county extension office or a qualified nutritionist, and always include a good poultry vitamin and mineral premix that contains manganese, choline, biotin and vitamin D3.
Keep calcium and phosphorus in the right balance; never give layer feed, extra limestone or eggshells to chicks and broilers unless a nutritionist says so.
Store feed off the floor on pallets in a cool, dry, rat-proof store, use it within a few weeks of manufacture, and never use mouldy or caked feed, especially during the rainy seasons.
Give broilers a lighting programme with a daily dark period after the first week, as advised by your hatchery or feed supplier, to slow excessive early growth and let birds rest and move.
Keep stocking density reasonable, provide enough feeders and drinkers, and keep litter dry and loose so birds stay active and legs stay strong.
Buy chicks from reliable hatcheries with well-fed parent flocks, and give improved kienyeji chicks some safe access to sunlight once they are old and strong enough.
Walk the flock every day, and act early when you see the first few birds sitting or limping, because the cause is usually the same for the whole flock.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan broiler farm, leg weakness hits directly at income. Lame birds cannot compete at the feeder and drinker, so they grow slowly and the flock becomes uneven at market time, which buyers and hotels pay less for. Feed is still being spent on birds that may end up as culls, so feed conversion (how much feed it takes to make a kilo of meat) gets worse. Some birds die from dehydration, trampling or secondary infections, and badly deformed birds are hard to sell or may be rejected by processors. Birds lying on wet litter get breast blisters and dirty skin, lowering carcass quality. For smallholders raising a few hundred broilers or improved kienyeji, even a modest number of culls can wipe out the profit from a batch. There is also the extra cost of changing feed, supplements and vet visits, and the stress and labour of caring for lame birds.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends on the cause, how early it is caught, and how badly birds are affected. Birds with early rickets or mild weakness often recover well once the feed is corrected, usually within a week or two. Birds with a fully slipped tendon, bones that have set in a bent shape, or severe tibial dyschondroplasia rarely return to normal and are often best culled humanely or sold early if they are otherwise healthy. The rest of the flock can usually be protected quickly by fixing the ration, improving feed storage and managing growth and housing. If the problem keeps coming back batch after batch, the feed source, premix or lighting programme is almost always the reason and should be reviewed with a nutritionist.

faqs.q: Is leg weakness contagious? Will it spread to my other birds?
faqs.a: Nutritional leg weakness and perosis are not infectious and do not pass from bird to bird. Many birds get it at once because they all eat the same faulty feed or live in the same conditions. However, some infections such as bacterial arthritis, reovirus or Marek's disease can also cause lameness, so if joints are hot and swollen, birds are sick in other ways, or many die suddenly, ask your vet to check.

faqs.q: Can a bird with a slipped tendon be fixed?
faqs.a: Usually not. Once the tendon has slipped off the hock and the bones have grown twisted, correcting the feed rarely straightens the leg. Correcting the diet helps prevent new cases and helps birds with early, mild weakness. Badly affected birds that cannot walk to food and water should be humanely culled or, if otherwise healthy, marketed early after discussing with your vet.

faqs.q: Why are my broilers sitting down at three or four weeks old?
faqs.a: Broilers grow extremely fast, and around three to five weeks their legs are under the most strain. Common reasons include an unbalanced or diluted feed, poor premix, mouldy feed, 24-hour lighting that pushes growth too fast, overcrowding and wet litter. Check the feed first, make sure there is a dark period each night, keep litter dry, and get your vet or feed supplier to look at a few birds.

faqs.q: Can I just add crushed eggshells, bone meal or limestone to help their legs?
faqs.a: Not without advice. Too much calcium is as harmful as too little: it upsets the calcium-phosphorus balance, can make leg problems worse and can damage the kidneys. Leg weakness can also come from missing manganese, choline, biotin or vitamin D3, which eggshells do not provide. Ask your vet or a nutritionist which nutrient is short before adding anything.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell birds with leg weakness?
faqs.a: The leg problem itself does not make the meat unsafe for people. Birds that are thin, sick, badly blistered or dehydrated are not suitable for sale, and any bird treated with medicine must complete the withdrawal period before it is slaughtered. If in doubt, ask your vet or meat inspector.

faqs.q: Do kienyeji chickens get this too?
faqs.a: Free-range kienyeji chickens that scavenge and get sunshine rarely get leg weakness. But improved kienyeji chicks kept indoors in brooders on cheap or home-mixed feed can develop rickets or perosis just like broilers. Give them a proper chick and grower feed with premix, and safe outdoor access once they are strong enough.

products.role: Supplies vitamins A, D3 and E; vitamin D3 is needed to absorb and use calcium and phosphorus for strong bones, so it can support birds and flocks where a vet or nutritionist suspects rickets or low vitamin D intake, used alongside a corrected, balanced ration and at the level they advise.

Provides calcium and phosphorus for bone building in home-mixed rations that are short of these minerals; it should only be added on the advice of a nutritionist or vet, because extra calcium or phosphorus in an already complete commercial feed can upset the balance and make leg problems worse.

leg-weakness.imagePrompt: A young white broiler chicken sitting on dry wood-shavings litter in a poultry house, with one leg visibly twisted outward at a swollen, flattened hock joint while other birds stand in the soft-focus background.
leg-weakness.seoDescription: Leg weakness and perosis in broilers and chicks: spot slipped tendons, bowed legs and sitting birds, learn the feed causes, first steps and prevention.

card.headline: Thin, soft or misshapen eggshells
card.look: Eggs crack easily, feel rubbery or come out with no shell at all. Some are wrinkled, rough, chalky, pale or oddly shaped, and the flock lays fewer eggs than usual.
card.action: Check the feed, calcium source, water and heat in the house today, and call your vet quickly if birds also look sick, cough or die.

detail.summary: Poor eggshell quality means hens lay eggs with thin, soft, rough, wrinkled, pale or misshapen shells, or no shell at all. It is often paired with a drop in the number of eggs laid. It is a sign, not one single disease. The cause may be poor feeding, hot weather, old hens or infections such as Infectious Bronchitis (IB) or Egg Drop Syndrome (EDS). It matters because cracked and soft eggs cannot be sold, hens learn to eat broken eggs, and a small drop in lay quickly eats into profit.
detail.cause: A hen builds an eggshell over about 20 hours in the shell gland. The shell gland is the part of the oviduct (egg tube) that works like a small factory. Most of this work happens at night. The shell is almost all calcium carbonate. The hen takes the calcium from her feed and from a store held in special bones called medullary bone. To use calcium well she needs enough vitamin D3. Phosphorus must also be in the right balance with calcium. If any one of these is short, or the balance is wrong, shells come out thin or soft. Hot weather causes problems in two ways. Panting hens eat less feed, so they take in less calcium. Heavy panting also changes the chemistry of the blood, so less calcium and less carbonate reach the shell gland. Age matters too. As hens get older their eggs get bigger, but the amount of shell stays about the same, so the shell is stretched thinner. Infections damage the oviduct directly. IB is caused by a coronavirus that attacks the airways, kidneys and oviduct. It leaves wrinkled, thin, rough or misshapen shells and watery egg whites. If chicks catch IB very young, the oviduct can be scarred for life. EDS is caused by an adenovirus that attacks the shell gland. It causes thin, soft or shell-less eggs and pale brown shells, often in hens that otherwise look healthy. Other things can add to the problem. These include mould poisons (mycotoxins) in feed, salty water, stress and fright that make hens hold eggs too long, some medicines, and diseases such as Newcastle disease and Mycoplasma.
spread: Nutritional causes do not spread from bird to bird. They come from feed that is low in calcium, phosphorus or vitamin D3, or poorly balanced. This often happens with cheap or poorly mixed layer mash, home mixes without enough limestone, or kienyeji hens fed only kitchen scraps and grain.
Heat triggers it during the hot, dry months before the long rains, and in hot areas such as the Coast, Lake region and northern lowlands. Poorly ventilated iron-sheet houses make it worse.
Infectious Bronchitis spreads very fast through the air, in droppings, and on people, crates, egg trays, vehicles and new birds. It can pass through a whole house in a few days.

Egg Drop Syndrome can pass from hen to chick through the egg. It also spreads through contaminated egg trays, needles, water and droppings. Ducks and geese can carry the virus without showing signs, so keeping them with layers adds risk.
Stress can trigger short-term shell problems. Examples are predators at night, loud noise, moving birds, rough handling, vaccination or sudden changes in feed or light.
Mouldy feed, especially damp maize stored in the rainy season, can carry mycotoxins. These harm the liver and reduce calcium and vitamin D use.
Mixing flocks of different ages, and buying point-of-lay pullets from unknown sources, brings in viral and Mycoplasma infections.
detail.atRisk: Laying hens of every type can be affected. This includes commercial layers such as brown hybrids, improved kienyeji, Kuroiler and Kenbro, and free-range indigenous hens. Older hens are most at risk, usually after about 60 to 70 weeks of age, because their shells naturally get thinner. Young pullets just starting to lay are also at risk. They may lay a few odd eggs at first, and they are hit hardest by EDS, which usually strikes around the start of lay or peak lay. Very high-producing commercial hybrids need the most calcium and suffer first when feed falls short. Flocks in deep-litter houses with poor airflow, or in hot lowland areas, suffer most in the hot dry season. Free-range and backyard kienyeji flocks given no layer mash or shell grit often lay thin-shelled eggs. Flocks that were never vaccinated against IB, or that share space with ducks and geese, carry extra infection risk.

early: A few more cracked eggs than usual in the nest or tray, especially eggs that break when you pick them up.
Shells that feel thinner, rougher or sandy to the touch, or have chalky white spots and bands.
Brown-egg flocks start laying paler, washed-out eggs.
Occasional soft, rubbery eggs with only a skin (membrane), often found under the perch in the morning.
Hens found eating eggs, or broken shells and yolk smeared in the nest boxes.
A slight drop in the daily egg count, or hens eating less feed and drinking more on hot afternoons.
advanced: Many shell-less or soft-shelled eggs every day, and a clear fall in the egg count over several days.
Wrinkled, ridged, flattened, pointed or oddly shaped eggs, which is a strong hint of Infectious Bronchitis.
Watery, runny egg white when eggs are cracked into a bowl, also typical of IB.
Hens that are lame, sit a lot, or cannot stand well (sometimes called cage layer fatigue), with soft keel bones or beaks in severe calcium or vitamin D3 shortage.
Coughing, sneezing, rattly breathing or watery eyes in the flock alongside poor shells, pointing to infection.
Hens with swollen bellies that stand upright like a penguin and do not lay, which can follow oviduct damage from early IB.
A strong egg-eating habit spreading through the flock, and some deaths if a serious disease is behind it.

lookalikes.name: Newcastle disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Newcastle disease can also cause soft and shell-less eggs and a sharp egg drop. But it usually comes with sudden deaths, green diarrhoea, gasping, twisted necks, paralysis or swollen heads. Newcastle disease is notifiable in Kenya. If you see these signs, stop all bird and egg movement and report to your County Veterinary Officer straight away.

lookalikes.name: Mycoplasma synoviae (eggshell apex abnormality)
lookalikes.howToTell: This bacterial infection gives a typical pattern. The pointed end of the egg has a rough, thin, cracked or glassy cap, while the rest of the shell looks normal. Hens may also have swollen hocks or foot pads, or mild breathing signs. A vet confirms it with blood tests.

lookalikes.name: Natural moult, broodiness or end of the laying cycle
lookalikes.howToTell: In a natural moult, hens drop many feathers and stop laying, but shells on the few eggs laid are usually normal. Broody hens sit on the nest, fluff up and peck when disturbed. Old hens lay large eggs with thin shells, but they are otherwise healthy and the change is slow, over weeks.

lookalikes.name: Parasites (red mites, lice and worms)
lookalikes.howToTell: Heavy parasite loads cause a gradual fall in egg numbers and pale combs, and sometimes poorer shells. Look for tiny red or grey mites in cracks of perches at night, lice at the base of feathers, or worms in droppings. Shells improve after parasite control and good feeding.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or poultry extension officer starts with the flock history. They will ask about age, breed, feed brand and type, how calcium is given, water source, house temperature, vaccination record, recent stress and when the problem began. They will examine the eggs, so keep several days of abnormal eggs aside, labelled by date. The type of defect gives strong clues. Wrinkled shells with watery whites suggest IB. Pale, thin and shell-less eggs in healthy-looking young hens suggest EDS. A rough tip suggests Mycoplasma. Thin shells in old hens suggest age. They will examine live birds for breathing signs, lameness, parasites and body condition. Blood samples may be sent to a laboratory, such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete or a regional veterinary lab. These tests look for antibodies to IB, EDS, Newcastle disease and Mycoplasma, often comparing samples taken a few weeks apart. A post-mortem on one or two sick or culled birds can show oviduct damage, soft bones or other disease. A feed sample can be tested for calcium, phosphorus and mycotoxins. To prepare, write down daily egg counts and cracked-egg counts. Keep your vaccination cards, feed bags and labels, and a sample of the current feed in a clean dry bag. Have one or two typical sick birds ready, alive and isolated.
firstSteps: Count eggs every day and record how many are normal, cracked, soft or shell-less. A written record helps the vet find the cause quickly.

Check the feed bag. Laying hens must be on proper layer mash or layer pellets, not grower, chick or broiler feed, and not grain alone. If you mix your own feed, check your recipe with an extension officer or nutritionist.
Give free access to clean crushed limestone or oyster shell grit in a separate feeder, especially in the afternoon, so hens have calcium at night when the shell is formed.
Make sure there is plenty of clean, cool drinking water at all times, and that drinkers are not blocked or left empty during the hot part of the day.
Cool the house on hot days. Open side curtains or windows, improve airflow, shade iron roofs, avoid overcrowding, and feed in the cooler early morning and evening.
Collect eggs at least two to three times a day, remove broken eggs quickly, and darken or curtain nest boxes to stop egg-eating.

Watch for coughing, sneezing, diarrhoea, twisted necks or sudden deaths. If you see them, separate sick birds, stop selling or moving birds and eggs, and call your vet or County Veterinary Officer at once.
Do not start antibiotics or other medicines on your own. Wait for advice from a vet, because many drugs are not allowed in laying hens and leave residues in eggs.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on the cause, so the vet will first find out what is behind the problem. For nutritional causes, the main treatment is correcting the diet. This may mean changing to a better layer feed, adding limestone or oyster shell, fixing the calcium and phosphorus balance, and adding vitamin D3 where it is lacking. Vitamin D3 and minerals should only be added as advised, because too much vitamin D3 or calcium can also harm hens, especially the kidneys. For heat stress, the vet will advise on housing, cooling, water and possibly electrolytes or other heat-stress supplements. For mycotoxins, the vet will advise removing the mouldy feed and may recommend a toxin binder. There is no medicine that cures Infectious Bronchitis or Egg Drop Syndrome. Antibiotics do not kill these viruses. Care focuses on good nursing, warmth or cooling as needed, clean water, good nutrition and preventing secondary bacterial infections. A vet may prescribe an antibiotic only if there is a real bacterial infection, for example when Mycoplasma or E. coli is confirmed. Drug classes sometimes used in poultry include tetracyclines, macrolides such as tylosin, and others. However, many antibiotics are not allowed for hens producing eggs for people to eat, and those that are allowed have an egg withdrawal period. This is a set number of days after treatment when eggs must be thrown away, not sold or eaten. Always follow the vet's instructions and the label. Using antibiotics without need breeds antimicrobial resistance, which makes future infections in birds and people harder to treat. For old hens with naturally thin shells, the vet may simply advise planning to replace the flock. Expect nutritional problems to improve within a couple of weeks of correcting the feed. Virus damage may take longer, and some damage may never fully recover.
prevention: Feed a complete, good-quality layer mash or pellet from a reputable miller, and store it dry and off the floor. Layer feed has roughly three to four times more calcium than grower feed.

Do not give layer feed too early, as high calcium can damage the kidneys of growing pullets. Use a pre-layer or follow your feed supplier's advice, usually switching around the time the first eggs appear.
Offer coarse limestone grit or crushed oyster shell in a separate feeder, especially for free-range and kienyeji hens, and top it up in the afternoon.

Vaccinate against Infectious Bronchitis according to a schedule from your vet or hatchery, usually starting in chicks with boosters before lay. Where EDS is a problem in your area, ask your vet about EDS vaccination of pullets before they begin laying.
Buy chicks and point-of-lay pullets only from trusted, licensed hatcheries and suppliers with vaccination records. Keep new birds apart for at least two weeks before mixing.
Keep ducks and geese away from layer houses and water sources, as they can carry the EDS virus.
Practise good biosecurity. Clean and disinfect egg trays and crates, limit visitors, use a foot dip, and avoid sharing equipment with other farms.
Build or adapt houses for heat. Use good cross-ventilation, roof insulation or shade, correct stocking density, plenty of drinkers, and feeding in the cooler hours.
Control mites, lice and worms on a regular plan agreed with your vet, and keep perches and nest boxes clean.
Keep records of age, egg numbers and shell quality, and plan to replace old flocks before shell quality and profit fall too far.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan farm, poor shells hit income fast. Cracked, soft and shell-less eggs cannot be sold in trays to shops, hotels or middlemen, and even slightly rough or pale eggs fetch a lower price. Broken eggs make nests dirty, attract flies and teach hens to eat eggs, a habit that is hard to stop. The hens still eat the same costly feed while laying fewer good eggs, so the feed cost per tray rises sharply. With IB, the drop in lay and shell quality can last for weeks, and pullets infected young may never lay well. EDS can stop a young flock from reaching its peak. In small and medium flocks this can turn a profitable batch into a loss, and it can delay loan repayments and school fees that depend on egg sales.
detail.humanHealth: The causes of poor shells, such as feed shortages, heat, IB and EDS, do not infect people. However, cracked, thin and dirty eggs let bacteria such as Salmonella get inside more easily. Do not sell or eat cracked or leaking eggs raw or lightly cooked. Cook eggs well, wash your hands after handling eggs and birds, and keep eggs cool and clean. If your vet prescribes any medicine, respect the egg withdrawal period, and throw away eggs laid during that time, so that drug residues do not reach consumers.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends on the cause. When the problem is feed, missing calcium, low vitamin D3 or heat, shells usually improve within a couple of weeks after the cause is fixed, and egg numbers often recover. With EDS, egg production and shells often improve over several weeks, but the flock may not return to full peak. With IB in adult hens, laying often recovers partly, but some hens keep laying poor eggs. Hens infected as young chicks may have permanent oviduct damage and never lay well. In old hens, thin shells are part of normal ageing and will not fully reverse, so replacing the flock is often the best choice. Early action, good records and quick vet advice give the best chance of saving production.

faqs.q: Can I just give my hens crushed eggshells instead of buying limestone?
faqs.a: Yes, clean crushed eggshells can add some calcium, especially for small kienyeji flocks. Bake or boil them first so they are dry and free of germs, and crush them so they no longer look like eggs, or hens may learn to eat eggs. Eggshells alone are often not enough for high-producing hybrids, so still feed a proper layer feed and offer limestone or oyster shell grit as well.

faqs.q: Why do I find soft eggs under the perch in the morning?
faqs.a: Soft or shell-less eggs laid at night usually mean the hen did not have enough calcium, or her shell gland could not finish the shell. Common reasons are low-calcium feed, no grit in the afternoon, heat stress, fright at night, young pullets just starting to lay, or a disease such as EDS or IB. If only a few eggs are affected, check feed and calcium first. If many hens are affected, or birds look sick, call your vet.

faqs.q: Will antibiotics fix thin shells or an egg drop?
faqs.a: No, not in most cases. Most shell problems come from feed, heat, age or viruses such as IB and EDS, and antibiotics do nothing against these. Using antibiotics without need wastes money, leaves residues in eggs and builds drug resistance. A vet may prescribe one only when a bacterial infection is confirmed, and then you must follow the egg withdrawal period.

faqs.q: My hens are vaccinated against IB. Why do I still see wrinkled eggs?
faqs.a: Vaccines lower the risk but do not give perfect protection. The vaccine may have been stored badly, for example not kept cold, or given wrongly, or the boosters may have been missed. There are also many types of IB virus, and the one on your farm may differ from the vaccine type. Old age, Mycoplasma or poor feed can also cause odd shells. Talk to your vet about testing and reviewing your vaccination plan.

faqs.q: At what age should I replace my layers?
faqs.a: Most commercial layers lay best in their first year of production, and shell quality and egg numbers slowly fall after that, often from around 70 to 80 weeks of age. The right time depends on egg prices, feed costs and how well the flock is still laying. Keep records of eggs per day and cracked eggs, and when income no longer covers feed and other costs, plan to sell the old hens and bring in a new batch.

faqs.q: How can I stop my hens from eating eggs?
faqs.a: First fix the cause of weak shells, because broken eggs start the habit. Collect eggs often, at least two to three times a day. Make nest boxes dark, soft and enough in number, about one box for every four or five hens. Remove broken eggs and wipe nests at once. Avoid overcrowding and boredom by giving some greens or scattering a little grain. Persistent egg-eaters may need to be culled, as they teach others.

products.role: A layer feed additive added to a complete layer ration to support egg production and shell quality. It helps laying hens get the nutrients they need for strong shells, alongside proper layer feed, free-choice limestone or oyster shell, IB vaccination and good heat management. It does not cure infections such as IB or EDS.

Supplies vitamins A, D3 and E. Vitamin D3 is needed for hens to absorb and use calcium for shells, so this can help where the diet is short of vitamin D3, such as during recovery from stress or in poorly fortified home-mixed feeds. Use it only as the label or your vet directs, because too much vitamin D3 can harm hens. It supports good nutrition and is not a replacement for a balanced layer feed or vet diagnosis.

poor-eggshell-quality.imagePrompt: A realistic close-up photo of a cardboard egg tray on a rustic wooden table in a Kenyan poultry house, holding normal brown eggs alongside several pale, thin, wrinkled, rough and misshapen eggs and one soft shell-less egg, in natural daylight.
poor-eggshell-quality.seoDescription: Thin, soft or misshapen eggshells and fewer eggs? Learn causes—calcium, vitamin D3, heat, age, IB, EDS—first steps and prevention for Kenyan layer farmers.

card.headline: Pale comb and restless hens at night
card.look: Hens have pale combs and wattles, lay fewer eggs and refuse to roost or go into nest boxes. Tiny grey-red mites hide in perch cracks, or white egg clusters sit at the feather base around the vent.
card.action: Check the house and the birds with a torch at night, then call your vet or a qualified agrovet before using any spray or powder.

aka: Chawa wa kuku (Swahili for chicken lice)
Utitiri (Swahili, commonly used for chicken mites and other tiny parasites)
detail.summary: Mites and lice are tiny external parasites that live on chickens or in their housing. They feed on blood, skin or feathers. They are very common in Kenyan flocks, from kienyeji chickens to commercial layers. Heavy infestations cause anaemia (a shortage of red blood cells, which shows as pale combs), stress, egg drop and sometimes death. They are rarely a sudden killer, but they quietly cost farmers eggs, feed and birds every day until they are controlled.
detail.cause: Several different parasites are involved. The poultry red mite (Dermanyssus gallinae) is a blood-sucking mite about the size of a full stop. It does not live on the bird. It hides by day in cracks in perches, nest boxes, walls and roofs, and it crawls onto roosting birds at night to feed. It is grey or whitish when hungry and turns red after a blood meal. It can survive for several months in an empty house without feeding. Northern fowl mite (Ornithonyssus sylviarum) and the closely related tropical fowl mite (Ornithonyssus bursa) live their whole life on the bird, mostly around the vent. They also suck blood, and they make the feathers there look dirty and grey-black with scabby skin underneath. Chicken lice, such as the body louse and the shaft louse, are wingless insects, pale yellow-brown and quick-moving. They live on the bird all the time and chew skin scales and feather material rather than sucking blood. They glue their eggs, called nits, in clusters at the base of feathers. Blood-feeding mites take blood every night, so heavy numbers cause anaemia, weakness and, in chicks or sitting hens, death. Lice and mites both cause constant itching and irritation. The bird feeds and rests poorly, damages its own feathers and puts less energy into growth and eggs.
spread: Red mites crawl between birds and around the house, and they are carried into new houses on second-hand crates, egg trays, nest boxes, perches, sacks and timber.
Northern fowl mites and lice pass directly from bird to bird through close contact, especially when birds are crowded on perches or in transport crates.
Newly bought birds, birds returned unsold from market, and birds borrowed for breeding often bring lice and mites into a clean flock.
Wild birds, such as sparrows and pigeons, that nest in or near the poultry house can carry mites and lice to your chickens.
People can carry mites on clothing, boots and hands when they move between infested and clean houses.
Warm weather speeds up the red mite life cycle, so numbers can build up very quickly in hot, dry spells and in warm lowland areas.
Dirty, cracked wooden housing, old litter and nest material that is never changed give mites ideal hiding and breeding places.
detail.atRisk: All chickens can be affected, including layers, broilers, breeders, kienyeji and improved kienyeji birds, ducks, turkeys and pigeons. Laying hens and breeders are most at risk because they stay in the same house for a long time, giving parasites time to multiply. Broilers are kept for a short time, so they are less often badly affected. Sitting (brooding) hens and young chicks suffer most from red mite, because they cannot escape the night-time feeding. Some sitting hens abandon their eggs or die on the nest. Free-range and backyard flocks in old wooden or mud-and-timber houses with many cracks are commonly affected. Older, sick, poorly fed or injured birds, and birds with trimmed or damaged beaks, cannot preen well and carry heavier lice loads. Red mite problems often worsen in hot periods and in warm areas. Northern fowl mite tends to do better in cooler conditions, so it may be seen more in highland flocks. Lice can be found all year round.

early: Birds are restless at night, unwilling to go onto perches, or try to sleep on the floor or in unusual places.
Hens avoid nest boxes and start laying eggs on the floor.
Birds scratch, peck and preen at themselves more than normal, especially under the wings and around the vent.
Small red or dark spots appear on eggshells, which can be crushed red mites or their droppings.
Small grey-white or reddish mites are found in perch ends, joints and cracks when you press white tissue into them, or a grey-white powdery deposit (mite droppings and shed skins) builds up there.
Parting the feathers below the vent shows small moving lice, or clusters of white-cream eggs glued to the base of the feathers.
Mites crawl onto your hands and arms when you collect eggs or handle birds, and you may feel itching afterwards.
advanced: Combs and wattles become pale pink or almost white because of anaemia from blood loss.
Egg production drops noticeably, and eggs may be smaller with more spotted or dirty shells.
Birds become weak, dull and thin, and they eat less or waste feed.
Feathers around the vent, tail and under the wings look ragged, dirty, grey or blackened, and the skin underneath is scabby and thickened.
Feather loss and bald patches appear, and some birds begin feather pecking each other.
Large clusters of red mites are visible on perches, in nest boxes and in wall cracks, sometimes with a sour smell.
Chicks, sitting hens and weak birds die, sometimes found dead on the nest or the floor in the morning.
Growth in young stock slows, and the flock becomes more likely to catch other diseases.

lookalikes.name: Sticktight fleas
lookalikes.howToTell: Sticktight fleas are very common in Kenyan backyard flocks. They are small dark brown or black fleas that stay firmly attached in clusters on the comb, wattles, earlobes and around the eyes, and they do not move away when touched. Mites hide in the house or around the vent, and lice run quickly through the feathers.

lookalikes.name: Scaly leg mite
lookalikes.howToTell: Scaly leg mite burrows under the leg scales, which become raised, thickened, crusty and chalky-white. The damage is on the legs and feet, not in the feathers, and the birds do not usually become pale from blood loss.

lookalikes.name: Natural moult or feather pecking
lookalikes.howToTell: During a moult, birds lose feathers in an orderly way, new pin feathers grow, combs stay a normal colour and no lice or mites are found. With feather pecking, other birds are seen pulling feathers, often on the back and tail, and careful checks of the bird and house show no parasites.

lookalikes.name: Other causes of pale combs and egg drop (coccidiosis, worms, infectious diseases, poor nutrition)
lookalikes.howToTell: Coccidiosis often causes bloody or watery droppings, and heavy worm loads may show worms in droppings or at post-mortem. Diseases such as Newcastle disease or infectious bronchitis bring breathing, nervous or egg-shape signs. If you find no mites or lice at night and on the birds, ask your vet to look for these causes.

detail.diagnosis: Mites and lice are usually confirmed by looking carefully, and a vet or trained animal health assistant can do this on the farm. They examine birds by parting the feathers under the vent, under the wings and on the back to look for lice, nits and fowl mites. Because red mites hide by day, the vet may inspect the house at night with a torch, press white paper or tissue into perch joints and cracks, or use simple traps. A common trap is rolled corrugated cardboard tied under perches and checked after a few days. Samples of parasites can be put in a small sealed container or on sticky tape and examined under a magnifying glass or microscope to identify the exact type. That matters because red mites must be treated in the house, while lice and fowl mites must be treated on the bird. The vet will also check how pale the birds are and may look for other diseases that cause anaemia and egg drop. If birds have died, a post-mortem can rule out other causes. To help, you can prepare records of daily egg numbers, feed use, deaths and when the problem started. Note any new birds brought in recently. Keep a few parasites in a closed jar, and be ready for an evening visit if red mite is suspected.
firstSteps: Inspect the house after dark with a torch. Look along perches, perch ends, nest boxes and wall cracks, and examine several birds under the vent and wings so you know what you are dealing with.
Protect yourself while working. Wear long sleeves, tuck trousers into boots, wash your hands and arms afterwards, and change and wash your work clothes, because mites will crawl onto people.
Separate badly affected, very pale or weak birds into a clean, separate pen so they can rest, eat and drink without competition.
Make sure all birds have plenty of clean, cool drinking water and good quality feed, because anaemic birds need extra support to rebuild blood.
Remove old litter and nest material, and burn it or bury it well away from the poultry house. Then scrape and sweep out droppings and dust from perches, corners and cracks.
Provide a dry dust-bathing area of fine dry soil or sand so birds can clean themselves naturally, and keep it dry and under shelter.
Stop moving, selling, buying or lending birds, crates and equipment until the problem is controlled, so you do not spread parasites to neighbours.

Write down egg production, deaths and what you found. Then call your vet or a qualified agrovet. Do not use any spray, powder or dip on the birds or in the house until they advise you, because many chemicals are toxic to chickens or leave residues in eggs.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on which parasite is present and must be chosen and prescribed by a vet or qualified animal health professional, using products registered for poultry. For lice and northern or tropical fowl mites, which live on the bird, the vet may recommend treating the birds directly. This is usually a powder, spray or dip containing an acaricide (a chemical that kills mites and lice), such as a pyrethroid like permethrin, or another approved product. For red mite, the main target is the house, because most mites are hiding in cracks, not on the birds. After a thorough clean-out, the vet may advise spraying perches, nest boxes, walls and cracks with an approved acaricide. Inert dusts based on silica or diatomaceous earth, which damage the mite's outer skin and dry it out, may be used in the house. In some countries, newer treatments given through drinking water are registered for red mite; your vet will know what is available and legal in Kenya. Most products do not kill eggs, so a follow-up treatment is usually needed after the young hatch, and the vet will set this timing. Repeating the same chemical too often can make mites resistant, so vets may rotate between different drug classes. Every product has an egg and meat withdrawal period, which is the time after treatment when eggs and meat must not be eaten or sold. Follow it exactly.
