Never use cattle dips or crop pesticides on chickens. Very anaemic birds recover slowly, and the vet may advise supportive care with good nutrition and vitamins. Antibiotics have no effect on mites or lice and should only be used if the vet diagnoses a separate bacterial infection.
prevention: Quarantine all new or returning birds in a separate pen for at least two to three weeks, and check them under the vent and wings for lice and mites before they join the flock.
Inspect the flock and house regularly, at least every week or two. Look at night, check perch cracks with white tissue, or use cardboard traps, so you catch red mite while numbers are still low.
Build or repair housing with smooth surfaces and as few cracks as possible. Use removable perches and nest boxes that can be taken out, scrubbed and sun-dried.

Clean thoroughly between flocks. Remove all litter, scrape and wash with detergent and hot water, let the house dry in the sun and leave it empty for as long as practical before restocking. Remember that red mites can survive for months without birds.
Change nest box material often. Keep litter dry, and do not store old sacks, trays or timber inside the poultry house where mites can hide.
Keep wild birds, especially sparrows and pigeons, out of the poultry house with wire mesh, and remove their nests from the eaves and roof.
Avoid using second-hand crates, egg trays and equipment without cleaning them well first, and do not share equipment with neighbours.

Give birds a dry dust bath area and feed a balanced diet with enough protein, vitamins and minerals, so they can preen well and cope better with parasites. Follow your vet's advice on a planned parasite control routine.
detail.impact: Mites and lice rarely wipe out a flock overnight, but they steadily drain a farm's income. Laying hens put their energy into fighting irritation and replacing lost blood instead of making eggs, so egg numbers drop and some eggs are smaller or spotted. Spotted or dirty eggs fetch a lower price at market and from egg traders. Birds eat feed but turn less of it into eggs or meat, so the cost of each tray of eggs rises. Hens avoid nest boxes, which leads to more floor eggs, more broken and dirty eggs and more wasted time. Sitting kienyeji hens may abandon their eggs or die, and chicks may be weakened or killed, reducing the number of birds a farmer can raise and sell. Feather damage and feather pecking can lead to wounds and more losses. Stressed, anaemic birds fall sick more easily with other diseases, adding treatment costs. The workers who collect eggs may also suffer itchy mite bites. On a commercial layer farm, an unnoticed red mite problem can become expensive and slow to clear because the house itself is infested.
detail.humanHealth: Poultry red mites and fowl mites can bite people, especially farm workers and those who collect eggs, and cause itchy red spots or rashes. They cannot complete their life cycle on humans and do not set up a lasting infestation on people. However, they can be a real nuisance, and bites can become infected if scratched. Mites may also come into houses if chickens roost near or inside the family home. Wear long sleeves when working in an infested house, wash after handling birds, and keep poultry sleeping away from human living areas. Chicken lice do not live on people. A second risk is chemical residues. Only use acaricides registered for poultry, as prescribed by a vet. Never use cattle dips, crop sprays or household insecticides on birds. Strictly observe the egg and meat withdrawal periods so that no chemical residues reach your family or customers.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good when the problem is found early and treated properly. Birds with lice or light mite loads usually recover quickly once the parasites are controlled, and egg production often improves over the following weeks. Very anaemic birds, sitting hens and chicks may take longer to recover, and some may not survive. Feathers regrow only at the next moult. Red mite is the hardest to clear because it hides in the house and survives long periods without feeding. Success depends on thorough cleaning, correctly timed repeat treatments and regular checks afterwards. Reinfestation is common if new birds are not quarantined or wild birds keep entering the house. A planned routine of inspection and prevention matters more than any single treatment.

faqs.q: Can I use cattle dip or tick spray on my chickens?
faqs.a: No. Cattle dips and many tick sprays are made for cattle, not birds. They can poison chickens, and they leave residues in eggs and meat that are dangerous for your family and customers. Only use products registered for poultry, at the strength and timing your vet prescribes, and follow the egg withdrawal period on the label.

faqs.q: I sprayed the birds but the mites came back. Why?
faqs.a: This is very common with red mite. Red mites spend most of their life hiding in cracks in the perches, nest boxes and walls, not on the birds, so spraying only the birds misses most of them. Most treatments also do not kill the eggs, so a new generation hatches after a few days. Effective control usually means a thorough clean-out of the house, treating the hiding places, a correctly timed follow-up treatment and regular checks. Ask your vet to plan this with you.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell eggs while my flock is being treated?
faqs.a: It depends on the product. Some products have a withdrawal period during which eggs must be thrown away. Others are approved with no egg withdrawal when used correctly. Always ask your vet and read the label, and do not sell or eat eggs until the withdrawal time has passed. Inert dusts and cleaning do not normally create residues, but chemical sprays and powders can.

faqs.q: Do kienyeji chickens that roam free also get mites and lice?
faqs.a: Yes. Free-range and kienyeji chickens are often affected, especially sitting hens and chicks kept in dark, cracked wooden or mud houses or in boxes and baskets at night. Free-ranging birds that can dust-bathe in dry soil often keep lice numbers lower, but red mite in the night shelter can still be serious. Check the sleeping place and nests regularly, not just the birds.

faqs.q: Does a wood ash or soil dust bath really help?
faqs.a: Dust bathing is a natural behaviour that helps chickens clean their feathers and can reduce lice and fowl mite numbers. A dry, sheltered dust bath of fine soil or sand is a good part of prevention. It will not clear a heavy infestation by itself, and it does little against red mites hiding in the house. Use it alongside cleaning, inspection and vet-advised treatment, and keep the dust dry so it does not cake or irritate the birds' eyes and lungs.

faqs.q: Can mites and lice from my chickens live on me or my children?
faqs.a: Chicken lice do not live on people. Red mites and fowl mites can crawl onto people and bite, causing itchy spots, but they cannot breed and live on humans. Keep chickens sleeping away from the house, wear long sleeves when cleaning, and wash and change clothes after working with birds. Once the flock and house are cleared, the bites should stop.

products.role: A liquid vitamin and mineral supplement that can help birds recover from the stress and blood loss of a heavy mite or lice infestation and support the return of egg production. Use it alongside vet-prescribed parasite control and house cleaning, as it does not kill mites or lice.

mites-and-lice.imagePrompt: Close-up realistic photo of a brown laying hen with a noticeably pale pink comb sitting on a rough wooden perch in a simple Kenyan poultry house, with a small cluster of tiny reddish-grey mites visible in a crack of the perch beside her feet.
mites-and-lice.seoDescription: Poultry mites and lice in Kenya: spot red mite, fowl mite and lice early, protect egg production, clean the house and know when to call the vet.

card.headline: Pale comb and worms in droppings
card.look: Birds look dull, thin and pale in the comb and wattles, grow slowly or lay fewer eggs. You may see white, spaghetti-like worms or small flat, rice-like segments in fresh droppings.
card.action: Collect fresh droppings and ask your vet or agrovet-linked vet to confirm which worm it is before you deworm the whole flock.

detail.summary: Internal worms are parasites that live in a chicken's gut and feed off the bird or compete for its food. They are very common in kienyeji and other free-range birds, and in deep-litter houses where litter is old and damp. Worms rarely kill birds quickly, but they quietly steal growth, eggs and money, weaken immunity and make birds more likely to fall sick from other diseases. With regular checks, the right dewormer from a vet and good litter and range management, they are very controllable.
detail.cause: Several types of worm affect poultry. The large roundworm (Ascaridia galli) is a thick, white worm several centimetres long that lives in the small intestine; it robs the bird of nutrients, damages the gut lining, and in heavy cases worms can block the intestine. The caecal worm (Heterakis gallinarum) is small and lives in the caeca, the two blind pouches near the end of the gut; on its own it does little harm in chickens, but it can carry the parasite that causes blackhead (histomoniasis), which is serious in turkeys and sometimes in chickens. Hairworms (Capillaria species) are very thin and hard to see; they burrow into the lining of the crop or intestine and can cause real damage even in small numbers. Tapeworms (such as Raillietina and Davainea) are flat, segmented worms that hook onto the gut wall; the bird passes small white segments in its droppings. Together these worms reduce how well the bird absorbs food, cause inflammation and sometimes blood loss in the gut, and lower the bird's ability to fight off other infections. The result is poor growth, poor feathering, paleness and fewer eggs.
spread: Roundworm and caecal worm eggs pass out in droppings and become infective on the ground or in litter after some days; birds pick them up while scratching, pecking and feeding.
Worm eggs are tough and can survive for many months in damp soil, shaded runs and old litter, so the same ground keeps reinfecting birds.
Earthworms can carry roundworm, caecal worm and hairworm eggs, and birds that eat earthworms after rain often pick up heavy burdens.
Tapeworms need a middle host: birds become infected by eating beetles, ants, houseflies, snails, slugs or earthworms that carry tapeworm larvae, so free-range birds are most exposed.
Feed and water containers placed on the ground get contaminated with droppings, spreading eggs to the whole flock.
New birds bought from markets or neighbours often bring worms into a clean flock.
Overcrowding, wet litter and keeping birds on the same run for years all build up worm numbers over time.
detail.atRisk: Free-range and semi-free-range kienyeji chickens are most at risk because they scratch soil and eat insects, earthworms and snails every day. Birds in deep-litter houses are also at risk when litter is old, wet or rarely changed. Young growing birds, from a few weeks to a few months old, usually suffer most because they have not built resistance, while older birds often carry worms with fewer signs but keep contaminating the ground. Layers in their production period lose eggs when burdened. Worm burdens tend to rise during and after the long and short rains, when soil is moist and earthworms, snails and insects are plentiful. Turkeys kept with chickens are at special risk of blackhead carried by caecal worms. Broilers on fresh litter for a short cycle are usually less affected, but problems appear when litter is reused between batches.

early: Birds eat normally or even more but stay thin or grow more slowly than expected.
The comb and wattles look paler or duller red than usual.
Feathers look rough, dull or ruffled and moulting seems slow.
Layers produce fewer eggs, and some eggs may be smaller or have paler yolks.
Droppings become looser or slightly watery, sometimes with more mucus.
Small white flat segments, like grains of rice, or thin white worms are seen in fresh droppings or on the litter.
advanced: Birds become clearly weak, thin with a sharp breastbone, and stand hunched with drooping wings.
Combs and faces are very pale, showing anaemia (shortage of blood).
Persistent diarrhoea, sometimes with mucus or a little blood if hairworms or heavy burdens damage the gut.
Egg laying drops sharply or stops in affected layers.
Young birds may die suddenly from a heavy roundworm burden blocking the intestine, with masses of worms found inside at opening.
Birds catch other diseases more easily, and the flock seems to be always sick with something.
In turkeys, and occasionally chickens, sulphur-yellow droppings and depression may signal blackhead spread by caecal worms.

lookalikes.name: Coccidiosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Coccidiosis usually strikes young birds quickly, often after rains or in wet litter, with blood-stained or reddish-brown droppings, huddling and deaths within days. Worms cause a slower, longer loss of condition and you may see actual worms or segments. A vet can tell them apart with a faecal test or by opening a dead bird.

lookalikes.name: Red mites, lice and other external parasites
lookalikes.howToTell: External parasites also cause pale combs, poor laying and weakness. Check birds and perches at night with a torch for red mites, and part the feathers around the vent for lice and their eggs. If you find these, the cause is on the outside, though birds can have both problems at once.

lookalikes.name: Poor nutrition or mycotoxin-contaminated feed
lookalikes.howToTell: Unbalanced feed or mouldy maize causes poor growth, weak eggshells and dullness across the whole flock, often soon after a new feed batch. There are no worms in droppings, and a faecal test is negative. Check feed storage, smell and colour, and whether the problem started with a feed change.

lookalikes.name: Chronic respiratory disease or gapeworm
lookalikes.howToTell: Respiratory problems cause sneezing, wet eyes, rattling or gasping, with birds stretching the neck to breathe. Gapeworm is a worm that lives in the windpipe and causes gaping and head-shaking, which is different from gut worms. Gut worms cause no breathing signs.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will look at the flock history, body condition, comb colour, laying records and droppings. The most useful test is a faecal examination, where fresh droppings are mixed with a special solution and checked under a microscope for worm eggs; this can show which type of worm is present and roughly how heavy the burden is. Tapeworms are often confirmed by seeing their segments in droppings, as their eggs do not always show up well in the test. The surest check is a post-mortem, where the vet opens a sick or recently dead bird and examines the crop, intestines and caeca for worms and gut damage; hairworms, which are hard to see, are often found this way. The vet will also rule out coccidiosis, mites and other diseases. To prepare, collect several fresh dropping samples from different parts of the house into a clean, labelled container or bag and keep them cool, note the age and number of birds, egg records, feed type, when you last dewormed and with what, and whether birds free-range. If a bird dies, keep it cool (not frozen) and take it to the vet or county veterinary laboratory quickly.
firstSteps: Look closely at fresh droppings and litter, and note whether you see round white worms, flat rice-like segments or nothing visible, then write it down.
Separate the weakest, thinnest birds into a clean, dry pen so they can eat and drink without competition and are easier to watch.
Make sure all birds have constant access to clean, fresh drinking water and a good balanced feed in raised feeders and drinkers, not on the ground.
Remove wet, caked litter and replace it with fresh dry litter, and avoid spreading droppings from the house onto the run.
Collect fresh dropping samples and contact your vet or County Veterinary Officer to confirm the type of worm before buying any dewormer.
Keep records of birds affected, egg numbers, weights if you have them, and any deaths, as this helps the vet and shows whether treatment works.
Stop buying or selling birds and stop sharing equipment with neighbours until you know what you are dealing with.
Wear boots or shoe covers and wash hands after handling birds and litter, as good hygiene protects your other flocks and family.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment is with a dewormer, called an anthelmintic, chosen by the vet for the type of worm and the kind of birds. Different drug groups work on different worms: piperazine acts mainly on large roundworms; levamisole works on roundworms and some others; benzimidazoles such as albendazole, fenbendazole and flubendazole cover roundworms, caecal worms and hairworms, and some also act on tapeworms; tapeworms often need a specific product such as praziquantel or niclosamide. Most poultry dewormers are given in drinking water or feed to the whole flock, and the vet may advise repeating treatment after a period to kill worms that hatch from eggs left in the environment. Doses and timing must come from the vet and the product label, because too little lets worms survive and encourages resistance, while the wrong product simply will not work on that worm. Very important: many dewormers have egg and meat withdrawal periods, meaning eggs and meat must not be eaten or sold for a set time after treatment, and some products are not allowed at all for laying hens whose eggs are eaten. Ask the vet specifically about the egg and meat withdrawal for the product used. Antibiotics do not kill worms; they should only be used if the vet finds a bacterial infection alongside the worms. Rotating between dewormer groups as advised by the vet, and deworming based on need and testing rather than blindly, helps slow down worm resistance. After deworming, birds usually regain appetite, condition and comb colour over the following weeks, and laying recovers gradually.
prevention: Deworm on a regular schedule agreed with your vet, often linked to the rains and to key points like before point of lay, and check droppings in between so you treat only when needed.
Keep deep litter dry and clean by fixing leaking roofs and drinkers, turning litter often, and removing wet patches; replace all litter between batches of birds.
Raise feeders and drinkers off the ground, or hang them, so droppings do not fall into feed and water.
Rotate free-range runs where possible, resting ground for some months, and avoid keeping birds on the same small, muddy patch year after year.
Improve drainage and sunlight in runs, as sun and dry conditions kill many worm eggs, while shade and mud preserve them.
Control the middle hosts of tapeworms by reducing flies, beetles and snails around the house through good manure management and keeping grass short.
Isolate new birds for about two to three weeks, check their droppings and deworm them on vet advice before mixing them with your flock.
Do not keep turkeys together with chickens on the same ground, because caecal worms from chickens can spread blackhead to turkeys.
Feed a balanced diet with enough protein, vitamins and minerals so birds are better able to tolerate low worm burdens and recover quickly.
Avoid overcrowding, as more birds per square metre means more droppings and faster build-up of worm eggs.
detail.impact: Worms are one of the most common hidden causes of poor profits on Kenyan poultry farms. Kienyeji and improved kienyeji birds take longer to reach market weight, so feed costs rise and selling is delayed. Layers lay fewer eggs and may produce smaller eggs, which directly cuts daily income, especially for farmers supplying local shops and hotels. Birds with heavy worm burdens have weaker immunity, so outbreaks of coccidiosis, Newcastle disease and respiratory infections can be worse, and vaccines may not protect as well. Feed is wasted because birds eat but do not convert it into meat and eggs. There are also costs from dewormers, lost egg sales during withdrawal periods, and occasional deaths of young birds. Because the losses are slow and quiet, many farmers do not notice them until production is already low.
detail.humanHealth: The common chicken worms (roundworms, caecal worms, hairworms and chicken tapeworms) are not known to infect people, so handling infected birds is not a direct worm risk to your family. The main human health concern is drug residues: dewormers can pass into eggs and meat. Always follow the egg and meat withdrawal period given by the vet or on the product label, do not sell or eat eggs or meat during that time, and never use dewormers in laying hens unless the vet confirms the product is approved for layers. Wash hands after handling birds, litter and droppings, as droppings can carry other germs such as Salmonella.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good for most flocks when the worm type is identified and the right dewormer is used together with better litter and range management. Birds with mild to moderate burdens usually regain condition, comb colour and laying over a few weeks. Very young birds with heavy burdens, birds already badly weakened, and flocks with other diseases at the same time recover more slowly, and some may not recover fully. Without changes in hygiene and ground management, reinfection is very likely, especially on free-range land after the rains. Repeated use of the same dewormer without testing can lead to worms that no longer respond, so following vet advice matters for long-term success.

faqs.q: How often should I deworm my kienyeji chickens?
faqs.a: There is no single rule for every farm, because it depends on how much your birds free-range, the season and how much worm build-up there is on your land. Many vets advise regular deworming at set times, often around the rainy seasons and before birds start laying, and checking droppings in between. Ask your vet to help you set a plan for your farm rather than deworming blindly every month, which wastes money and builds resistance.

faqs.q: Can I eat eggs from hens I have just dewormed?
faqs.a: Not until the withdrawal period is over. Many dewormers leave residues in eggs for a period of time, and some are not approved for laying hens at all. Ask your vet which product is safe for layers and exactly how long to discard eggs. Do not sell eggs during that period either.

faqs.q: I see small white flat pieces in the droppings. What are they?
faqs.a: These are most likely tapeworm segments, which look like grains of rice and may move slightly when fresh. Tapeworms are not killed by every dewormer; some common products like piperazine work only on roundworms. Show a sample to your vet so they can choose a product that covers tapeworms, and reduce flies, beetles and snails that spread them.

faqs.q: Do herbal remedies like garlic, pawpaw seeds or aloe get rid of worms?
faqs.a: Many farmers use these traditionally, and some may support general gut health, but there is not enough reliable evidence that they clear worm burdens the way a proper dewormer does. Do not rely on them alone if birds are already sick or thin. Use a vet-recommended dewormer, and treat herbal practices only as an extra alongside good hygiene and nutrition.

faqs.q: My birds were dewormed but are still thin. Why?
faqs.a: Possible reasons include the wrong product for that type of worm, an incorrect amount, birds being reinfected immediately from dirty litter or ground, worm resistance to the drug, or another problem such as coccidiosis, mites, poor feed or mouldy feed. Take fresh droppings to the vet for testing a couple of weeks after treatment and review your litter, feed and range management.

faqs.q: Do broilers need deworming?
faqs.a: Broilers raised on fresh, dry litter for a short cycle usually pick up few worms and often do not need routine deworming. Problems arise when litter is reused, birds are kept longer, or they free-range. If you see poor growth or worms in droppings, ask your vet, and remember meat withdrawal periods before selling.

products.role: After vet-prescribed deworming, this liquid vitamin and mineral supplement can help birds recover from the stress of a worm burden and support a return to normal laying in layers. It does not kill worms and is used alongside the dewormer and better hygiene.

A liquid tonic that can help support appetite and growth in thin, recovering birds once worms have been treated by a vet, helping them regain condition. It is not a dewormer and does not replace treatment or good litter management.

internal-worms.imagePrompt: A realistic close-up photo of a thin brown kienyeji hen with a noticeably pale, pinkish comb standing on dry deep litter, with a fresh dropping beside her feet showing a few thin white roundworms.
internal-worms.seoDescription: Internal worms in chickens: spot pale combs, poor growth, egg drop and worms in droppings. Learn causes, vet deworming and prevention for Kenyan farms.

card.headline: Bare, pecked backs and bleeding vents
card.look: Birds have patches of missing feathers on the back, tail or around the vent, and some have red, raw or bleeding skin. Other birds chase them and peck at the wounds, and you may find pulled-out feathers on the floor or see birds eating feathers.
card.action: Remove any bleeding or wounded birds at once into a separate, quiet pen so the flock cannot keep pecking them, then find and fix the cause in the house.

detail.summary: Feather pecking is when chickens pull at and eat the feathers of other birds in the flock. Once the skin is broken and blood shows, the red colour attracts more pecking, and it can quickly turn into cannibalism, where birds tear at flesh and can kill each other. It is a behaviour and management problem rather than an infection, but it spreads through a flock fast, because birds copy each other. It causes deaths, lost eggs, wasted feed and real suffering, so it needs action the same day you notice it.
detail.cause: Chickens are natural foragers and spend much of their day pecking at the ground, seeds, insects and grass. When that urge has nowhere to go, birds redirect their pecking onto each other's feathers. The main triggers are overcrowding, light that is too bright or kept on too long, heat and poor ventilation, boredom with nothing to scratch or peck at, and feed that is short of protein, especially the sulphur-containing amino acid methionine (an essential building block of protein that birds need to grow feathers), or short of salt and other minerals. Hunger from empty feeders, too few feeders or drinkers, sudden changes in feed, and stress from mites, lice or disease make it worse. Once a bird has a bare patch or a small wound, the exposed skin and blood draw attention, and other birds peck harder. In layers, vent pecking often starts when a hen lays a large egg or has a prolapse (part of the oviduct pushed out through the vent), leaving red tissue showing. Repeated pecking damages skin and muscle, causes bleeding and pain, opens wounds to bacterial infection, and in severe cases birds can bleed to death or have their intestines pulled out.
spread: Too many birds in too little space, which raises stress and means birds cannot get away from aggressive flock mates.
Very bright light, white light shining directly on birds, or long lighting hours, which makes birds more active and aggressive.
Boredom in birds kept indoors on bare floors or in cages with nothing to scratch, forage or dust-bathe in.
Feed short of protein, methionine, salt or other minerals, including home mixes that are poorly balanced or diluted with too much maize bran.
Heat, poor airflow and ammonia smell in the house, which irritate birds and increase restlessness.
Too few feeders and drinkers, or feed and water running out, so birds compete and fight.
Birds copying each other: once one or two birds start pecking, others learn the habit quickly.
Any bird with a wound, prolapse, injury, or bare skin from mites, lice or mating damage, which becomes a target.
detail.atRisk: Any chicken can be affected, but the problem is most common in commercial layers and improved breeds kept in deep-litter houses or cages, where crowding and bright lighting are more likely. Pullets coming into lay and hens at peak production are at high risk of vent pecking, especially when large eggs or prolapses occur. Broilers and growing chicks can start toe pecking and feather pecking when brooders are crowded, too hot or too brightly lit. Kienyeji chickens on free range rarely have serious outbreaks because they can forage, but improved kienyeji kept fully confined can be affected. Risk rises during hot dry months, when birds are kept in for long periods, when stocking is increased without enlarging the house, and when feed prices push farmers to cut protein or switch feed suddenly.

early: Birds pulling or nibbling at the feathers of other birds, especially around the tail, back and wings.
Loose feathers lying on the floor, or birds seen picking up and eating feathers.
Thinning feathers or small bare patches on the back, rump and base of the tail.
Some birds hiding in corners, under feeders or on high perches to avoid others.
Increased restlessness, noise and chasing in the house, often worse when lights are on or in the hottest part of the day.
Chicks pecking at each other's toes in the brooder.
advanced: Large areas of bare skin on the back, tail and wings, sometimes with red, scabbed or raw skin.
Bleeding from the vent, back, comb, toes or tail, with blood stains on feathers, eggs or walls.
Groups of birds attacking one bird and pecking at open wounds.
Swollen, torn or prolapsed vents, sometimes with tissue pulled out.
Sudden deaths of birds found with torn vents or deep wounds.
Drop in egg production, more eggs with blood on the shell, and birds pecking at and eating eggs.
Weak, depressed injured birds that stop eating, which may develop smelly, infected wounds.

lookalikes.name: Natural moulting
lookalikes.howToTell: In a moult, birds lose and regrow feathers on their own, often after a period of lay or stress, and new pin feathers appear evenly across the body. There is no chasing, no blood and the skin is not damaged. With pecking, bare patches are on the back, tail and vent, and you see birds actively pulling feathers.

lookalikes.name: Mites and lice
lookalikes.howToTell: External parasites cause dull, damaged or missing feathers and itchy, restless birds. Part the feathers around the vent and under the wings: you will see small crawling lice, clusters of eggs at the base of feathers, or tiny red mites, which are easiest to find at night in perches and cracks. Parasites can also trigger pecking, so both may be present.

lookalikes.name: Mating damage from cockerels
lookalikes.howToTell: Hens kept with cockerels can lose feathers on the back of the neck and on the back where the cockerel stands and grips. The damage is on hens only, matches mating positions, and you do not see hens attacking each other. Too many hens per cockerel, or one favoured hen, makes it worse.

lookalikes.name: Prolapse or egg binding
lookalikes.howToTell: A hen with a prolapse has red or pink tissue sticking out of the vent and may strain, stand upright like a penguin or sit fluffed up. This is a medical problem in its own right, but the exposed tissue quickly attracts vent pecking. If one hen has a damaged vent but the rest of the flock looks normal, check for prolapse first.

detail.diagnosis: Feather pecking and cannibalism are usually recognised from what the farmer and vet can see: the pattern of feather loss, the wounds, and birds actively pecking. The real work is finding why it started. A vet or poultry extension officer will look at the house size and number of birds, light brightness and hours, temperature and ventilation, number of feeders and drinkers, litter condition, and the feed being used. They will examine birds for mites, lice, prolapse and signs of other disease, and may check whether the feed is properly balanced or recommend a feed analysis. If birds have died, a post-mortem (opening the dead bird to examine the organs) can confirm the cause of death and rule out other diseases. Before the visit, prepare: the number of birds and the size of the house, the age and breed, the name and type of feed and any recent feed changes, your lighting routine, when the problem started, how many birds are injured or dead, and egg records if you keep layers.
firstSteps: Remove every bird with a bleeding or open wound straight away and keep it in a separate, quiet pen with its own feed and clean water until it has fully healed and feathered over.
Remove dead birds promptly so the flock cannot peck at them, and dispose of them safely by burying deeply or burning.
Reduce light brightness: dim the bulbs, use lower-wattage or red bulbs, shade windows from direct sun, and avoid leaving lights on longer than your feeding programme needs.
Give birds something to peck at: hang cabbage, sukuma wiki or green grass, scatter a small amount of grain in clean litter, and provide a dust-bathing area or bundles of hay or straw.
Check that feeders and drinkers are full, clean and enough for the number of birds, so no bird has to fight to eat or drink.
Improve airflow and cool the house during hot hours by opening vents, removing wet litter and providing shade outside.
If the house is crowded, move some birds out or open up more space as soon as possible.
Check your feed: make sure you are using the correct complete feed for the birds' age and type, and call your vet or feed supplier to discuss protein and salt levels before making changes.
Record how many birds are injured or dead each day, and call your vet or extension officer if the problem continues, wounds look infected or birds keep dying.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no single medicine that stops feather pecking; the vet's main job is to help you fix the cause and care for injured birds. Wounds are usually cleaned and treated with an antiseptic spray, often a coloured spray such as a purple or blue wound spray, which also hides the red colour that attracts pecking. Some vets suggest anti-peck sprays or bitter-tasting products on feathers. Badly injured birds may need to be humanely culled if they are suffering and unlikely to recover. Antibiotics are only needed if wounds become infected, and they must be prescribed by a vet, used for the full course as directed, and never used as a substitute for fixing the management problem; overuse of antibiotics breeds resistant bacteria (antimicrobial resistance) that make future treatment harder for both animals and people. If any drug is used, follow the withdrawal period on the label and from your vet before selling or eating eggs or meat. The vet or a nutritionist may advise correcting protein, amino acids, salt or minerals in the feed. In some systems, beak trimming is used to reduce damage, but it causes pain and stress, must only be done by a trained person at the right age, and does not remove the need to fix housing, light and feed. Expect improvement over days to weeks once the cause is corrected, but the habit can persist in a flock, so management changes must be kept up.
prevention: Do not overcrowd: give each bird enough floor, feeder and drinker space, and build or extend the house before increasing bird numbers. A widely used Kenyan extension guideline for adult layers on deep litter is about four to five birds per square metre, but ask your extension officer what suits your breed and housing.

Manage lighting carefully: use only the light hours your layers or broilers actually need, keep the light soft and even, avoid bare bright bulbs hanging low, and shade direct sunlight coming through windows.

Feed a complete, balanced commercial feed or a well-formulated home mix for the correct age and type of bird, with enough protein, methionine and other amino acids, salt and minerals, and avoid sudden changes in feed.
Keep birds busy: provide greens, scattered grain in the litter, hay bundles, perches and dust-bathing areas, and allow safe free-range time where possible.
Keep the house cool and well ventilated, keep litter dry and fresh, and do not let ammonia build up.
Control mites and lice regularly by checking birds and perches, and treat with products recommended by your vet or agrovet.
Keep birds of similar age and size together, avoid mixing strange birds into an established flock, and keep a suitable number of hens per cockerel.
Collect eggs often, provide enough dark, comfortable nest boxes, and check daily for prolapsed or injured birds so you can remove them before pecking starts.
detail.impact: Feather pecking and cannibalism can cost a Kenyan poultry farmer heavily. Birds die from wounds and bleeding, and each lost layer is lost income for the rest of her laying life. Birds with poor feather cover lose more body heat, so they eat more feed to stay warm while laying fewer eggs, which raises feed costs at a time when feed is already the biggest expense. Egg production drops from stress, and egg eating and blood-stained eggs reduce what you can sell. Broilers with damaged skin and scars fetch lower prices. Treating wounds, isolating birds and culling all take time and money, and once the habit is established in a flock, it can keep flaring up until the birds are sold.
detail.humanHealth: Feather pecking itself does not spread to people. If a vet prescribes antibiotics or other drugs for infected wounds, you must observe the withdrawal period before selling or eating eggs or meat, so that drug residues do not reach consumers. Wear gloves or wash your hands well with soap after handling wounded or dead birds, as wounds and droppings can carry bacteria such as Salmonella.
detail.outlook: Most birds with mild feather loss recover well and regrow their feathers once the cause is removed, often by the next moult. Birds with small wounds usually heal if they are separated quickly and kept clean. Birds with deep wounds, torn vents or prolapses have a poorer outlook, and some may need to be humanely culled. The flock outlook depends mainly on how fast the farmer acts: if crowding, light, boredom and feed problems are corrected early, outbreaks usually settle, but if they are ignored, the behaviour can become a fixed habit in the flock and keep causing losses.

faqs.q: Why have my chickens started eating each other?
faqs.a: It usually begins as feather pecking caused by stress, crowding, bright light, heat, boredom or feed that is short of protein or salt. Once a bird bleeds, the red colour attracts more pecking and it turns into cannibalism. Look at your house, lights and feed first, and remove any wounded bird immediately.

faqs.q: Should I add salt to the drinking water to stop pecking?
faqs.a: Salt shortage can be one cause of pecking, and some farmers have heard of adding salt to water. However, too much salt is poisonous to chickens and can cause wet droppings and death. Do not guess. Check that you are using a proper complete feed, and ask your vet, extension officer or feed supplier before adding any salt.

faqs.q: Can I put a wounded hen back with the flock?
faqs.a: Only when the wound has fully healed, there is no visible red skin or scab, and feathers have started to grow back. Put her back at night when birds are calm, and watch closely for the next few days. If she is attacked again, remove her and keep her separate longer.

faqs.q: Will red bulbs really help?
faqs.a: Many farmers find that red or dimmer light calms birds and makes blood and bare skin less visible, which reduces pecking. It helps most when combined with fixing crowding, feed and boredom. Make sure your layers still get the light hours they need for egg production.

faqs.q: Is beak trimming necessary?
faqs.a: Beak trimming reduces the damage pecking causes, but it is painful and stressful, must only be done by a trained person, and does not fix the reason birds are pecking. Good space, soft light, enrichment and balanced feed are the first line of prevention. Discuss with your vet whether trimming is appropriate for your system.

faqs.q: My hens are also eating their eggs. Is that related?
faqs.a: Often yes. Egg eating shares many causes with feather pecking, including boredom, crowding, too few or too bright nest boxes, and shortage of protein or calcium in the feed. Collect eggs often, remove broken eggs quickly, provide dark comfortable nests, and make sure layers get a proper layer feed.

products.role: Methionine is an essential amino acid needed for protein metabolism and feather growth, and shortage of it is one known trigger for feather pecking. Where your vet or feed advisor finds the ration is short, it can be used as a feed supplement to help balance the diet and support feather regrowth, alongside correcting crowding, light and management. It does not stop pecking on its own.

A vitamin and mineral supplement that can support birds recovering from the stress of a pecking outbreak and help injured birds and stressed layers return to production, used together with isolating wounded birds, vet wound care and fixing the cause in the house.
