feather-pecking.seoDescription: Feather pecking and cannibalism in chickens: causes, signs, first steps and prevention for Kenyan farmers – crowding, light, boredom and diet.

card.headline: Straining hen with red tissue at vent
card.look: The hen stands upright like a penguin, pumps her tail and strains again and again without laying an egg. In prolapse, a red or pink moist bulge of tissue sticks out of the vent.
card.action: Move the hen at once to a quiet, clean, dim pen away from the flock so others cannot peck her, and call your vet.

aka: Pick-out (when other hens peck the prolapse)
detail.summary: Egg binding means an egg is stuck inside the hen's oviduct (the egg-making tube) or in the cloaca (the shared chamber just inside the vent) and she cannot push it out. Prolapse means part of the oviduct or cloaca has been pushed out through the vent, often after heavy straining. Both problems are emergencies because the hen can die from exhaustion, shock, infection or being pecked by other birds. They usually point to a flock problem with calcium, body condition or the age at which pullets start laying.
detail.cause: Laying an egg needs strong, well-timed muscle contractions in the oviduct and good lubrication. Calcium is needed both to build the shell and to make these muscles squeeze properly. When a hen is short of calcium, or of vitamin D3 which she needs to use calcium, her oviduct muscles become weak and the egg stops moving. Very large eggs, double-yolk eggs, misshapen or soft-shelled eggs can also get stuck. Young pullets that start laying before their bodies are big and mature enough, and fat hens with a lot of fat around the oviduct, have the most trouble. As the hen strains hard and repeatedly, the lining of the oviduct and cloaca can be pushed out through the vent; this is a prolapse. The exposed tissue swells, dries, gets dirty and is very attractive to other hens, who peck it. Pecking can pull out the intestines and kill the hen quickly. Infection of the oviduct, dehydration, cold, stress and lack of exercise all make egg binding and prolapse more likely.
spread: Egg binding and prolapse are not contagious; they do not pass from bird to bird, but several hens can be affected when the whole flock shares the same feeding or management problem.
Feeding chick or grower mash, maize bran, kitchen scraps or poorly mixed home-made rations to laying hens can leave them short of calcium and trigger the problem.
Lighting pullets for long hours, or feeding them heavily too early, can push them into lay before their bodies are ready, which raises the risk of prolapse at the start of lay.
Overfeeding energy-rich feeds and keeping hens in small cages or crowded houses with little exercise makes them fat and more likely to bind or prolapse.
Hot weather reduces feed intake, so hens eat less calcium just when they need it, and dehydration from lack of clean water makes laying harder.
Stress from handling, transport, predators, loud noise or sudden changes in feed can upset laying and lead to retained eggs.
Once one hen has a bleeding or protruding vent, other hens learn to peck vents, and cannibalism can spread through the flock as a behaviour.
detail.atRisk: Laying hens of any breed can be affected, but the risk is highest in young pullets just coming into lay and in older, overweight hens. Commercial layer hybrids, which lay many eggs, are at higher risk if their feed is not balanced for calcium. Improved kienyeji and free-range hens fed mainly on scraps or bran without a calcium source are also at risk. Hens that lay unusually large or double-yolk eggs, birds kept in cages or crowded houses with little exercise, and flocks under heat stress during the hot, dry months before the long rains are more likely to have problems. Bright lighting in the house and overcrowding increase the risk that a prolapse turns into pecking and cannibalism.

early: The hen goes in and out of the nest box many times, or sits in the nest for a long time without laying.
She stands very upright with legs wide apart in a penguin-like stance and walks stiffly or waddles.
Her tail pumps or bobs up and down as she strains, and you may see her abdomen tightening.
She is quieter than usual, fluffs her feathers, eats less and may drink more or less than normal.
Droppings may be few, small or watery because the stuck egg presses on the gut.
When you gently feel the abdomen near the vent, you may feel a firm, egg-shaped lump.
The vent may look swollen, moist or pulsing.
advanced: Red, pink or dark purple moist tissue sticking out of the vent, sometimes with an egg visible inside it.
The hen sits on the ground, cannot stand or walk properly, and may seem to lose use of her legs because the egg presses on nerves.
Pale or bluish comb, fast or open-mouth breathing, and deep weakness or collapse from exhaustion and shock.
Dried, dirty, swollen or blackened prolapsed tissue that smells bad, which means infection or tissue death.
Bleeding or torn tissue at the vent from other hens pecking, and blood on the feathers of the hen or her pen mates.
Sudden death, sometimes with the hen found with her insides pulled out by other birds.

lookalikes.name: Egg yolk peritonitis
lookalikes.howToTell: Here yolk has fallen into the belly and caused infection. The hen also stands upright like a penguin, but the belly is soft, swollen and may feel like a water bag, and there is usually no hard egg-shaped lump near the vent and no tissue sticking out. She is often sick for days with poor appetite and stops laying.

lookalikes.name: Vent gleet (cloacitis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Vent gleet is an infection of the vent. You will see a dirty, smelly, white or yellow discharge and caked feathers around the vent, but the hen is not usually straining hard and there is no egg stuck or tissue protruding.

lookalikes.name: Vent pecking injury without prolapse
lookalikes.howToTell: Bleeding or wounds at the vent can come from pecking alone, especially in crowded, brightly lit houses. Look closely: in a pecking injury there is no swollen bulge of tissue turned out of the vent and no egg stuck, but there are wounds and missing feathers.

lookalikes.name: Coccidiosis or severe diarrhoea
lookalikes.howToTell: Birds with coccidiosis may hunch and strain, but they pass watery, often bloody droppings, several birds are usually sick at once, and young growers are more affected. There is no egg lump and no penguin stance linked to the nest box.

detail.diagnosis: A vet usually confirms egg binding by watching the hen's behaviour and gently feeling her abdomen and vent. Often the egg can be felt, and sometimes a gloved, lubricated finger inserted carefully into the vent can touch it. In clinics with equipment, an X-ray or ultrasound scan can show where the egg is, whether the shell is hard or soft, and whether there is more than one egg. For prolapse, the vet examines the tissue to see which part has come out, whether an egg is trapped inside, and whether the tissue is still healthy, infected or dead. If several hens are affected or dying, the vet may do a post-mortem (an examination of a dead bird) to look for calcium problems, fat around the oviduct, infection or egg peritonitis, and may ask about feed. To help, prepare notes on the hen's age, when she started laying, what feed and any supplements the flock receives, how much water is available, lighting hours, how many birds are affected, and recent egg size and shell quality. Keep a sample bag of the feed you are using in case it needs checking.
firstSteps: Separate the hen immediately into a quiet, clean, dim, warm box or pen with soft bedding, away from other birds that might peck her vent.
Wear gloves or wash your hands well before and after handling her, because the vent area carries germs.
Offer clean, fresh water within easy reach, as dehydration makes laying harder; do not force water into her beak.

For a suspected stuck egg with no prolapse, you can soak her lower body in a basin of comfortably warm (not hot) clean water for about 15–20 minutes to relax her muscles, then dry her well and keep her warm in the quiet box.
Gently apply a little clean petroleum jelly or clean cooking oil just around the vent with a gloved finger, but do not push deep inside or try to pull the egg.
Never try to break or crush the egg inside the hen yourself, as sharp shell pieces can cut the oviduct and cause fatal bleeding or infection.
For a prolapse, keep the exposed tissue clean and moist by rinsing gently with clean lukewarm water, and protect it from flies, dirt and drying out until the vet advises you.

Record what you have seen, how long she has been straining, and check the rest of the flock for other hens straining, laying soft-shelled eggs or pecking vents, then call your vet or the nearest animal health assistant.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on how long the hen has been straining, whether the egg can be felt, and whether tissue has prolapsed. For egg binding, a vet often starts by giving calcium, for example calcium gluconate or another calcium preparation, because many bound hens are low in calcium and this can help the oviduct muscles contract again. The vet may also give fluids, warmth and gentle lubrication, and can sometimes ease the egg out manually. Hormones that make the oviduct contract, such as oxytocin, are only used by a vet after checking that the egg is not stuck in a way that could cause the oviduct to tear. If the egg will not move, the vet may carefully draw out the egg contents with a needle and then collapse and remove the shell pieces; this is skilled work and should not be tried at home. For prolapse, the vet cleans the tissue, may reduce swelling, gently pushes it back into place, and may place a temporary stitch around the vent to hold it while it heals. Pain relief or anti-inflammatory drugs such as meloxicam may be used. Antibiotics are only needed if there is infection or damaged tissue; they should be prescribed by the vet and used fully and only as directed, because careless antibiotic use breeds resistant germs (antimicrobial resistance) that affect both animals and people. Many drugs have an egg and meat withdrawal period, which is the time after treatment when eggs and meat must not be eaten or sold, so ask your vet for it. Recovering hens usually need several days of rest in a dim pen and may stop laying for a while. In commercial flocks, badly damaged or repeatedly prolapsing hens are often culled humanely, as treatment may not be worth it. Never give drugs or injections yourself without a vet's prescription.
prevention: Feed laying hens a proper layer mash that contains enough calcium for shell building, and do not let them live mainly on maize bran, scraps or grower feed once they are laying.
Offer a separate free-choice calcium source such as clean crushed oyster shell or limestone grit in a small feeder, so each hen can take what she needs, especially in heat or peak lay.

Do not feed layer mash to young growing pullets long before they start laying, because too much calcium too early can damage their kidneys; switch to layer feed around the point of lay as advised by your feed supplier or extension officer.
Make sure birds get vitamin D3, from sunlight for free-range hens or from a good premix or vitamin supplement for housed birds, because they cannot use calcium well without it.
Bring pullets into lay at the right age and body weight: do not increase lighting hours or push feed too early, and weigh a sample of pullets to check they are growing evenly before lay starts.
Prevent hens from getting too fat by avoiding excess energy feeds, giving the right daily amount, and allowing space to walk, scratch and exercise.
Provide clean, cool drinking water at all times, more drinkers in the hot season, and good shade and ventilation to reduce heat stress.

Reduce vent pecking by avoiding overcrowding, keeping light in the house dim rather than very bright, giving enough nest boxes in a dark corner, and removing any bleeding or prolapsed hen immediately.
Collect eggs often, keep nest boxes clean, and watch for soft-shelled, thin-shelled or very large eggs, which are early warnings of calcium or management problems.
Keep records of laying, egg size and any binding or prolapse cases so you can spot patterns and talk them over with your vet or extension officer.
detail.impact: A bound or prolapsed hen stops laying, and many die if not helped quickly, so each case is a direct loss of a productive layer and her future eggs. When several hens are affected, it usually means a feed or management problem is lowering egg numbers and shell quality across the flock, with more cracked, soft and unsaleable eggs. Prolapse often leads to vent pecking and cannibalism, which can kill healthy birds too and make the flock nervous and less productive. For a smallholder with a small kienyeji or layer flock, losing even a few hens around the point of lay is a serious blow, as they have already been fed and raised for months. Vet visits, treatment, culling of damaged birds and withdrawal periods on eggs add extra costs.
detail.humanHealth: Egg binding and prolapse themselves do not infect people. However, the vent area of chickens can carry germs such as Salmonella and E. coli, so wear gloves when handling an affected hen, wash your hands well with soap and water afterwards, and keep children away. If your vet treats the hen with antibiotics or other drugs, follow the egg and meat withdrawal period exactly, as eating or selling eggs or meat too soon can leave drug residues that harm consumers and add to antimicrobial resistance.
detail.outlook: Hens with a simple stuck egg that are helped early, especially when low calcium is the cause, often pass the egg and recover well within a day or two. The longer a hen strains, the more exhausted and dehydrated she becomes and the poorer her chances. A small, clean prolapse that is pushed back quickly and kept away from other birds can heal, but larger prolapses, dirty, dried or dead tissue, and tissue that has been pecked carry a much poorer outlook. Some hens bind or prolapse again in later laying cycles, particularly if they are fat or lay very large eggs. Fixing the flock's calcium, vitamin D3, body condition and lighting is the best way to stop new cases.

faqs.q: Can I break the egg inside my hen to help her pass it?
faqs.a: No. Breaking the egg yourself is dangerous. Sharp shell pieces can cut the oviduct, causing heavy bleeding or infection, and leftover egg material can lead to peritonitis. If warm soaking, rest and lubrication around the vent do not help within a few hours, call your vet, who can safely remove the egg contents if needed.

faqs.q: Should I push the prolapse back in myself?
faqs.a: Your first job is to keep the tissue clean, moist and protected from pecking, and to call your vet. A vet or trained animal health assistant can show you how to clean and gently replace the tissue, and may place a stitch to hold it. Pushing it back with dirty hands, or using force, can tear the tissue and introduce infection. If you cannot reach a vet, ask for guidance by phone before you try.

faqs.q: Why are my young pullets prolapsing just as they start laying?
faqs.a: This usually happens when pullets start laying before their bodies are big and mature enough, often because lighting hours were increased too early, or they were fed to come into lay quickly but are underweight or uneven in size. Fat pullets and those laying large first eggs are also at risk. Talk with your extension officer about the right lighting programme and target body weights, and make sure they move onto a balanced layer feed with a calcium source at the right time.

faqs.q: Is giving extra calcium to my hens enough to stop egg binding?
faqs.a: Calcium is very important, but it is not the only factor. Hens also need vitamin D3 to use calcium, enough clean water, the right body condition, exercise and good lighting. Too much calcium given to young growing birds can harm their kidneys. The best approach is a good layer feed plus a free-choice calcium source like oyster shell for laying hens, sunshine or vitamin D3, and good management overall.

faqs.q: Can I still eat eggs from a hen that had egg binding or prolapse?
faqs.a: If the hen was not given any drugs, her eggs are generally safe once she is healthy again, though any egg that came out with blood, pus or dirt should be thrown away. If your vet gave her antibiotics or other medicines, do not eat or sell her eggs or meat until the withdrawal period your vet gives you has passed.

faqs.q: Will a hen that prolapsed once do it again?
faqs.a: Some do, especially if they are overweight, lay very large eggs or the flock's calcium and management problems are not fixed. Watch her closely in the following weeks, keep her in good body condition, and make sure her feed is balanced. In commercial flocks, hens that prolapse repeatedly are often culled, because they are likely to suffer again and may attract pecking.

products.role: Added to layer feed to support egg production and shell quality, helping the flock lay well-formed, properly shelled eggs as part of a balanced ration and good management that lower the risk of egg binding; it is a preventive aid, not a treatment for a hen that is already bound or prolapsed.

Supplies vitamin D3, which hens need to absorb and use calcium for strong shells and normal oviduct muscle contractions, along with vitamins A and E; useful for housed layers with little sunlight as part of prevention, alongside proper calcium feeding and vet advice.

egg-binding.imagePrompt: A brown laying hen standing very upright in a penguin-like stance on straw bedding in a simple Kenyan poultry house, tail lowered and pumping, with a small pink moist bulge of tissue visible at the vent, soft natural light.
egg-binding.seoDescription: Egg binding and vent prolapse in hens: spot straining, penguin stance and red tissue at the vent, give first aid, and prevent it with calcium and good care.

card.headline: Swollen, water-filled belly and blue comb
card.look: Fast-growing broilers, often the biggest males, stand upright like a penguin with a tight, swollen belly that feels like a water balloon. They pant with open beaks, have a dark bluish-red comb and wattles, and some die suddenly, often near the end of the growing cycle.
card.action: Improve fresh-air ventilation and fix brooding temperature at once, and call your vet to open a dead bird and confirm the cause.

detail.summary: Ascites is a build-up of fluid in the belly of broiler chickens. It happens when the bird's heart and lungs cannot supply enough oxygen for its very fast growth, so the heart becomes overloaded and fluid leaks out of the blood vessels. It is not an infection and does not spread from bird to bird, but it is common in Kenya's highland broiler areas and causes heavy losses late in the cycle, after most of the feed money has already been spent.
detail.cause: Modern broilers grow extremely fast, and their muscles demand a lot of oxygen. Their lungs, however, are small and rigid for their body size. When oxygen is short, because of high altitude, a cold house, stale air, ammonia, dust or lung disease, the bird's blood vessels in the lungs tighten. The right side of the heart, which pumps blood through the lungs, has to push much harder. Over days and weeks it becomes thick, then stretched and weak, and its valve starts to leak. Blood backs up into the veins and the liver, pressure rises, and clear yellowish fluid (plasma) seeps out of the liver into the belly. This fluid is the 'water' in water belly. The bird also makes more red blood cells to try to carry more oxygen, which thickens the blood and makes the heart work harder still, so the problem feeds itself. Extra salt (sodium) in feed or water makes the body hold more fluid and worsens it. Damage to the lungs or liver from mouldy feed (mycotoxins), respiratory infections, carbon monoxide from charcoal brooders, and some nutrient shortfalls such as low vitamin E can add to the load.
spread: Ascites does not spread from bird to bird; it is triggered by conditions on the farm and by the bird's own fast growth.

High altitude is a major trigger, because the air holds less oxygen; farms in places like Nakuru, Eldoret, Nyandarua, Nyeri, Kiambu and the Nairobi highlands see more cases than coastal or lowland farms.

Cold brooding, especially on cold nights in June to August and during the rains, forces chicks to burn more energy and use more oxygen to keep warm, and this early stress often shows up as ascites weeks later.
Poor ventilation lets ammonia, dust and carbon dioxide build up; houses closed tightly with polythene or sacks to keep warmth in are a common cause.
Charcoal jikos or other burners inside a closed brooder release carbon monoxide, which blocks oxygen in the blood and damages the heart and lungs.
Very fast early growth from high-energy pelleted feed fed freely from day one increases oxygen demand beyond what the lungs can handle.
Too much salt in feed or water, for example salty borehole water, home-mixed rations with salty fish meal (omena), or adding table salt or electrolytes for long periods, makes fluid build-up worse.
Respiratory diseases such as infectious bronchitis, Newcastle disease, mycoplasma (CRD) or aspergillosis (fungal lung infection from mouldy litter) damage the lungs and push birds into ascites.
detail.atRisk: Commercial broilers (such as Cobb, Ross and Arbor Acres) are by far the most at risk, especially the fastest-growing males. Signs usually appear from about the third week to slaughter, although the damage often starts during brooding. Farms at higher altitude, houses that are cold at night, and houses that are tightly closed with poor airflow carry the highest risk. It is most common during cold months and the long and short rains, when farmers close houses to keep birds warm. Improved kienyeji types (such as Kenbro, KALRO improved kienyeji or Kuroiler) and free-range indigenous chickens grow more slowly and are rarely affected. Layers can occasionally be affected but much less often than broilers.

early: Birds that are slower and quieter than flock mates, spending more time sitting and less time at the feeder.
Panting or breathing with the beak open, even when the house is not hot.
Comb, wattles and face turning dark red or bluish-purple (cyanosis, meaning poor oxygen in the blood), especially after the bird moves.
Slightly fuller-looking lower belly, sometimes with feathers on the belly looking thin or wet from lying down.
Some birds look smaller or uneven compared with the rest, while others are the biggest birds in the house.
A rise in daily deaths among the heaviest, best-looking males, which is often the first thing a farmer notices.
advanced: Tight, swollen belly that feels soft and fluid-filled, like a water balloon, when gently pressed.
Bird stands very upright, like a penguin, with legs wide apart to balance the heavy belly.
Reddened or purplish skin over the belly, which may look shiny and stretched.
Heavy, laboured breathing with the whole body moving, and the bird struggles to walk to feed and water.
Bird gasps or collapses when chased or handled, and may die suddenly during catching or loading.
Sudden death, with the dead bird showing a swollen belly and dark comb.

lookalikes.name: Sudden death syndrome (flip-over)
lookalikes.howToTell: Also kills big, fast-growing broilers, but the bird dies within moments, often found on its back, with no swollen belly and no fluid inside at post-mortem. Ascites birds are sick for days first and have a fluid-filled belly.

lookalikes.name: Yolk sac infection (omphalitis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Affects chicks mostly in the first week, with a wet, swollen, smelly navel and a swollen belly from an infected yolk. Ascites usually appears from three weeks onward and the belly fluid is clear yellow and does not smell.

lookalikes.name: E. coli peritonitis and other bacterial infections
lookalikes.howToTell: Birds often have fever signs, diarrhoea or airsac disease, and the belly contains cloudy, cheesy or foul-smelling material rather than clear fluid. A vet's post-mortem tells the difference quickly.

lookalikes.name: Aflatoxin poisoning or other liver damage
lookalikes.howToTell: Mouldy feed causes poor growth across the whole flock, pale or yellow mottled liver, poor feathering and weak immunity. It can contribute to ascites, so the vet may find both; feed testing helps confirm it.

detail.diagnosis: Ascites is usually confirmed by post-mortem (opening a dead bird). The vet looks for clear yellowish fluid in the belly, often with jelly-like clots, a heart that is enlarged and floppy with a thickened and stretched right side, a swollen, congested or shrunken liver, and dark, congested lungs. The vet may compare the weight of the right side of the heart with the whole heart to confirm right heart overload. They will also check for underlying causes such as lung infection, airsac damage, fungal growth from mouldy litter, or liver damage from mycotoxins, and may send samples to a laboratory (such as a county or KALRO/Kabete veterinary lab) for disease tests, feed mycotoxin tests or water salt tests. To help, keep two or three freshly dead or very sick birds cool (not frozen) in a clean bag, note the age of the flock, daily deaths, which birds are dying (big males or all sizes), the feed brand and batch, the water source, brooding method and night temperatures, and any vaccinations or treatments given.
firstSteps: Open up ventilation straight away so fresh air flows through the house, especially near the roof and above bird height, while avoiding cold draughts blowing directly on the birds.
Check for ammonia: if the smell stings your eyes or nose when you bend down to bird level, the air is too dirty; remove wet, caked litter and add fresh, dry litter.
Remove any charcoal jiko or burner from a closed brooder, or make sure fumes are vented outside, because carbon monoxide is deadly and worsens ascites.
Keep the house at a steady, comfortable temperature; watch the birds, since huddling means too cold and spreading to the walls with panting means too hot.
Handle birds as little as possible and do not chase them, because stressed ascites birds can collapse and die from the extra effort.
Make sure clean, fresh water is always available, and stop adding salt, salty electrolytes or home remedies to the water unless your vet advises it.
Do not try to drain the belly with a needle or knife; it does not cure the bird and causes pain, infection and death.
Record daily deaths and the age, sex and size of birds affected, keep a few fresh dead birds cool for the vet, and call your vet or County Veterinary Office for a post-mortem.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no medicine that reliably cures a broiler with an advanced water belly, and most such birds will not recover; the vet will usually advise humane culling of badly affected birds to end their suffering. The real treatment is at flock level, to stop more birds from developing it. The vet will typically advise on better ventilation and steady temperatures, reducing early growth rate (for example a lighting programme with a dark period at night, or a period of controlled feeding, or switching to mash or a lower-energy feed for part of the cycle), and checking feed and water for excess salt. If the post-mortem shows an underlying infection such as a bacterial respiratory disease, the vet may prescribe an appropriate treatment for that infection only. Antibiotics do not treat ascites itself, and using them without a clear bacterial cause wastes money and increases antimicrobial resistance (germs becoming resistant to drugs), which harms animal and human health. Diuretics (drugs that make the body lose water) have been tried in some settings, but results are inconsistent and they are not a routine answer. Any drug must be prescribed by a vet, and the meat withdrawal period (the time you must wait after the last dose before slaughter or sale) must be followed strictly, which matters greatly in broilers that are close to market age. Expect losses to slow within days to a couple of weeks once ventilation and growth management are corrected, although birds already damaged may keep dying.
prevention: Brood chicks warm and steady from day one, with a pre-heated house and dry litter, because cold stress in the first two weeks is one of the biggest causes of ascites later.
Ventilate well at all ages: use adjustable curtains that open from the top, leave ventilation gaps under the roof, and never seal the house completely with polythene, even on cold nights.
Use safe heat sources such as electric brooders, gas brooders or well-vented charcoal brooders placed so that fumes go outside, and never leave a smoking jiko in a closed brooder.

On highland farms, slow early growth slightly using a lighting programme with some hours of darkness each night, or a feeding plan agreed with your vet or feed supplier; birds catch up later with little loss of final weight.
Check the salt content of your water if you use a borehole, and avoid adding salt, salty fish meal or long-term electrolytes to home-mixed feed; buy feed from reputable millers.
Store feed off the floor in a dry, airy store, use it while fresh, and never feed mouldy feed, because mycotoxins damage the liver and lungs.

Keep litter dry and free of mould to prevent aspergillosis, and vaccinate against Newcastle disease, Gumboro (IBD) and infectious bronchitis as advised by your vet, since lung damage from disease increases ascites.
Avoid overcrowding, buy chicks from reputable hatcheries, and keep records of deaths per day so you can spot a rising trend early and act.
detail.impact: Ascites hits the broiler farmer at the worst time, because birds usually die in the last weeks of the cycle when nearly all the feed, chick and brooding costs have already been paid. The best, heaviest males are often the ones lost. Surviving affected birds grow poorly, waste feed, and give uneven flock weights that brokers and hotels may pay less for. Birds with ascites are rejected at slaughterhouse inspection, and they often die during catching and transport. On highland farms with cold nights and closed houses, repeated ascites losses can make the difference between profit and loss for a small broiler business, and they also erode confidence in broiler farming as a reliable income.
detail.humanHealth: Ascites is not an infection and cannot pass to people. However, birds with water belly are sick and should not be sold or eaten; they are condemned at meat inspection. If your vet prescribes any drug for an underlying problem, observe the full meat withdrawal period before selling or eating birds, to avoid drug residues in chicken meat.
detail.outlook: For an individual bird with a clearly swollen, fluid-filled belly, the outlook is poor; most die or need to be culled. Birds showing only early signs, such as panting and a dark comb, may stabilise if conditions improve quickly. For the flock, the outlook is good when the farmer acts early: improving ventilation, stopping cold stress, checking salt and feed quality, and managing early growth usually bring losses down in the current batch and prevent them in the next. Flocks at high altitude, in cold seasons, or with underlying lung disease will continue to have some risk, so prevention must become a routine part of every batch.

faqs.q: Is water belly contagious? Will it spread to my other birds?
faqs.a: No. Ascites is not caused by a germ and does not pass from bird to bird. But if one bird has it, the same conditions (cold, stale air, altitude, fast growth) are affecting the whole flock, so more birds are likely to develop it unless you fix the house and management. Your vet should still check dead birds, because a lung infection can be the hidden trigger.

faqs.q: Can I remove the water with a needle to save the bird?
faqs.a: No. Draining the belly does not fix the overworked heart, the fluid comes back quickly, and the bird often dies from shock or infection. It is also painful for the bird. Birds with an advanced water belly should be humanely culled, and your effort should go into protecting the rest of the flock.

faqs.q: Why do my broilers in the highlands get it, but my cousin's in Mombasa do not?
faqs.a: At high altitude the air is thinner and holds less oxygen, and nights are colder. Broilers grow so fast that their lungs struggle even at sea level, so in the highlands their hearts are pushed much harder. Cold nights also make farmers close houses tightly, cutting fresh air. That is why farms around Eldoret, Nakuru, Nyandarua and similar areas need extra care with ventilation, warmth and growth rate.

faqs.q: Will antibiotics or electrolytes help my flock?
faqs.a: Antibiotics do not treat ascites, and using them without a vet's diagnosis wastes money and builds drug resistance. They only help if the vet finds a bacterial infection that is contributing. Many electrolyte products contain sodium (salt), and extra salt can actually make fluid build-up worse, so do not add them for long periods without your vet's advice. Clean, fresh water is what the birds need.

faqs.q: If I slow down their growth, will I lose money at market?
faqs.a: A short period of slower growth early in the cycle, through a lighting programme with some dark hours or controlled feeding agreed with your vet or feed supplier, usually lets birds catch up later. Many farmers find that fewer deaths in the last weeks more than make up for a small difference in growth. Talk to your vet about a plan that fits your altitude, house and market age.

faqs.q: Should I switch to improved kienyeji birds if ascites keeps happening?
faqs.a: Improved kienyeji types grow more slowly and are rarely affected by ascites, so they can suit cold highland farms with simple housing. But they take longer to reach market weight and sell into a different market. Before switching, try fixing brooding, ventilation, safe heating and feed quality, because these changes often solve the problem in broilers.

products.role: Mixed into feed as a mycotoxin binder, it helps reduce the harm from aflatoxin and ochratoxin in feed, which can damage the liver and lungs and add to the load that pushes broilers into ascites. It supports good feed storage and buying fresh feed; it does not treat birds that already have water belly.

Where your vet or feed supplier suspects the ration is low in vitamins, this vitamin A, D3 and E supplement can help support the bird's antioxidant defences and general health during stressful brooding and fast growth. It is an aid alongside proper ventilation, warmth and growth management, not a cure for ascites, and should be used as directed on the label.

ascites.imagePrompt: A white commercial broiler chicken standing upright like a penguin on wood-shavings litter inside a simple Kenyan poultry house, with a visibly swollen, rounded lower belly, open-beaked panting and a dark bluish-red comb and wattles, soft natural daylight.
ascites.seoDescription: Ascites (water belly) in broilers: spot the swollen belly, blue comb and panting early, learn the causes and how to prevent it on Kenyan farms.

card.headline: Swollen foot pad with black scab
card.look: The bird limps or avoids standing on one foot. Underneath, the centre of the foot pad is swollen, warm and round, often with a hard, dark brown or black scab in the middle.
card.action: Separate the limping bird onto soft, clean, dry bedding and ask your vet or animal health officer to examine the foot before the infection goes deeper.

detail.summary: Bumblefoot is an infection of the underside of a bird's foot. It usually starts when germs, most often Staphylococcus bacteria, get into a small cut or crack in the foot pad and form a pocket of pus. It begins as a mild limp but can spread into tendons, joints and bone if ignored. It is common in heavy birds, cockerels and birds kept on rough perches or wet, dirty litter, and it mostly comes from problems in housing and hygiene that the farmer can fix.
detail.cause: The main cause is the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus, a germ that normally lives on the skin of birds and people and in dust and litter. Other bacteria such as E. coli, Streptococcus and Pseudomonas may also be involved. These germs cannot easily get through healthy skin. Trouble starts when the foot pad is damaged by a splinter, sharp stone, wire, rough or very narrow perch, a hard landing from a high perch, or skin that has gone soft and cracked from standing on wet, ammonia-rich litter. Once inside, the bacteria multiply and the body walls them off. Birds do not make runny pus like mammals. Their pus is thick and cheese-like, and it forms a firm core, sometimes called the 'kernel' or 'plug', under the scab. As the infection grows, the foot swells and becomes painful. In long-standing cases the infection can spread into the tendon sheaths, the toe and leg joints and even the bone, which is much harder to treat. In rare severe cases bacteria can get into the blood and make the bird very ill.
spread: Small cuts, punctures and splinters from rough timber perches, broken wire floors, nails, glass or sharp stones in the run let bacteria into the foot.
Wet, caked litter, especially during the long and short rains or around leaking drinkers, softens the skin and burns it with ammonia, causing cracks where germs enter.
Perches that are too high make heavy birds land hard on their feet, bruising the pad again and again.
Perches that are too thin, round metal pipes or smooth plastic make birds grip hard and put pressure on one spot of the pad.
Being overweight, as in broilers and heavy cockerels, puts extra pressure on the feet and raises the risk.
Poor nutrition, especially low vitamin A or biotin (a B vitamin), weakens the skin of the feet so it cracks more easily.
It is not usually passed from bird to bird like a flu, but pus from a burst abscess contaminates litter and perches, raising the germ load for other birds with damaged feet.
detail.atRisk: Heavy birds are most at risk: broilers near market weight, heavy dual-purpose breeds, and adult cockerels and roosters. Laying hens jumping down from high perches or nest boxes are also often affected. Kienyeji chickens on free-range are generally less affected than confined birds, but they still get it from thorns, sharp stones and rough night perches. Deep-litter houses with poor ventilation, leaking drinkers or overcrowding are high risk, especially in the rainy seasons when litter stays wet. Birds kept on wire floors, concrete or hard bare ground, older birds, and birds fed poorly balanced homemade rations are also more likely to develop it. Ducks and geese kept on hard, dry ground away from water can get a similar foot problem.

early: The bird limps slightly, shifts weight between feet, or stands on one leg more than usual.
The bird is slow to get onto the perch or prefers to sit on the floor.
When you turn the foot over, the pad looks slightly red, shiny or swollen, or has a small brown or dark spot.
The pad may feel a little warmer than the other foot.
Small cracks or rough calloused skin on the bottom of the foot.
advanced: A clear round swelling in the centre of the foot pad, sometimes extending between the toes, feeling firm or hard.
A hard, dark brown or black scab in the middle of the swelling, which covers a core of thick, yellow-white, cheese-like pus.
Obvious limping, refusing to walk or stand, and spending most of the time sitting.
Swollen toes or a swollen hock (ankle) joint if the infection has spread.
Reduced eating and drinking because the bird does not want to walk to the feeder, leading to weight loss.
Laying hens drop in egg production and cockerels stop mating because of pain.
In very advanced cases, a bad smell from the foot, an open draining sore, a fluffed-up dull bird, and toes that stay bent or stiff.

lookalikes.name: Scaly leg mite
lookalikes.howToTell: Mites lift and thicken the scales on the shanks and toes, which look rough, crusty and chalky. The foot pad itself is usually not swollen with a single black scab, and several birds are often affected.

lookalikes.name: Infectious synovitis (Mycoplasma synoviae) or joint infection
lookalikes.howToTell: The swelling is mainly in the hock joints and the joints of the toes rather than the middle of the foot pad. Often many birds in the flock are lame at once, and some may have breathing signs or greenish droppings.

lookalikes.name: Articular gout
lookalikes.howToTell: Joints of the toes and legs become swollen with white, chalky deposits that can be seen under the skin. It is linked to kidney damage, excess protein or calcium, or poor water intake, and there is no central black scab on the pad.

lookalikes.name: Marek's disease
lookalikes.howToTell: Young birds become lame or paralysed, often with one leg stretched forward and the other back, but the feet look normal with no swelling or scab. The eyes may turn grey and birds may waste away.

detail.diagnosis: Most cases are recognised by careful examination. The vet or animal health officer will pick up the bird, compare both feet, feel for heat, swelling and pain, and check the toes and hock joints to see how far the infection has gone. Bumblefoot is often graded from mild (a red or calloused pad) to severe (deep abscess with joint or bone involvement), which guides treatment. If the bird needs antibiotics, or if several birds keep getting it, the vet may take a swab of the pus for culture and sensitivity testing at a county, KALRO or private laboratory. This shows which bacteria are present and which drugs will work, which is important because Staphylococcus can be resistant to some antibiotics. In valuable birds, an X-ray may be used to check the bone. If birds die or many are lame, a post-mortem at a veterinary laboratory can rule out other causes such as Mycoplasma or gout. To help, note how many birds are lame and for how long, describe the perches, floor and litter, mention any recent rains or leaks, bring a sample of the feed label or ration recipe, and list any medicines already given.
firstSteps: Separate the lame bird into a small clean pen or box so it does not compete for feed and so pus does not contaminate the main house.
Give it soft, clean, dry bedding such as fresh wood shavings or dry grass, and a low perch or none at all so it does not have to jump.
Place feed and clean water right next to the bird so it can eat and drink without walking far.
Wear gloves when handling the foot and wash your hands well with soap afterwards, because Staphylococcus can infect cuts on human skin.

Gently wash the foot with clean warm water and dry it well to see the problem clearly, but do not cut, squeeze or pick off the scab yourself, as this can push infection deeper and cause heavy bleeding.
Check the feet of all the other birds, especially cockerels and heavy birds, and note how many show early redness or swelling.
Look around the house for the cause: sharp objects, rough or high perches, broken wire and wet litter, and fix them straight away.
Record the bird's details, date and what you see, then call your vet or animal health officer, especially if the swelling is large, the bird stops eating, or toes and joints are swollen.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on how deep the infection is. Very mild cases with only redness or a small callus may improve simply by correcting perches and litter and keeping the foot clean and dry, under advice from your vet. For a true abscess with a black scab, the vet usually cleans and disinfects the foot, softens the scab, then carefully opens the swelling and removes the scab and the whole cheese-like core. Leaving part of the core behind is a common reason for the problem coming back. The wound is flushed with an antiseptic such as diluted povidone-iodine or chlorhexidine, sometimes packed with a wound dressing, and bandaged with padding to take pressure off the pad. Bandages are usually changed every few days until the wound heals, which can take a few weeks. The bird should stay in a clean, soft, dry pen during this time. Pain relief may be given. Antibiotics are not needed for every case. A vet may prescribe them, either applied to the wound or given by mouth or injection, when the infection is deep, spreading into joints, or the bird is unwell, ideally guided by a culture result. Commonly used drug groups include penicillins, tetracyclines, sulphonamide combinations and others chosen by the vet; never use antibiotics without a prescription, and never give doses based on guesswork. Using antibiotics wrongly helps bacteria become resistant, making future infections in birds and people harder to treat. Any antibiotic or other drug comes with a withdrawal period: eggs and meat from treated birds must not be sold or eaten until the time stated on the label or by your vet has passed. Severe cases where bone or joints are badly damaged may not heal well, and the vet may advise culling for welfare reasons.
prevention: Use perches made of smooth, rounded natural wood that is wide enough for the bird to rest its whole foot on, roughly the width of a broom handle or wider for heavy breeds, and sand down splinters.
Keep perches and nest boxes low, especially for heavy breeds and broiler breeders, so birds do not land hard on their feet.
Keep litter dry and loose: fix leaking drinkers and roofs, raise drinkers on a platform, turn the litter regularly and remove wet, caked patches, especially during the long and short rains.
Make sure the house has good ventilation to remove moisture and ammonia, without strong cold draughts on the birds.
Walk through the house and run regularly to remove nails, wire, broken glass, thorns and sharp stones, and repair broken wire floors.
Avoid overcrowding, because crowded houses get wet litter quickly and birds injure each other's feet.
Feed a well-balanced commercial or properly formulated ration with enough vitamins (especially vitamin A and biotin), minerals and protein, and avoid letting heavy birds become overweight.
Check the feet of your birds every few weeks, especially cockerels and heavy birds, so problems are caught early when they are easy to fix.
Clean and disinfect the house, perches and equipment between batches, and put in fresh dry litter for each new flock.
detail.impact: Bumblefoot rarely kills birds directly, but it quietly costs money. A lame bird eats and drinks less, so broilers grow slowly and reach market weight later, and layers lay fewer eggs. Cockerels with painful feet stop mating, which lowers fertility and hatchability in breeding and kienyeji flocks. Treatment takes time, bandages and vet visits, and severe cases may have to be culled. Where many birds are affected, it is a warning sign that litter, perches or nutrition are wrong, and those same problems also raise the risk of coccidiosis, breast blisters and respiratory disease. In broiler flocks, damaged foot pads also lower carcass quality and can reduce the value of birds and chicken feet sold to buyers.
detail.humanHealth: Staphylococcus aureus, the main germ in bumblefoot, can also infect people, causing skin boils or infected wounds, and some strains are resistant to common antibiotics. Always wear gloves when handling or cleaning an infected foot, cover any cuts on your hands, and wash your hands well with soap and water afterwards. Burn or bury used bandages and pus-soaked material. If a bird has been treated with antibiotics or other drugs, do not eat or sell its eggs or meat until the withdrawal period given by your vet or on the label has ended, to avoid drug residues that harm people and encourage antibiotic resistance.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good when bumblefoot is caught early, while it is only redness, a small callus or a shallow scab, and the housing problem is fixed. Most such birds recover fully. Once a deep abscess has formed, recovery is still possible with proper cleaning, core removal and bandaging, but it takes weeks and the problem often comes back if perches and litter stay the same. When the infection has spread into joints, tendons or bone, healing is slow and uncertain, and the foot may stay stiff or misshapen. Heavy birds, older birds and birds that keep standing on wet or hard surfaces recover more slowly.

faqs.q: Can I cut out the black scab myself at home?
faqs.a: It is better to let a vet or trained animal health officer do it. The foot has a good blood supply and can bleed heavily, and if part of the cheese-like core is left behind, the infection usually comes back. Cutting with dirty tools can also push germs deeper into the joints. What you can do safely is isolate the bird, keep it on soft clean bedding, wash and dry the foot, and call for help.

faqs.q: Is bumblefoot contagious to my other chickens?
faqs.a: It does not spread like Newcastle disease or a cold. However, pus from a burst abscess adds germs to the litter and perches, and any other bird with a cut or cracked foot can pick them up. When several birds have it, the real cause is usually shared: rough or high perches, sharp objects or wet litter. Fixing the house protects the whole flock.

faqs.q: Can I eat eggs from a hen with bumblefoot?
faqs.a: Bumblefoot itself does not make eggs unsafe, as long as you handle the bird with clean hands and keep eggs clean. The concern is medicines. If the vet has given antibiotics or other drugs, do not eat or sell the eggs or meat until the full withdrawal period has passed. Ask your vet what that period is for the specific product.

faqs.q: Will putting antibiotics in the drinking water cure it?
faqs.a: Usually not, and it is not a good idea to do this without a vet. The pus in bumblefoot is walled off in a hard core that drugs reach poorly, so the core usually needs to be removed. Treating a whole flock through the water for one lame bird wastes money, leaves residues in eggs and meat, and helps bacteria become resistant. Only use antibiotics when a vet prescribes them for that case.

faqs.q: Why does bumblefoot keep coming back in my flock?
faqs.a: Repeated cases almost always point to the environment or diet. Check that perches are smooth, wide and low, that litter is dry and not caked, that there are no nails, wire or sharp stones, and that birds are not overcrowded or overweight. Also make sure the ration is balanced, because lack of vitamins such as vitamin A and biotin weakens foot skin. In treated birds, the infection can also return if part of the core was left behind.

faqs.q: Do free-range kienyeji chickens get bumblefoot?
faqs.a: Yes, though less often than heavy confined birds. Kienyeji chickens can injure their feet on thorns, sharp stones, broken glass or rough night perches in the kitchen or store where they sleep. Check their feet when you catch them, give them a smooth wooden perch at night, and keep the sleeping area dry and clean.

products.role: A liquid vitamin and mineral supplement that can help a bird recovering from bumblefoot keep up its condition while it is eating less and coping with the stress of handling and bandaging. It supports recovery alongside the vet's foot treatment and improved housing; it does not treat the infection.

Supplies vitamin A, which helps keep skin, including the foot pads, healthy, plus vitamins D3 and E. It can help where the ration may be short of these vitamins, as one part of preventing cracked, weak foot skin. Use it alongside a balanced feed, dry litter and good perches, not as a cure.
